#940. Inside the mind games that will decide Arsenal v Man City

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Mikel Arteta was punished by Pep Guardiola after a crucial selection in the Carabao Cup final, now, Miguel Delaney writes, he holds the experience and power to land a decisive blow on their bitter title rivals

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Manchester City have a lot of bigger concerns right now but some of Enzo Maresca’s staff have naturally been conscious of the noise around David Raya. The goalkeeper was not wearing a sling at Tuesday’s Champions League match against Borussia Dortmund, after he had so conspicuously been photographed sporting one on London’s busiest street just two days before.

It’s certainly true the injury suffered at Newcastle United is nowhere near as bad as first feared, with contact on a nerve having apparently caused the initial issue.

Some on the City side have wondered whether Mikel Arteta is using it to play his usual games. The manager likes to use media and even official squad photos to keep opposition guessing.

It would be especially understandable here, since this position could go a long way to deciding Sunday’s game.

The entire decision on Raya, in fact, draws out so many of its strands and storylines.

Both sides are especially attuned to it since it was as recently as March's Carabao Cup final that Pep Guardiola’s response to the Kepa Arrizabalaga selection essentially decided that game.

It might even have been the Catalan’s last piece of genius in England. Arsenal couldn’t play out of the press without Raya's passing, and City gradually shut them down. The tactical effect of it was so pronounced that it framed the thinking of both clubs ahead of April’s suffocatingly tense Premier League showdown.

That 2-1 City win might well go down as one of those influential defeats, rather than decisive victories, because of the effect on Arsenal. They actually gleaned confidence and instruction, to win all of their remaining games.

And now they're champions, and intent on asserting exactly what that means - with Raya's injury currently the primary concern.

Except, aside from it looking 50-50 over whether Raya will be involved, Guardiola certainly won’t be. The man responsible for that tactical thinking isn't there. And even if there is now debate over Maresca’s exact quality as a coach, he’s not Guardiola.

The dysfunction of his own pressing system, and City’s newly profound susceptibility to counter-attacks, also means they may not be able to execute any such approach in the same way… but then very little about City is the same.

The very consequence of this match might even change.

It all adds to the feel of this being a defining game for this most peculiar of seasons.

Arsenal can win to emphatically kill City’s title challenge… but will that even be a title challenge? City can win to transform the entire dynamic around the top of the table, but will the outcome of their appeal skew it in a way the Premier League has never seen?

Or, what if they win and then win their appeal - however unlikely legal figures currently think that is - to then go on a run?

It’s an absurd context, and that for a fixture that has recently been freighted with greater meaning.

And it is because of that recent history that Arsenal do feel they owe City one.

Arteta is said to feel it was absolutely crucial they won the title before Guardiola left and the verdict of the long-running Premier League case came in.

It was about proving it on their own terms. And now, with City precarious, they want to fully prove their superiority; to emphasise this can be their era; to put City out of the picture.

Despite enduring two comebacks for draws in their last two matches, the Arsenal squad are in a good mood.

They feel they played excellently for 160 minutes of those games and that just continuing that will have them in good stead over an awkward run of fixtures.

Or, as one figure told the Independent: “We are due to hammer someone”.

And, as another said separately: “We need to hammer City on Sunday”.

Everyone at Arsenal knows that is much easier said than done.

Despite all of City’s recent problems, the rivalry of this fixture might just be the type of game Maresca’s side require. It might cause them to dig deep.

That of course may depend on how deep their problems actually are.

One recent argument coming out of City has been that this is all just tactical, and individual moments in individual games are going against them.

It’s just that the idea this slump is solely down to tactical/technical issues feels… a stretch.

Really, City are in a situation of remarkable extremes.

Even the departure of Guardiola would have been enough to distort an entire season. If City are obviously better structured than Manchester United after Sir Alex Ferguson or Arsenal themselves after Arsene Wenger, it is still adapting to the absence of one of the most psychologically imposing figures in football. His presence was immense.

That alone creates a vacuum, that is arguably manifesting in City's dysfunctional midfield.

That area also poses significant tactical questions about Guardiola's successor. Insiders familiar with both Chelsea and Leicester City can’t help notice familiar flaws in Maresca’s teams, especially as regards the balance. City are just so easy to get at.

You can even map previous Chelsea form onto this season. Maresca’s first season at Stamford Bridge in 2024-25 started well, to the point of being talked of as title challengers, only to endure a winter drop-off surrounded by the same tactical discussions.

The City squad are going through a situation no one in English football history has ever experienced. You can even extend that to European football, despite various controversies, given how long this entire process has been.

Another line from inside the club is that they are as adamant with the players as they are with everyone else: that they will overturn this verdict, and big questions will instead be posted to the rest of the Premier League.

Some at rival clubs even think that one element of City’s belligerent response, at least in public, has been as a message to the players.

They need to radiate a sense of business as usual so as to convince the squad, because they do need the actual football business to indeed be as it usually is. They know they need to keep them focused.

That’s just very difficult to do when the potential consequences could come this season, which recent results arguably show.

Because, even if the players themselves honestly insist they are genuinely fully focused, this is still a story that has major implications for their careers. They may have to take big decisions. Some might even be thinking this is a waste of a season in a short career.

That is going to at least have some effect, even if it is subconscious.

It creates a cloud of doubt, and this in a sport that demands more intensity of focus than ever before. The opposition manager, Arteta, demands it more than anyone else. Guardiola himself was a huge influence in this.

Both have abruptly discarded numerous players if they sensed that a necessary tunnel vision had been obscured by even 1 per cent.

And that is exactly what a situation like this does. It's too big to just completely shut out.

Without it, City might have even been better able to work around some of the tactical issues.

In short, even if performances have been OK, this does not look like a team playing to optimum level.

Neither do Arsenal but they don’t feel too far off. They're primed. City might well need that challenge to rouse themselves.

Either way, it is already a fixture that feels like it has the makings of a huge result. And also a result that might mean absolutely nothing by the end.

#939. Underperforming Manchester City are an accident waiting to happen

Enzo Maresca had two home games in four days to get Manchester City into decent shape for Sunday’s clash against Arsenal, which now feels like a must-win. On Tuesday, however, they ended up being taunted by Rasmus Hojlund on another evening that raised more questions than answers.

It is now one win in seven for Maresca, who cannot keep a clean sheet and has a £327m midfield that have played well individually, but is yet to form a unit. Worryingly, their reliable source of goals, Erling Haaland, had his quietest game of the season. It required Rayan Cherki to rescue a point against Napoli.

Maresca needs to find a solution in the next five days before heading to the Emirates to face the champions in what could be a defining weekend for the season. Defeat would put them nine points off the pace, with Maresca still trying to find his best combination of players to pick.

Club captain Rúben Dias was on the bench here and Josko Gvardiol was left out of the draw against Fulham at the weekend, which also ended as a draw rather than a morale-boosting win to get City out of their slump.

There is enough quality in City’s midfield to trouble Arsenal, but the conundrum for Maresca is how to fit them all into his system. Elliot Anderson was pushed towards the right against Napoli rather than in a central position to control the game, while Ayyoub Bouaddi was often alongside “inverted” full-back Nico O’Reilly.

Bouaddi showed his attacking instincts with City’s first equaliser; incredibly his first goal as a professional. There cannot be many £86m players who have yet to score in senior football. Enzo Fernandez also started against Napoli but was quiet before being taken off for the last half an hour.

“We have so much quality, so it’s about getting the quality out in every player. We have to regroup, stay positive and bring energy on the pitch and try to do our best.

“We go to the champions, so it’s the most difficult game of the season going to the champions away. We need a top performance from every single player.”

A penny for the thoughts of Khaldoon Al Mubarak and Aleksander Ceferin, who sat next to each other in the Etihad directors’ box.

Khaldoon has been the chairman of a club under siege after the Premier League found them guilty of breaking financial rules. They could be punished with a points deduction that would mean they miss out on the Champions League, the blue-riband tournament of Uefa, of which Ceferin is president.

Ceferin will want figures like Haaland and entertainers like Cherki to be playing among Europe’s elite, although this City team look far from contenders for this year’s edition. At the moment they will take any kind of win.

City were giving a debut to their new orange kit, but a change of strip did not bring a change of fortune. Their jerseys have been likened to Irn Bru, but the most of the running was made by Napoli, whose midfield was made in Scotland from girders. Kevin De Bruyne has been lined up for a January move to PSV Eindhoven, with the Dutch club working on a deal to land one of the Premier League’s greatest players when the window opens.

De Bruyne, 35, has been at Napoli since the start of last season but it is understood that a move away from the Serie A club is now on the horizon. He is still under contract at Stadio Diego Armando Maradona so PSV will pay a fee to land him as they look to retain their Eredivisie title.

At Manchester City, De Bruyne won six Premier League titles and was part of their Treble-winning team that won the Champions League. During the last 18 months at Napoli he has suffered injury issues, had a row with team-mate on the pitch and was quoted as saying he was glad Antonio Conte left as head coach.

“Not a lot I can say for the moment,” said De Bruyne when asked about his future. “I have played at 100% until now and obviously I am not 20 years old, I am turning 36.

“There is a lot of things going in my mind but there is not a lot to say. I am playing good football, trying to help the team to do well and it has been a bit of a challenging season with a lot of things happening.”

It is matchday five of the Champions League as Manchester City host Napoli at the Etihad. These sides last met back in September 2025, with Manchester City winning 2-0 at home courtesy of goals from Erling Haaland and Jeremy Doku. Manchester City’s cause was helped by an early red card for Napoli’s Giovanni Di Lorenzo. Napoli’s only win over Manchester City came all the way back in November 2011 when they won 2-1 after a double from Edinson Cavani.

Manchester City have won three of their opening four Champions League matches this season, with their only defeat coming at home against back-to-back champions PSG. They drew 1-1 at home against Fulham in the league on Saturday, which means they are now without a league win in four games.

“We are always looking to win games, no matter the competition,” Manchester City boss Enzo Maresca said. “For sure, the four games in a row in the Premier League that we did not win has been a shame. Tomorrow [tonight] we have a chance to win the game and continue our path in the Champions League that at the moment has been very good. First of all, it is important to qualify and then probably, if you are not able to finish in the top eight, you have two more games that with the amount of games that we have, it is always important to reduce games. So the target is to try and finish in the top eight.”

Napoli, managed by Massimiliano Allegri, have struggled thus far in this season’s Champions League, winning just one of their opening four games and are all the way down in 27th. They come into tonight’s match off the back of a 1-0 home win over Torino in Serie A on the weekend courtesy of former Manchester United midfielder Scott McTominay’s winning goal. However, they still sit down in eighth in the Italian top flight, a massive 14 points off the top through just 12 games.

“This match will not be decisive,” Allegri said. “It is a simple mathematical equation, but obviously we will try to do well, even against a great team like Manchester City. It will be a beautiful and fascinating challenge and we want to play to the best of our ability. Ultimately, our goal is to qualify. We must not repeat the mistakes we made in Porto, where we played a great game for 70 minutes and then let ourselves go, conceding chances too easily. We will have to be able to play both with and without possession.”

Team news from the Etihad to follow shortly.

#938. Why Nvidia CEO's affair with alleged Chinese spy matters for AI race

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has apologized for an affair with a woman the US believes was spying for China. The story could have profound implications for the world's most valuable company and the global AI race.

Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang's admission to an affair with a woman whom US intelligence officials believe was working as a spy for China could have profound implications for the $5 trillion (€4.47 trillion) company.

The Financial Times first reported on Huang's affair with Alice H., an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based customer of Nvidia, which has been suspected of trying to circumvent export controls to get advanced Nvidia chips into China.

The newspaper reported that the US government and its intelligence community believe she was recruited as a spy by China's Ministry of State Security intelligence agency.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

US government officials drafted a memo about the allegations shortly before US President Donald Trump traveled to Beijing for a summit with Xi Jinping in May.

Huang's relationship with the alleged Chinese spy has exposed him and the company to criticism that it may have allowed China to obtain valuable trade secrets as Beijing tries to gain an edge in the race to develop advanced AI models.

Nvidia is initiating an investigation led by independent board members and an external law firm. It said in a statement that Huang "has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort."

"The board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders," the company said Sunday. "While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board's inquiry will examine all available information."

The company's shares fell in early trading on Monday.

While US intelligence officials have not commented publicly on the claims, Trump — with whom Jensen Huang has a close relationship — has backed the Nvidia boss.

"He's an honorable guy," said Trump. "I have not spoken to him ​about it. I just know he's a ​fine person, but you never know what is going on. I hope everything's fine."

Tim Culpan, an Asia tech reporter who has covered Nvidia and Huang closely for years, told DW that while Nvidia's fundamental strengths as a company remain in place, Huang is hugely personally damaged by the story.

"They're still going to make great chips and they're going to sell them to millions of customers around the world who want the best AI chips in the world," he said.

"His opinion is going to carry a lot less weight now. And that, in the long term, will flow through to Nvidia and Nvidia's own corporate interests. So it won't be immediate. It's really a fact that he doesn't have the sway or the power that he might have had one week ago simply through this."

Richard Windsor, a tech analyst and the founder of research company Radio Free Mobile, said the news could be very serious for Nvidia given how much the company has revolved around Huang for decades.

"This problem is particularly acute because Jensen Huang is very hands-on, meaning that the key decisions that led to its success were ultimately taken by him and because there is no obvious successor," he said.

"I suspect we are about to find out just how much the market thinks that the company is dependent on its iconic founder and CEO."

Nvidia and Huang's attitude toward China and potential Chinese customers has been a bone of contention with US intelligence officials — despite Huang's close relationship with Trump.

Huang has repeatedly lobbied Trump to ease restrictions on the sale of Nvidia chips to China. A 2025 export control deal heavily curbed sales, but Trump subsequently permitted the export of older H200 Nvidia chips to China in return for the US government receiving a cut of the sales.

However, that deal has been complicated and bogged down by Washington's strict export-license review. China has also initiated import controls, despite strong demand from Chinese companies. China lacks access to the most advanced AI-capable chips. Beijing wants to develop its own alternatives but has struggled to catch up.

Huang has argued that Chinese dependence on Nvidia's chips would prevent rivals such as Huawei from catching up and boosting China's ambitions to dominate AI supply chains.

However, that argument has been dismissed by many US intelligence officials. They fear that unlimited Chinese access to the most advanced Nvidia chips would boost China's domestic AI sector, lead to its AI models catching up with the leading US models and see the chips being used in Chinese military applications.

The US-China rivalry has become a central theme in the global AI story, with both countries seeking to gain an upper hand in the technology. Leading US AI executives such as Anthropic's Dario Amodei have argued that US AI companies can't afford to take a prolonged pause to allow safety standards in AI to catch up, if they're going to prevent Chinese firms from gaining an advantage.

Washington's central fear over Huang's affair is that it could have led to Beijing obtaining vital trade secrets or other key information about how Nvidia makes its most advanced chips.

Windsor thinks Huang will survive the "severe test" due to his importance to the company. He also cast doubt on the extent to which Beijing and its leading tech firms have learned from Nvidia's chips, pointing to China's own chip ambitions and commitment to have its firms buy its own semiconductors.

"I am far from convinced that Chinese AI has materially benefited from technology or illicit chip imports that it gained from Nvidia," he said.

The news comes at a particularly challenging moment for Nvidia, which has benefited massively from the AI boom thanks to its position as the leading maker of cutting-edge semiconductors needed for AI applications.

Nvidia's valuation has soared dramatically in recent years as companies rushed to buy its chips, becoming the world's first $5 trillion company in October 2025.

However, doubts over the sustainability of the $9 trillion capital expenditure AI boom have sparked a major sell-off in stocks related to the boom in recent weeks. The Democrats' sweeping victories in the US midterms have added to the doubts, given the strength of voter opposition to data center construction in the US.

Manchester United's No.1 was dependable last season - but hasn't seemed himself this term

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

There were other factors that led to Manchester United’s 4-0 defeat to Liverpool besides Senne Lammens’ performance, like Leny Yoro’s red card after only eight minutes. Down to 10 men for the majority of the match, Mauricio Pochettino’s debut as manager became about damage limitation from that point on.

And yet in the post-match analysis, Manchester United’s first-choice goalkeeper still found himself scrutinised. “If he’s in the right position, he saves it comfortably,” argued Danny Murphy on Match of the Day, highlighting Lammens’ positioning for Dominik Szoboszlai's opener.

It wasn’t the first time a Lammens mistake has been highlighted this season. While the Belgian was widely hailed for his performances in his debut Premier League campaign after joining from Royal Antwerp, the malaise around him at Old Trafford has dragged him down. He, like many of his United teammates, is under-performing.

Before the November international break, Lammens was blamed for two goals in the chaotic 4-4 draw with Aston Villa, too easily beaten at his near post by Alysson for Villa’s first and spilling a shot for Nicolas Jackson to make it 2-0 after only four minutes. He was shaky throughout.

There was also Lammens’ ill-judged decision to come rushing off his line against Bournemouth, giving Evanilson the chance to finish into an empty net in a 3-0 win for the Cherries at Old Trafford. The messy own goal conceded by Manchester United in the 1-1 draw away to Fulham was another that involved Lammens.

Like so many at United right now, Lammens is clearly low on confidence. His struggles can be traced back to the World Cup where he made a blunder that led to Belgium’s exit from the tournament, spilling a shot for Mikel Merino to score a late winner for Spain. Lammens hasn’t been the same since that moment.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

There are, however, some mitigating factors to explain the goalkeeper’s form. For starters, Lammens is having to make more saves this season. Last season, the 24-year-old averaged 2.4 saves per 90 minutes in the Premier League, whereas this season that number has increased to 3.6 saves per 90 minutes.

Only Crystal Palace have conceded more Expected Goals (xG) in the Premier League this season than Manchester United. Lammens is being afforded very little protection by the players in front of him, as demonstrated by United’s shambolic defensive performance at Anfield on Sunday.

For comparison, Manchester United conceded the fourth-lowest xG over the course of the 2025/26 Premier League campaign. Their sudden defensive drop-off is somewhat unexplainable, but it goes a long way to reasoning why Lammens is struggling so much. He’s simply having to do more. He’s being overwhelmed.

Lammens hasn’t actually regressed much in terms of his save percentage. This season, the Belgian is ranked 16th in the Premier League for this metric, whereas last season he was 14th. Lammens has never been anywhere near the most effective shot-stoppers in this regard.

Like so many at United right now, Lammens is clearly low on confidence

It’s possible Lammens over-performed last season. Without the Belgian settling so quickly after arriving as an emergency upgrade on Andre Onana and Altay Bayindir, it’s difficult to envisage Manchester United finishing third. His saves did a lot to mask some of United’s structural deficiencies.

No goalkeeper in the Premier League last season prevented more goals than Lammens (6.4). That ranked him ahead of the likes of Gianluigi Donnarumma, Emi Martinez, Jordan Pickford, Alisson Becker and David Raya. It was perhaps unrealistic to expect someone still so young in goalkeeper years to maintain such a high level.

“This break came at the ideal moment for me,” said Lammens in the last international break during which he played the full 90 minutes in back-to-back games for Belgium against Turkey and Italy, saving a penalty against the latter. “These have been difficult weeks for me at Manchester United.”

Life for Lammens didn’t get any easier in his first match back from international duty, although the Belgian’s seven saves prevented the scoreline from being even more humiliating for Manchester United. There were moments when Lammens showed the sort of form that made him so eye-catching last season.

Pochettino might find a way to steady Manchester United at the back. The Argentine set up the Old Trafford outfit with a back three in possession before Yoro’s red card completely changed the dynamic of the match. With 11 men on the pitch, Pochettino should find it easier to implement a defensive game plan, although that’s something Michael Carrick never managed.

This could help Lammens rediscover his best form. If not, Manchester United will need their goalkeeper to eliminate the errors from his performances on his own accord, otherwise a relegation scrap at the bottom of the Premier League table could be unavoidable. Lammens can’t count on getting any more help any time soon.

#936. The biggest fear behind the Premier League’s controversial move to digital football tickets

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The Premier League’s decision to fully introduce digital tickets this campaign has sparked a ‘secret civil war’, writes Miguel Delaney, with fans increasingly concerned that the season ticket could be about to disappear for good - with significant consequences

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

It is described as the Premier League’s “secret civil war”, except it’s very public. So much so that it affects the majority of those who fill stadiums every single week. It affects the lifeblood of football… but then the entire point is that this isn’t something tangible you can touch.

This season’s full introduction of digital tickets has affected fan behaviour and community.

You can see it in queues outside games. You can hear it in discussions on the difficulty of “passing on” tickets, and arguably even atmosphere.

Duncan Drasdo of the Manchester United Supporters Trust says, “it absolutely impacts fan culture”.

The Football Supporters’ Association say they are “monitoring” how it progresses but it all plays into a deeper sense, that there is a long-term aim to eventually end season tickets altogether.

Multiple clubs contacted for this article strenuously dispute this, and many are quite strident on their position.

The move comes from a vote in the summer of 2024, where there was effusive support for the mandatory introduction of digital tickets from the start of this season. This essentially means doing away with old physical tickets - although clubs can still give them out in special cases - for ones now scanned. And, if holders can’t go, they can pass to selected family and friends, or put on the club exchange.

There are two primary arguments the clubs make. One is cutting down on touting, which they insist is still absolutely rife. Club sources say the data showed networks where people were running 50-60 season-ticket accounts, and there was financial gain. They argue that runs contrary to the idea of the season ticket being personal to a fan for their loyalty, and insist the only action - achieved through hidden barcodes - is against abuse.

The other is increasing safety, and knowing everyone who is in the stadium. It inherently conditions better behaviour, since anyone can be tracked.

Fan groups accept parts of these arguments, and would acknowledge that a lot of their clubs directly engage, but sympathy has been eroded by direct experience. Almost immediately, there were long queues outside games, many of which have lingered. Most pertinently, though, there is the sudden negating of what has long been normal. Every season-ticket holder will know it, as will those who use their tickets. “Passing on” is a lot more difficult, as clubs increase obligation for the ticket to be used in some form.

“And passing it on is absolutely fan culture,” says Gareth Roberts, of Liverpool’s Spirit of Shankly group. Drasdo adds: “It’s what creates community.”

A common complaint is that it now involves more laborious processes, and doing it unofficially potentially risks a ban, when you used to be able to just hand it to someone.

“Not just talking about Liverpool here, but I do know of fans who do get worried about it,” Roberts says. “There are so many rules and regulations to take in, it’s almost like taking an exam. It feels a heavy load to be a supporter.

“Through not filling in the initial form as they wanted, I have one mate who can’t go to Champions League games and two who can’t go to cups. The assumption is that everyone is digitally literate, but they don’t.”

This has practical concerns, too, if a fan can’t go at short notice.

“We’ve been saying there should be ways to do this,” Roberts says. “You’re not setting up a business and earning from this. OK, there are touts but they have to think of ways to not impinge on traditional fans.”

Darren Epstein, a Gold Rep at Arsenal, says the complication of it all is under-appreciated: “In days gone by, we’d be talking about managers and tactics. Now it’s when away tickets go on sale, collections, ID checks, and points - points being the loyalty points you get on buying an away ticket.

“It feels like a constant battle to ensure you get to a game. Although, changes have undoubtedly improved the ability of many fans to get to games they never have been able to before, which many of course feel is a good thing.”

A connected complaint is that this is one more factor affecting traditional atmospheres.

“If it’s the club re-selling the ticket on the exchange, it changes the profile of the support, introducing a random fan into a group of mates,” Drasdo says. “In the old standing sections you were able to congregate with friends but the introduction of all-seater stadia meant people got split up by where their seats were and we lost that mobility which is the key to atmosphere."

Tom Concannon of the FSA, speaking as a Newcastle United fan, says: “Atmospheres are worsening because of it in my opinion. Tickets are going to those wanting to experience the atmosphere rather than contribute to it.” Roberts adds: “Atmosphere is dependent on youth vibrancy. The Kop is pretty old now.”

Even in simple terms, it’s a lot harder to pass on tickets to children who may not have a phone, but that clubs actively need to get that match-day buzz. Fan representatives would similarly say it doesn’t help that the Premier League’s clubs’ ticketing working group only has heads of ticketing on it, rather than actual match-going fans.

Such concern feeds into a deeper tension in all of this, between being a supporter and being a customer. An irony is that it means fans have less control over what they pay for. As one executive says, “if you’ve bought your season ticket, you should have no obligation to sit in the seat”.

Another perspective is that clubs are being more strict and trying to get control of every ticket they can. One industry figure points to how the same data from digital tickets has allowed clubs to see just how often tickets are passed on, and it has stunned them. One club has estimated that 20-25 per cent of tickets are passed on, which they also see as running contrary to what a season ticket is supposed to be.

Or, as some fans put, they realised they could monetise. Tickets not passed on can be put on the ticket exchange, where FSA research shows prices are considerably higher than the average for a season-ticket seat.

Club sources would say they deliberately decoupled the season-ticket price from match-by-match, to recognise the value of a season-ticket holder.

Drasdo offers a different view: “A common phrase we hear from our fans is ‘the club are the biggest touts of all’, which is essentially a reaction to the restrictions on usage and the premium prices we see when season ticket holders' tickets are resold by the club.

“A major problem we’ve had at United is stretching the gap in price between season ticket holders and member ticket prices which causes the club to focus on how season ticket holders pass on their tickets when not personally attending.”

Another knock-on has been what Roberts describes as the “normalisation” of fans who don’t have season tickets paying fees to become members to go into lotteries for tickets. Some clubs even charge for transferring. Most clubs have unlimited membership, meaning there is actually less chance of getting a ticket.

“We’ll never really know how many tickets end up in the hands of actual fans,” Concannon says. “Hospitality numbers are on the rise.”

Clubs would nevertheless insist they are acutely conscious of this, and they have to allow opportunities for fans on long waiting lists, or who otherwise feel shut out of being able to go to games. That has fostered tension between supporters, as well as between supporters and clubs. Fans who speak out often find themselves shouted down by others who say “if you don’t pay it, I will”.

And yet such demand comes at a different cost, as anecdotal evidence suggests a lot of long-time supporters are being worn down. “There’s an underbelly of that growing, that clubs don’t realise,” Roberts argues. “If you’re constantly made to jump through these hoops.”

Such weariness has even been deepened by two other concerns. One is this long-time fear that clubs actually want to get rid of season tickets, so they can sell more seats for higher prices. Club sources are adamant that is not the case, as illustrated by how season tickets stripped from some fans are redistributed to those on the waiting list. Whether that is true or not, a step like this could serve as a halfway step for the future.

Clubs themselves would point to escalating player costs and fans wanting the best possible team on the pitch but, as with redundancies, this is dismissed. “A nonsense notion,” Concannon says, “£25 from every fan at every Premier League game only just paid the agents’ bills last season.”

One chief executive actually links the entire issue to the financial rules. “The point of forcing bums on seats should be atmosphere,” they say. “The ugly extra money-making for clubs is not on. Clubs do need protection - if they had cost-control protection they would not be fleecing fans.”

Some clubs would accept there could have been better communication. For now, if you go to a game this weekend, it’s what a lot of fans are talking about.

#935. Ten-man Bournemouth battle back to score Europa League victory at Celta Vigo

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Celta Vigo 1-2 Bournemouth: The Cherries lost Bafode Diakite to a 23rd-minute red card but battled back from going a goal behind to win in Spain

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Bournemouth moved a step closer to automatic qualification for the Europa League last 16 after coming from behind with 10 men to win 2-1 at Celta Vigo.

It was a remarkable 10th victory in a row in all competitions for Marco Rose’s side and it might have been the most satisfying of the lot for the manager, coming as it did after his team had found themselves a goal down and a man down at half-time.

The visitors looked in trouble when, minutes after Iago Aspas had curled Celta in front, Bafode Diakite was red-carded for a poorly timed tackle.

Bournemouth might have folded then, but instead they came roaring back, Alvaro Rodriguez heading them level almost immediately after the start of the second half.

A draw would have been an excellent result in the circumstances. Substitute Rayan had other ideas, waiting at the end of a rapid breakaway to sweep in the winner 12 minutes from time.

Victory against Viktoria Plzen in December will almost certainly now be enough to earn direct passage to the last 16.

Pablo Duran had the ball in the Bournemouth net after 10 minutes after it spilled back to him off Michele Di Gregorio, the goalkeeper relieved to see the offside flag go up against the Celta striker.

The stand-in keeper redeemed himself minutes later with a solid save from an outrageous bicycle kick by Aspas. It would have been a remarkable goal but the Celta great would not be denied. Bournemouth failed fully to get the ball away, and from the edge of the box Aspas curled a beauty in off the far post.

Bournemouth had gone behind in the first half of their last game in this competition at Sparta Prague. That night, the balance was tipped almost immediately in their favour by a red card for the Czech side, but here it was Rose’s team who found themselves down to 10 men.

Diakite made an honest attempt to win the ball but was late and his studs landed on the ankle of Couhaib Driouech. An initial yellow card was overturned following a VAR check and Bournemouth were on the ropes.

It had been the most challenging half of their debut European campaign, but within minutes of the start of the second period, they were level.

Amine Adli was left in space outside the box to send over a wonderful cross to the far post. Arriving there was Rodriguez, sneaking ahead of his defender to get a head on the ball and nod in the equaliser.

A wonderful counter-attack brought the Premier League side their winner. Adrien Truffert showed good strength out on left to outmuscle Sergio Carreira, and he fed the ball up to Marcus Tavernier. He might have shot himself but instead moved it on to Rayan who swept home.

#933. 37 years after fall of Berlin Wall: How divided are Germans?

Three artists share their thoughts on the reunification of East and West Germany. How do they perceive a shared "we" and what gives them cause for optimism?

When the Berlin Wall fell on November 9, 1989, ending East Germany's isolation from the West, the event was celebrated on both sides of the border. Yet, 37 years later, many people on both sides remain deeply skeptical of each other.

Surveys show that only a minority of respondents report feeling a strong sense of community between those from former East and West Germany, and many continue to perceive significant differences.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

We asked three artists from Germany with different perspectives on the history of the country's division to share their views.

Author Lea Streisand was born in 1979 and experienced the fall of the Berlin Wall firsthand while growing up in East Berlin.

In her books and essays, she has returned to her East German upbringing many times, using literature to process it.

The novel "Hufeland, at the corner of Bötzow" (2019, Ullstein), for example, recounts the period of reunification from a child's perspective.

"November 9, 1989, was simply incredible," she told DW. She was 10 years old at the time. When her mother bought her winter boots with the 100 Deutsche Marks she received from the West German state — a welcome gift given to all East German citizens — she was so disappointed that she felt like crying. But later, a friend of her parents' let her buy so many sweets at the supermarket that they lasted until Christmas.

"The disappointment really set in afterwards, with what happened over the course of the following year. It was unbelievable how quickly an entire system was suddenly swept away and a new one built up, as if to say, 'There you go. You're welcome'," Streisand recalled. "I think it was just too fast for people."

The people of East Germany, or the GDR, had brought about the fall of the Berlin Wall themselves through a civil rights movement and numerous demonstrations. For many, however, the goal was not to dissolve the state immediately but to reform it.

Among them was Anke Feuchtenberger, born in 1963 in East Berlin. Her childhood was spent in East Berlin and in the East German region of Western Pomerania, where she now lives again and feels "very much at home."

Today, she teaches at the University of Applied Sciences in Hamburg, meaning she spends time on both sides of the former divide. Feuchtenberger is often described as Germany's most influential comic artist. Her work has also garnered international acclaim.

"Back then, as artists, we tried to bring about a change through posters and flyers — to gain more freedom without immediately abolishing socialism," she explained.

At the time, the fall of the Berlin Wall stirred up mixed feelings in Feuchtenberger: "I soon realized that the creative and revolutionary aspects of our movement were very quickly being smothered by consumerism, and that nationalist tendencies — which had already been noticeable before — were coming to the fore," Feuchtenberger recalled. "That made me afraid."

Meanwhile, for photographic artist Simon Menner, born in 1978 in Emmendingen, in the West German state of Baden-Württemberg, Berlin was very far away. As Menner put it, he experienced the fall of the Berlin Wall as a child in a "rather abstract" way. Today, Berlin is his home.

In his experience, the way films and documentaries portrayed East Germany around the time of reunification was very bleak. "But West Germany in the '80s," he said, "was also bleak and very staid."

This uneven portrayal of the two parts of Germany is an issue that deeply concerns Menner — partly because he unwittingly contributed to it in a small way. Among other things, Menner's work explores the topic of surveillance and how it works.

In the archives of East Germany's Ministry for State Security, or Stasi — which are freely accessible today as part of the National Archives — he discovered a massive collection of photographs that both fascinated and horrified him and which he wanted to bring to the attention of a wider public.

His photo book "Top Secret" (2012, from publisher Hatje Cantz) features a selection of photos that offer a unique insight into the work of the Stasi. Some are eerie, while others are curious or even absurd.

Menner also tried to look into the photo archive of West Germany's Federal Intelligence Service. "I spent a year trying to gain access — without success," he said.

In hindsight, he now finds his artistic project problematic because he believes it is too one-sided, focusing exclusively on East Germany's past.

According to Menner, West Germany's intelligence services in the 1960s were not exactly models of virtue either, and he believes it is "actually high time" to critically examine this part of history as well. In his view, an honest examination of Germany's past as a whole is a prerequisite for genuine reconciliation.

Streisand believes literature can help foster mutual understanding. "Literature opens a window into experiences we haven't had ourselves," she said. "You can immerse yourself in the mind of someone who has had a different life than you have and understand what happened."

Interest in these stories remains strong. In 2023, Feuchtenberger published the nearly 500-page graphic novel "Comrade Cuckoo" (published by Reprodukt), which was the first graphic novel to be nominated for the Leipzig Book Fair Prize in the fiction category.

The story spans a childhood in the fictional East German village of Pritschitanow in the 1960s in the GDR to the post-Reunification era. In it, Feuchtenberger weaves autobiographical memories of her upbringing with fantastical and fictional elements.

The artist said she was surprised "that, so long after the fall of the wall, my stories have sparked such great interest in the West."

In particular, the fact that the main character, Kerstin, rarely sees her parents because they both work full-time is a topic that often comes up at readings. In the GDR, everyone had the right to work, she said. At the same time, it was a civic duty.

Could the West German interest in this stem from the fact that full-time employment for both parents has long been less common in the West? It's possible, said Feuchtenberger.

When looking toward their shared future, the two East German women are more optimistic than Menner, from West Germany.

"In Berlin, I often don't even notice anymore whether I'm in the West or the East," said Menner. "But when it comes to sociopolitical issues, politicians should listen to older and younger people more closely," he added, referring to the recent election successes of far-right Alternative for Germany, or AfD . "Otherwise, things are going to get difficult in the near future."

"It's very important to step outside our own bubble because people all over the world are facing problems. Constantly focusing on this German-German divide that has emerged between the groups doesn't help," said Feuchtenberger.

"For me personally, the whole issue of borders has somehow dissolved," she explained. This is due in no small part to the many trips abroad that have taken her to various places around the world.

Moreover, in her hometown near the Polish border, she observes how animals couldn't care less about the border. "They come from the east and the west and do whatever they want," she said. That's why she also gave "Comrade Cuckoo" the working title "A German Animal in a German Forest," "because I found the absurdity of an animal having a nationality so funny."

"This East-West thing — our children won't have any interest in it at all," said Streisand. "Young people don't care where their parents come from. Can I get a job that will support a family? Do I have to go to war? Right now, completely different things are relevant."

This article was originally written in German.

Kelly Somers shares her favourite post-match moments as the BBC's in-camp England reporter

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Kelly Somers has recalled a deeply personal moment with Sir Gareth Southgate after England’s victory over Germany at Euro 2020 – and a thoughtful gesture the former Three Lions manager made when she was pregnant.

Sir Gareth's England beat Germany 2-0 at Wembley in June 2021, 25 years after his decisive penalty miss against the same opponents in the Euro 96 semi-finals, and the result prompted an emotional reflection on the team-mates he felt he had let down all those years ago.

As the BBC’s England reporter, Somers was there to capture that reaction, and says it remains one of the standout conversations of her time following the national side.

Asked for her favourite interviews over her years covering England, Somers told FourFourTwo: “[Southgate] said he’d looked up to the big screen midway through the game and seen David Seaman sitting there.

“He said 'I know I can never undo any of the heartache I caused them, but hopefully this has gone a long way'. Hearing him say that was really special.”

Somers was also touched by an off-camera gesture delivered by Southgate during her pregnancy in 2023.

She said: “When I was pregnant in 2023, Gareth gave me a little England kit for my daughter in a gift bag.”

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“In true Gareth Southgate fashion, he said 'I didn’t actually know about your pregnancy, my team arranged this, but this is on behalf of the FA'.

"He didn’t want to take the credit for it, which I thought was lovely.”

Somers also picked out interviewing Ollie Watkins dramatic winner against the Netherlands in the Euro 2024 semi-final as a highlight.

She said: "It felt like I was talking to a boy from the park, I was speaking to someone at pretty much the pinnacle of their life.

“There was another where I had to wait for Jude Bellingham after a drugs test, and he came out in just his top and pants. I thought ‘This is all very weird!’ But he’s always very good in interviews."

Somers added: "To be the in-camp reporter is incredible, because pretty much every day you get 15 minutes with a different player, so I’ve got to know them. I love interviewing and the challenge of bringing out the human side of players.

"At the Euros in 2021, I did one with Jack Grealish where he spoke about his sister – he’s incredibly close to his family. When the interview ended, he said “I was getting emotional, I didn’t expect that.”

#931. Thomas Frank ‘close to a heart attack’ in dramatic first Crystal Palace win

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Jean-Philippe Mateta and Dwight McNeil scored late in a 2-1 Europa League victory over Real Sociedad

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Thomas Frank secured his first win as Crystal Palace boss but admitted his new side nearly nearly gave him a “heart attack” in the nervy final five minutes of their 2-1 Europa League comeback against 10-man Real Sociedad.

Chelsea loanee Mamadou Sarr broke the deadlock for the visitors in the 66th minute at Selhurst Park but Frank’s first home contest turned on its head when Jon Martin received a second yellow card six minutes later.

Jean-Philippe Mateta drew the sides level from the penalty spot and Dwight McNeil poked Palace into the lead from fellow substitute Jorgen Strand Larsen’s bicycle kick, but they were denied a chance to put the game away when Yeremy Pino’s penalty was saved.

“I think first and foremost to get it over the line, and (it was) an extremely important win for various reasons,” said Frank, who took charge of Premier League basement club Palace for the first time in Saturday’s league loss to Coventry.

“One, of course, confidence, and it relates to belief against an extremely good team. I think the first half we were compact and very disciplined in many ways. We missed the high-pressure situations we had, and I think we struggled to keep the ball well enough.

“Second half I felt we were much better in the high pressure, and I felt we kept the ball much better. I actually felt we got a bit more momentum in the second half but then, out of the blue, they scored the 1-0 goal.

“But what I really like is the belief from the players, what they showed, and that we are threatening on set-pieces, we cannot underestimate that.”

Unai Marrero’s save to deny Pino from the spot kept the Spanish side in with a chance of an equaliser and it nearly came at the death from Orri Oskarsson, whose effort was pushed away by Dean Henderson – his last of six saves on Thursday night.

“We know in football one moment can change the game,” Frank continued. “The penalty and the red card changed the game, then we still needed to score.

“To win still is important and we went brave, we went with the offensive substitutions and kept two strikers on the pitch, and that paid off.

“And then I think we were all close to getting a heart attack in the last five minutes.”

Frank agreed the win could be a significant turning point for Palace’s fortunes ahead of a critical Premier League clash with Hull on Sunday.

“That’s why it’s so important to keep doing the right things, keep believing, and keep going,” he said.

Palace’s Premier League survival remains the priority but the result also propelled the Eagles into play-off position in their European campaign, four places out of the top eight after five matches.

Asked about his ambitions for the European campaign – given Palace’s league position – Frank replied: “I think we want to aim high.

“We are ambitious for this tournament, and that’s why the win was so important.”

#930. Wirtz follows rich Liverpool heritage with star showing in win over Brugge

It had to be this way. Liverpool No 7s have historically defined matches against Club Brugge, so it was entirely appropriate that Florian Wirtz preserved that rich heritage.

The late Kevin Keegan thrashed home a free-kick at this stadium 50 years ago to win Liverpool the Uefa Cup and Sir Kenny Dalglish was the hero at Wembley in 1978 when his deft finish ensured the European Cup was retained.

That jersey means those who have subsequently worn it have had high standards to keep. Although this fixture did not carry the heft of past occasions, it was symbolic that Wirtz, the incumbent, decorated this contest and propelled Liverpool a step closer to the knockout phase.

On another night Alexander Isak would have expected his two goals to take the headlines, but he would have appreciated more than anyone the magic spells that Wirtz kept casting. The Swede had a glorious view of the strike that essentially secured three points in Belgium’s frozen north.

The idea of Brugge playing in the biggest club fixture of all, sadly, seems fanciful now given how much the footballing landscape has changed. But they are a progressive side, full of attacking wit, and they had ambitions and, on another evening, would have done some damage.

How often, though, do you see sides these days undo their good work by being overambitious when playing out from the back? Yann Sommer has had a distinguished career, the Swiss goalkeeper has played for Bayern Munich and Inter Milan, but he is 37 and his aberration was decisive.

He put Kyriani Sabbe in all manner of trouble with a loose pass, Bradley Barcola picked the right-back’s pocket and nudged it on swiftly to Dominik Szoboszlai, who in turn fed Isak. With the goal at his mercy from six yards, the striker was never going to miss.

Alexander Isak finds the back of the net to give Liverpool the lead against Club Brugge! 🔥 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/vZbiHKkpiy

“He is in a great moment,” Andoni Iraola, Liverpool’s head coach, said of his striker. “When the team is playing well and getting good results everyone looks better. In the second half we defended lower and knew there would be space to exploit. In one of those moments, he killed the game.”

Liverpool are not perfect, by any means, but the closer you watch them, the more obvious it is that they are grasping what Iraola wants. They will be a good team when it does click, but these are just the first steps of the journey. The first half proved it.

Some moves broke down with a misplaced pass and Brugge were often let off the hook when they were guilty of over-elaboration. Iraola wants Liverpool to be ruthless, but his mood soured for a period, not least when Victor Muñoz injured his knee in an incident when he was trying to win back possession.

“A knock on the knee and we have to test it,” Iraola said. “That was the worst part of the night. It is very early to tell but it was very painful at that moment. He was better after the game.”

So, too, was Iraola, who was especially pleased that Liverpool recorded their first Champions League clean sheet of the season and, in the process, stopped Brugge – who had scored in 19 consecutive games – from finding a way through.

There were several reasons this was the case: Jérémy Jacquet, for instance, never put a foot wrong – what a smart signing he has proved to be. He more than did his bit to retain order in the absence of Virgil van Dijk, who was given the chance to catch his breath before the Merseyside derby.

It was tough for Liverpool in the second period, as Brugge attacked the end of the stadium where their noisy ultras created a cacophony. Yet they handled the situation well, even if Iraola looked ready to combust at one stage, receiving a yellow card for protesting too much to the officials.

“I saw the referee beforehand, I know him from Spain and I knew this was coming,” Iraola said.

Perhaps his ire was fuelled by Liverpool squandering a fabulous chance on the hour to kill things off. A move that featured Wirtz and Isak exchanging passes with pinball precision ended with Szoboszlai bearing down on Sommer, but his shot was too close to the veteran.

He had to score and the grimace that followed had nothing to do with heavy strapping the Hungarian had on supporting his right knee. That miss would have been exacerbated in the 69th minute had Alisson Becker not made a superb save to deny Félix Lemaréchal, plunging to avert the danger.

Jürgen Klopp will not want any credit, but some seeds he planted have started to bloom. Similarly, Andoni Iraola will not ask for recognition, but his constant encouragement is reaping dividends.

Past and present do not always mix in football, yet in Florian Wirtz’s case, the manager who once took Liverpool to the summit of the game and the one who wants to return them to that exalted position in the future have proved to be the perfect blend.

Liverpool have travelled over to Belgium to take on Club Brugge on matchday five in the Champions League. These sides have met competitively three times before and they have all come in finals, resulting in famous nights for Liverpool. In 1976, Liverpool beat Club Brugge 4-3 on aggregate across two legs to win the Uefa Cup. Then, Kenny Dalglish scored the only goal of the game at Wembley back in May 1978 as Liverpool won the European Cup for the second straight season, becoming the first English side to do so.

Liverpool, who have won 13 of their previous 17 matches against Belgian sides, won their first three Champions League games, beating Atletico Madrid, LASK and Villarreal but lost 3-2 away at Fenerbahce on matchday four despite leading twice in that game. After tonight’s game in Belgium, Liverpool’s remaining games in the Champions League are against Porto, Inter Milan and Lens. Andoni Iraola’s side come into this game with a spring in their step after thrashing rivals Manchester United 4-0 at Anfield on Sunday.

“A win [against Manchester United on Sunday] is always great but you do not have time to celebrate with this schedule,” Iraola said. “By Monday, we were already watching analysis of Club Brugge. I have enjoyed analysing them [Brugge], they are very energetic and have had an incredible run of games. I think we will have to be at a very good level, otherwise it is going to be very difficult. They have players who can make the difference and obviously we do as well, so I expect quite an open game. We are both aggressive, both want to press, there will be spaces and hopefully we can win the one-vs-one battles.”

Club Brugge have made a strong start to this season’s Champions League; after losing their first game to Aston Villa, they have since won their next three, including wins over Inter Milan, Lens and PSV. That puts them on the same number of points as Liverpool and are just one place behind. In the Belgian Pro League at the weekend, they thrashed Mechelen 5-1 and they sit second in the Belgian top flight, one point behind Union SG.

“I am proud of the players and what they have achieved against Aston Villa, Inter, Lens and PSV,” Club Brugge boss Ivan Leko said. “We know we should be grateful to be here, but we really want to try to show that Belgian football is fun to watch and we can win matches. I am proud, but I know we are a big club. You are only as good as your last match. We know what happened in the past, so there is also a nice connection between both clubs and the supporters. It is a special fixture to play, but we are not here just to enjoy the Champions League; we want to win and that is what we are going to try to do tomorrow [tonight].”

#929. What is the Riemann hypothesis? A guide to the famed conjecture that rules prime numbers

German mathematician Bernhard Riemann formulated his famous conjecture in 1859.Credit: Smithsonian Libraries and Archives (CC0)

On 20 November, mathematicians made two competing announcements about solving the Riemann hypothesis — perhaps the most important open problem in mathematics.

The question had remained unanswered since it was formulated in 1859 by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann (1826–66). His statement is central to the theory of prime numbers, the whole numbers that cannot be evenly divided by any other number except themselves or 1.

AI is ‘the end of mathematics as we know it’ — where does the field go next?

AI is ‘the end of mathematics as we know it’ — where does the field go next?

The hypothesis concerns the distribution of primes, and it is important because these numbers are central to all of maths. “There is nothing more basic and more fundamental in mathematics that the prime numbers,” says Álvaro Lozano-Robledo, a mathematician at the University of Connecticut in Storrs.

Riemann arrived at his idea by studying prime numbers as waves — in a way that presages the way music recordings are compressed into mp3 files — and his hypothesis is usually described in abstruse-sounding language. But at its heart, the idea boils down to a statistical test that is familiar to any scientist who’s ever analysed data.

Nature breaks down the Riemann hypothesis.

Mathematicians want to know how predictable the prime numbers are. The German scientist Carl Friedrich Gauss (1777–1855), who many consider to be the greatest mathematician in history, had noticed in the late eighteenth century (when he was a teenager) that if you pick any whole number, the odds that it’s a prime depend on the number’s size. Primes slowly become sparser as numbers become bigger. Gauss observed that their frequency seems to depend on (or, is inversely proportional to) the number of digits. Roughly speaking, among numbers with k digits, one in every k of them is a prime.

In Riemann’s time, a half-century after Gauss’s guess, there was still no rigorous proof of this. In a landmark paper in 1859, Riemann stated his belief that the late Gauss, who had been one of his mentors at the University of Göttingen, had been right.

But Riemann — who was a “daring” thinker, says maths historian Rossana Tazzioli at the University of Lille in France — went much further. He proposed that Gauss’s “one in every k” guess was a good statistical prediction, meaning that the frequency of the primes should not fluctuate away from it too much. In other words, Riemann made a guess about the margin of error of Gauss’s prediction.

If true, this ‘Riemann hypothesis’ would make primes’ behaviour similar to that of a random process, such as a series of coin tosses. More precisely, he suggested that when you count the primes among the first n whole numbers, fluctuations would take a form that many scientists are familiar with: “The idea of the Riemann hypothesis is that the error term looks a lot like √n, which is what any random model will give you,” says Andrew Granville, a number theorist at the University of Montreal in Canada.

Mathematicians astounded by AI and human-written proofs of iconic Riemann hypothesis

Mathematicians astounded by AI and human-written proofs of iconic Riemann hypothesis

Such square-root terms pop up everywhere in data analysis, because they control the shrinking of a margin of error as the number n of data points grows.

In his paper, Riemann did much more than guess. He introduced tools that would constitute the basis for much of the work on number theory — the branch of mathematics that concerns integers, primes and divisibility — in the following centuries.

First, by developing new techniques in analysis — another word for advanced calculus — as he went along, Riemann constructed the ‘Riemann ζ function’ (ζ is the Greek letter ‘zeta’).

Riemann then showed that the function embodied an enormous amount of information about prime numbers. First, he proved that the solutions to the equation ζ (z) = 0 — where z is a point on a plane — encode the statistical distribution of prime numbers along the number line. To do so, Riemann employed a type of Fourier analysis, the type of maths that nowadays enables the compression of music into compact mp3 files by breaking sound waves down into sinusoidal components.

#928. Norway's ice hockey team says Russia replacing it at World Juniors

The wrangling over Russia's return to international ice hockey continues, with Norway saying it has been kicked out of the next major tournament to accommodate Russia. Switzerland has joined a "boycott."

With just weeks to go until the start of the 2027 World Junior Championship, it remains unclear who will be the 10th, and final, participant. This comes after the Norwegian Ice Hockey Association said the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) had said it had been removed from the tournament so that Russia could take part.

The move, which has yet to be publicly announced by the IIHF, comes in apparent response to the Court of Arbitration (CAS) ruling in late October, which ordered it to allow Russia to return to international play. The World Juniors is the first tournament affected by the CAS decision.

The IIHF barred Russia and Belarus from international play shortly after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

In a statement issued Saturday, the IIHF said it was "taking the necessary steps required by the CAS ruling and reviewing what conditions would need to be met to safeguard our Championships, protect the organization's financial stability and secure the long-term future of international ice hockey."

As of Monday, the IIHF website still listed Norway as one of the participants in the World Juniors, which is to be hosted by Edmonton and Red Deer, Alberta, beginning on December 26. But Swiss Ice Hockey has responded to Norway's statement, saying its team would not face Russia at the World Juniors — as would be the case if it replaces Norway in the schedule.

However, it's far from certain that Russia will actually be able to ice a team in the tournament, as just last week, the Canadian prime minister ruled out the possibility.

"While Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified ​war in Ukraine, as long as that's going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada," said Mark Carney.

"So, ​if you're asking specifically about the World Juniors, the Russians will not be there."

How this circle could be squared is unclear. Carney's pledge, coupled with the stated refusal by Finland, Sweden, Switzerland and others to face Russia in an international tournament, appears to have given the Norwegian Ice Hockey Association (NIHF) hope that its team could still play in the upcoming tournament. Several long-time corporate sponsors have also threatened to pull out if Russia is allowed to compete.

"This makes us hope that the last word has not been said about our participation in Canada in December," said NIHF General Secretary Petter Salsten.

"The Norwegian Ice Hockey Association is awaiting further information from the IIHF in the coming days."

Meanwhile, the German Ice Hockey Association (DEB) is still in discussions with the government in Berlin and the IIHF about how to proceed — or not — with hosting the Men's Ice Hockey World Championship in May.

"We intend to host the world championship in Germany next year, and I am very optimistic that we will succeed in doing so," DEB chairman Frank H. Lutz told German broadcaster MagentaSport on Saturday.

While he acknowledged the IIHF's CAS-ordered requirement to include Russia and reiterated the DEB's rejection of the court ruling, he provided no indication as to how this obstacle could be overcome.

Lutz, who said he would be in Berlin for more consultations this week, had previously said handing back Germany's hosting rights was a possibility — if only as a last resort.

On Friday, government spokesman Stefan Kornelius said Berlin supports the DEB's efforts to find a solution.

"However, given the boycotts that would follow Russia's readmission, that would effectively be impossible. For this reason, we intend to explore, through dialogue, how we can still ensure the tournament takes place."

Asked at the same press conference whether Germany could issue visas to a Russian team for the tournament, a Foreign Ministry spokesman indicated that this would be difficult under restrictions currently in place.

"At a time when Russia is waging a war of aggression against Ukraine, there can be no 'normalcy' — and we will certainly not pretend that there is," said spokesperson Martin Giese.

However, he did not categorically rule out the possibility.

It has been suggested that government officials could be choosing their words carefully out of concern for Munich's chances as it bids to host the Summer Olympics in 2036, 2040 or 2044.

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) recently lifted its sanctions on Russian athletes and suspension of the Russian National Olympic Committee, opening the door for their return to competition despite the ongoing war in Ukraine.

The thinking goes that the IOC would expect national Olympic committees who are bidding to host an Olympic Games — like the German Olympic Sports Confederation (DOSB) — to follow its lead.

Asked whether the debate over Russia's possible involvement in a hockey tournament could affect Munich's chances, government spokesman Kornelius said he didn't wish to "speculate on implications."

Still, with the IOC set to decide in the next few weeks whether Munich advances to the next stage of the process, one has to think that the issue could hardly have come up at a more inopportune time for the DOSB.

Be nice to people on your way up, because you'll meet them on your way down – whether you're Wayne Rooney at Everton, Theo Walcott at Southampton or just expecting to queue with the same crowd on a return flight from Madrid.

It's 8am on a Saturday though, and while plenty of the punters have dropped off luggage, FourFourTwo are doing no such thing, travelling light for a hit-and-run mission to Spain: yep, we're coming back here tomorrow.

Welcome to the era of 'Trip Snacking': the only sights we're taking in are Jose Mourinho's thousand-yard stare, Jude Bellingham's outstretched arms and the wonder of learning that Iago Aspas, pushing 40, is still getting wheeled out on the biggest stages of all. We're here for a prime cut of La Liga, and this time, you can keep your museums, palaces and fancy sky bars.

FourFourTwo have always loved a quick turnaround – the relentless nature of European away days practically dictates it – but the concept has officially gone mainstream. According to Hotels.com’s Unpack ’27 travel trends report, Trip Snacking is the defining travel trend of 2027. It's the rise of the one-night stay – the loan spell of the tourism world – precision-engineered to fit seamlessly around packed schedules and tighter budgets, with fans increasingly turning match-day into getaway-day. Count us in.

The numbers speak for themselves. Searches for one-night stays are up nearly 10 per cent year-on-year globally, and up 15 per cent among British travellers. Some 73 per cent of travellers booked a one-night stay in the past 12 months, and 79 per cent say they are planning to book one in the coming year, climbing to 83 per cent among Millennials and Gen Z.

While 42 per cent cite celebrating life milestones and 23 per cent simply need a quick reset between traditional holidays, a massive 49 per cent of Brits are doing it to attend concerts, shows and sporting events.

That's why we're here. Madrid is one of the biggest beneficiaries of the trend: weekend lodging searches to the Spanish capital during the football season are up 20 per cent year-on-year, while full-season searches have risen 25 per cent. It's a pattern repeating across Europe's major footballing hubs – demand has surged in Liverpool (up 100 per cent), Manchester (up 95 per cent), London (up 40 per cent) and Munich (up 10 per cent). Unsurprisingly, marquee European nights drive the biggest spikes, with Madrid searches jumping 70 per cent around a clash with Bayern Munich, and Manchester rising 25 per cent when Los Blancos came to town.

As an Official Partner of Real Madrid, Hotels.com arranged our stay at the five-star Barcelo Imagine – one of their top-rated picks for a Madrid football break, starting at £125 per night – purely for Real hosting Celta Vigo at the Bernabeu. On a 24-hour getaway, staying close to the action is half the battle.

A quick drop of the bags and we're out into the crisp Madrid afternoon. It's warm for November, ideal for a stroll up towards the Bernabeu, semi-newly renovated – looking a little like a giant airfryer – and packed with fans and tourists alike. Thanks to our hosts, FourFourTwo took in the action from the Hotels.com VIP box, situated just behind the goal. The PA system is booming – a little like we imagine Mourinho will be when Real return to the dressing room for the half-time break trailing by a goal. But we came here to have superstars, and the Special One appears obliging to treat us to a fair few from his bench.

A beautiful five-star hotel just a five-minute Uber from the Bernabeu, the Barcelo Imagine is a superb choice to stay at for Trip snacking. The seasonal outdoor pool is a great spot to take a dip, and guests can grab a bite to eat at Eat & Roll, which serves local and international cuisine and is open for breakfast. Other highlights at this luxurious hotel include 2 bars/lounges, a poolside bar and a fitness centre

Vinicius Jr has struggled early on this season but is now back to his sparkling best, grabbing the game by the scruff of the neck and toying with his full-back like a cat with string. Pretty soon after his introduction, the stadium is dancing to a samba rhythm, led by the Brazilian orchestrating with ease – and after Bellingham's punchy equaliser, Los Blancos really step up a gear. It's a lesser-known name, Carlos Espi, who grabs the winner from close range, letting out a primal roar in front of the Grada Fans, reflecting 80,000 relieved Madridistas, all exhaling at once.

In the end, Celta simply couldn't keep up, as we discuss after the game. This is where the true joy of the Madrid Trip Snack begins: a late dinner means midnight tapas, swapping stories, and dissecting the match over plates of jamon iberico and patatas bravas. Some 32 per cent of travellers say they have taken a one-night trip specifically for a sporting event – rising to 33 per cent among women – and turning a 90-minute match into a 24-hour cultural immersion feels like the ultimate life hack.

As Melanie Fish, Hotels.com spokesperson and travel expert, puts it: "Football fans aren't waiting for a week-long holiday anymore. They're turning matches into memorable 24-hour getaways, whether that's a weekend in Madrid or a European away game." For Trip Snackers, finding a good deal is key, and perks like free cancellation and earning £100 in Hotels.comCash after 10 nights make squeezing in a spontaneous trip much easier to justify.

Sunday morning allows for no such gentle reset – we're going back to the Bernabeu for a tour of the stadium, believe it or not – before heading off to the airport, roughly 24 hours after we arrived. We feel a little like an away team, jetting into the city just for the game, enjoying a warm down and getting back for Match of the Day 2 – but we crammed in enough football, croquettes and merch from the Real club shop that it feels like we were away longer than just a day.

An impressive 71 per cent of travellers agree that a Trip Snack holds them over until their next longer trip, and it is easy to see why. We do not always have the time, the annual leave, or the funds for a sprawling European tour. We cannot all travel the continent watching our team – especially when it's Real Madrid, who have been to Rome and Athens already this autumn, with London on tfhotelshe horizon.

Sometimes, you just need a quick fix. Sometimes it takes heading to the nation of tapas to realise you just need a bite over a buffet.
