#926. Levski Sofia fans hospitalised after violent clashes with Marseille supporters

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The Bulgarian Football Union has referred the incident to Uefa

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Marseille head coach Bruno Genesio said “we are living through violent times” after five Levski Sofia fans were hospitalised following violent clashes before their Europa League encounter with the French side.

Groups of supporters threw projectiles and flares and French outlet L’Equipe reported that there were Nazi salutes observed in the away section.

Ten minutes before kick-off at the Stade Velodrome a group of Marseille fans broke through into the away stand, which housed around 500 fans.

In the ensuing clashes five people, all Bulgarian, were injured and taken to hospital “with eye injuries, head trauma and a dislocated shoulder”, according to the Marseille police prefecture, while six others were treated on-site for more superficial injuries.

The police force said there was “no information at this stage regarding any arrests”.

Security were able to restore order and the game kicked off on time, although there were further incidents later on, particularly at half-time.

Genesio said: “We are living through violent times in our society, so this is very, very regrettable.” Julio Velazquez, head coach of the Bulgarian domestic champions, said: “It's a very regrettable episode. These are incidents which are unacceptable for football.”

The Bulgarian Football Union condemned the violence and said it had referred the incident to UEFA, calling for the harshest possible sanctions. It also demanded full cooperation and transparency from French authorities in investigating the attacks and identifying those responsible.

Levski said the club's priority is the safety and well-being of its fans. A statement read: “What happened tonight is particularly alarming given the extraordinary security measures put in place by the French authorities, as well as the restrictions imposed on our travelling supporters—restrictions that the club had already formally contested with UEFA.

“Despite the risks identified by the club prior to the match, the measures taken failed to provide adequate protection for our fans. This is completely unacceptable.”

Marseille also condemned the violence and said it is conducting “a thorough analysis of the circumstances in which these incidents took place.”

Bulgarian President Iliana Yotova called for those responsible to be held accountable and Prime Minister Rumen Radev said he had spoken to French president Emmanuel Macron about the violence at a European summit in Brussels.

A spokesperson for Macron’s office said: “He condemned in the strongest possible terms these acts of violence targeting Bulgarian supporters, which have no place in sport or in public spaces, and assured the Prime Minister that these acts would not go unpunished.”

Marseille won the game 1-0, with Amine Gouiri scoring a 28th-minute penalty.

#925. One person had a worse night than United keeper – the wretched referee

By the end of another utterly chaotic 90 minutes in the Manchester United soap opera, there was only one person who had endured a worse night than Senne Lammens.

Watching this game back will make for grim viewing for the United goalkeeper who, having been one of the club’s shining lights last season, is steadily becoming enveloped in a crisis of his own in this most torrid of campaigns.

But Roberto Rosetti, Uefa’s chief refereeing officer, might also want to sit Szymon Marciniak down after this and pick over the Polish official’s own nightmare performance. Marciniak denied United two goals, both of which should have stood, and in doing so ended up shining an even more brutal lens on Lammens’s calamitous display.

United’s Belgian goalkeeper was responsible for both of Sporting’s goals. He needlessly conceded a penalty in the first half, after a rush of blood to the head, that was converted by Luis Suárez, just 75 seconds after he had saved a spot-kick from the Sporting striker.

United had recovered from those bewildering few minutes to lead early in the second half, courtesy of two goals from captain Bruno Fernandes against his old club.

But, 10 minutes from time, Lammens committed the kind of howler that becomes worse and worse with every viewing. In doing so, he handed Sporting an equaliser and ensured United remain without an away win this season.

Lammens could have come to meet Iván Fresneda’s cross 100 times and probably dropped the ball only once. It was his and United’s misfortune that it should happen here. Suárez could barely believe his luck, although his finish was still accomplished, an acrobatic overhead kick from close range.

Senne Lammens with a gift for Luis Suárez to equalise for Sporting 🤯 📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/kOQ6HImlVc

One of the stars of last season for United, Lammens is being dragged down with the rest of them this time around. He had looked hesitant from the moment he was almost caught dealing with a back-pass by Suárez in the opening minutes. It set the tone for what was to come.

As if Mauricio Pochettino did not already have enough on his plate, United’s new head coach now has a goalkeeper problem.

Of course, this would not have been as costly a night for Lammens had Marciniak not made such a mess of things himself. United may have been their own worst enemies again, but there was little doubting Sporting were given a helping hand here by some truly wretched refereeing.

The worst of it was the denial of a perfectly legitimate equaliser late in the first half after Youri Tielemans was penalised for a perceived foul – it was nothing of the sort – that the referee had initially not blown for.

And then moments after Suarez made it 2-2, the Sporting goalkeeper Kaique Pereira flapped at Fernandes’s corner and punched the ball into his own net. Kaique’s blunder was already in motion by the time Patrick Dorgu barged into Kaique. But Marciniak was ordered to the pitch-side monitor by Piotr Lasyk, the VAR, and from there, he weakly decided Kaique had been infringed upon by Dorgu. It was a big let-off for the goalkeeper and the hosts.

To compounded United’s frustrations, they were then reduced to 10 men late on when Tielemans, who had been booked for protesting over the first disallowed goal, received a second yellow card. It means United have now had four red cards and conceded five penalties in their last five games and, four weeks shy of Christmas, are still searching for a win on the road.

The irony was that, amidst the chaos, there was a lot Pochettino will have liked about the performance. It was far from perfect but United at least had a structure, coherence and confidence about them for long periods. But for Lammens’s shocker and some dubious refereeing, United would surely have claimed just a fourth win this season.

The problem with this United side is they never seem too far away from an act of self-sabotage. Pochettino insisted on the eve of this game that his team were not fragile, but that assessment was challenged in the crazy 160 seconds when United conceded not one but two penalties.

In truth, they could feel hard done to by the award of the first in the 29th minute. Geny Catamo went down far too easily – and very late – after Lisandro Martínez swung out a leg. There was contact but it was of the very minimal variety. Martínez rushed off to Marciniak to remonstrate but his pleas fell on deaf ears. There was a sense of justice, then, when Lammens saved Suárez’s feeble penalty.

You would have thought that would be a confidence booster for Lammens, but in no time he had gone from hero to zero, with worse to follow.

A ball was swept in behind Noussair Mazraoui and Maximiliano Araújo gave chase. There was no need for Lammens to come careering out of goal but that is what he did. When he clumsily blocked off Araújo in the process, Marciniak wasted little time brandishing a yellow card and pointing to the spot. This time Suárez made no mistake from 12 yards.

One more in the win column for the Ewing Theory (that says teams can improve without their star player).

Laudrup told FourFourTwo: “As we weren’t able to qualify, I decided to focus 100 per cent on Barça. Yugoslavia went on to win the group, but because of the war, Denmark were suddenly given their place. They need to finish 24th or higher to avoid elimination. They only have two fewer points (after four games) in the Champions League than they do in the Premier League (after 11).

Few Manchester United fans expected a positive result from Mauricio Pochettino’s first game in charge at Anfield, but the bar will not be set so low for Sporting in the Champions League this evening.

The manner of the 4-0 defeat against Liverpool, even accounting for Leny Yoro’s early red card, was dispiriting but not unexpected. The next few weeks will reveal how Pochettino intends to get a grip on the job.

When it comes to United’s Champions League prospects, the comeback win over Roma at the tail-end of Michael Carrick’s tenure made their position less perilous, but avoiding outright elimination is the first target.

United are 19th in the table, with the top 24 teams going through. Those between ninth and 24th go into a play-off round before the last 16. After Sporting away, United host RB Leipzig and Bayern Munich before a trip to Villarreal so there are stiff tests to come.

Sporting are well-placed after three wins from four, but their Champions League schedule is rather one-sided: in their final three matches they travel to Roma, before playing Barcelona and Manchester City. They reached the quarter-finals of the competition last season, losing narrowly to Arsenal over two legs.

They are third in their league, having been weakened by the summer sales of Geovany Quenda (to Chelsea), Morten Hjulmand (to Atletico Madrid) and Ousmane Diomande (to Nottingham Forest). The vast majority of goals are scored by Colombian striker Luis Suárez.

Bruno Fernandes, United’s captain, returns to his former club tonight and there is hope Luke Shaw could be back at left-back. Pochettino must decide whether or not to stick with Matthijs de Ligt, who was extremely rusty at Anfield but may need the minutes.

Yoro’s one-game suspension was overturned by the FA, and he would have been available for this one in any case.

Arsenal were held to another Champions League draw, but one of the stars of the performance has a foot out of the door

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

One Arsenal star is in talks to leave the club, despite getting the nod last night to start against Borussia Dortmund.

The Gunners were held to a 1-1 draw by the Bundesliga leaders last night, despite creating a plethora of chances, finding themselves needing two wins from their next three Champions League fixtures to finish in the top eight of the league phase.

But despite Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta making six changes last night, one star is still “unhappy” and seeking an exit from N5.

Criticised at times during his tenure at the Emirates Stadium for a lack of rotation, Arteta seems to have changed approach this term and given more game time to his squad players.

Riccardo Calafiori and Kai Havertz were both unused substitutes last night against Dortmund, Ben White and Jurrien Timber have shared the right-back position, and Myles Lewis-Skelly has had ample opportunities despite the signing of Bruno Guimaraes.

Kepa Arrizabalaga, however, is “unhappy” with his role within the squad, with Sport Witness relaying a report from Spanish outlet El Desmarque that Valencia have approached the goalkeeper.

The most expensive goalkeeper of all time joined the Gunners in 2025 on a cut-price deal from Chelsea, following loans at Real Madrid and Bournemouth – and despite serving as the first choice at Dean Court, he has largely been a cup keeper for the Gunners.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Despite getting his chance last night, and as a substitute against Newcastle United at the weekend when David Raya went off injured, Arrizabalaga hasn't troubled his fellow Spaniard for the No.1 jersey, with the champions signing French custodian Ilian Meslier over the summer, too.

This new report states that the Basque is “unhappy with his secondary role at Arsenal”, and “eager to return” to La Liga, following rumours that he would depart over the summer after just a season in North London.

A move is described as “complicated”, however, with Arsenal unwilling to let the star go.

Arsenal have signed a goalkeeper every year since Arteta took the reins, with the likes of Mat Ryan, Aaron Ramsdale, Matt Turner and Neto all joining the club and leaving since 2019.

The Premier League champions have several good prospects between the sticks, too, with Tommy Setford on loan at Stevenage, academy prospect Jack Porter well thought of and Dane Lucas Nygaard having joined at the age of 18 in June 2024.

Arrizabalaga is worth €5 million, according to Transfermarkt. Arsenal host Manchester City this weekend when Premier League action resumes.

#923. Iran war oil shock drives dip in global emissions, study shows

Global carbon emissions are expected to fall slightly in 2026, but not because of major progress on climate action. Instead, it's high energy prices following the US attack on Iran that's driving the trend.

Global carbon emissions are set to slightly drop this year, a new study suggests, largely as a result of high energy prices in the wake of the US war on Iran and the disruption of supply through the Strait of Hormuz.

Emissions from oil, gas and coal are the main drivers of climate change. While over the past decade, these emissions have risen by 0.9% per year, they are expected to drop by 0.4% in 2026.

"It's downwards, which sounds good, but this is largely driven by the war in Iran, what's happened in the Strait of Hormuz," said the study's co-author Glen Peters, a scientist at the CICERO Center for International Climate Research in Norway.

"So in a way, a little bit of good news, but for the wrong reasons."

The study was released while global leaders are meeting in Turkey for the United Nations' COP31 climate conference.

The study published by international research group the Global Carbon Project found that oil emissions dropped by 1.9% in 2026, while natural gas fell by 0.3%. Coal emissions however continued to rise, by around 0.6%.

"A drop in emissions in ‌one year is not a peak unless it ‌is driven ​by structural change," Peters cautioned.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A structural change would mean that emissions would slowly rise to a peak and then slowly decline afterward, indicating a long term trend. That's not what happened though, Peters said. "What we see this year is [that] oil emissions are going up and then suddenly, bang, down 2%."

It is the third time in recent years that global carbon pollution has dropped. The previous declines were during the global economic crisis in 2009 and during the COVID pandemic in 2020. In each of those cases, emissions went back up once global economies recovered.

While the geopolitical shocks of the past year have been the driving factors behind the temporary emissions reversal, there has also been a rise in renewable energy contributing to the data. So while solar panels, wind farms and electric vehicles did make a difference, they were just not enough to cut emissions by themselves.

"The long-term answer remains the rapid deployment of clean energy technologies," according to co-author of the study, Pierre Friedlingstein, of the Global Carbon Budget Office at the University.

And even though emissions from fossil fuels dropped slightly, overall global carbon dioxide emissions still went up by about 1%, the study warns. The overall rise is because of land use changes like deforestation and peat fires, which increased too fast to be offset by the slight decrease in fossil fuel burning.

Syrian referee Hanna Hattab was replaced at half-time of the AFC Champions League Two match between Gol Gohar and Al Jazira

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

A referee has hit back at claims he was “drunk” while officiating an AFC Champions League Two match.

Footage has been widely shared on social media of Syrian referee Hanna Hattab looking visibly disoriented during a match between Iran's Gol Gohar and Al Jazira of the United Arab Emirates.

One particular incident raised eyebrows when Hattab showed a yellow card to Al Jazira’s goalkeeper for a foul that happened close to the halfway line, 40 yards away from him.

Hattab was then replaced at half-time with the fourth official taking over for the remainder of the game, which Al Jazira won 1-0.

Reports claimed Gol Gohar staff accused the referee of being drunk following erratic decision-making as similar accusations flooded in online.

But Hattab, who is part of the AFC's elite refereeing group, has refuted the allegations as “insult and defamation”, threatening legal action.

“I also confirm my full right to take all legal and judicial measures against anyone who published or made a statement or contributed to the insult and defamation of me, regardless of their position or status, whether they are an individual, an institution, or a sports entity.”

He also said he would issue a further statement following contact with the Syrian Arab Football Federation (SFA) which will “clarify all the details and facts related to what happened ... with full transparency and clarity.”

Omani journalist Issa Said, who covers Asian football, has since claimed on social media that what happened to Hattab was "due to a drop in his blood sugar, which caused him to lose concentration and focus".

The SFA have also put out a statement standing in support of Hattab, while stating it has requested his medical report from the match.

“The Main Referees Committee of the Syrian Arab Football Federation confirms that it stands in full support of international referee Mr Hana Khattab regarding the incident he was subjected to, following reassurance about his health,” it said.

“This comes after the committee was reassured of his well-being, following a number of discussions on social media concerning the incident. The committee emphasises its full support for him and its commitment to following up on the matter in all its details and developments.

“In this regard, the committee has requested that the Syrian Football Referees Committee provide the medical report relating to the referee, the match observers' report and the referee assessor's report. This is in order to establish the circumstances of the incident accurately and comprehensively and to complete the necessary procedures in this matter.

“The committee also confirms that it will provide the relevant authorities and the public with the findings as soon as the requested reports are received, in order to ensure accuracy and to obtain information from official sources.”

The Europa League game between Besiktas and Israel's Hapoel Beer-Sheva was suspended for around 30 minutes on Thursday when police clashed with fans of the Turkish club after they displayed a banner in support of Palestine.

The game, being played on neutral ground in Batumi, Georgia, was halted in the 26th minute but restarted after the interruption.

Turkey’s Haberturk broadcaster said Georgian police used pepper spray against the Besiktas fans, who also unfurled a Palestinian flag, prompting referee referee Morten Krogh to stop the game with the score 0-0.

In a statement, Besiktas accused the Georgian security forces of using “disproportionate” force against supporters before and during the game.

Georgian police entered the stands and ⁠used pepper spray on Besiktas fans, Turkish outlet NTV reported.

“We strongly condemn the security forces for their use of disproportionate force against our fans,” the club said. “We also extend our best wishes for a speedy recovery to all our fans affected by these incidents.”

The report added that Turkish fans chanted “Down with Israel” and that Besiktas players and director of football Onder Ozen spoke to supporters before play restarted to calm the situation.

The Turkish Football Federation condemned the treatment of Besiktas supporters on X, saying they were subjected to unacceptable behaviour and discrimination. It said it would press for an investigation.

The TFF’s statement read: “We strongly condemn the unacceptable attitudes, conduct and interference directed at Beşiktaş supporters, both inside and outside the stadium, before and during our club’s Uefa Europa League match against Hapoel Beer-Sheva in Georgia.

“No practice that disregards the universal values of sport, human dignity, mutual respect and the principles of fair play, or that involves discrimination, exclusion or security failures, can be tolerated.

“Nor can there be any question of remaining silent in the face of such conduct, which endangers our supporters’ safety and targets their fundamental rights and freedoms.

“As the Turkish Football Federation, we declare unequivocally that we will follow this matter to its conclusion to ensure that the events are fully investigated, those responsible are identified and the necessary sanctions are imposed without delay.

“There must be no tolerance for covering up these events, allowing those responsible to evade accountability or permitting similar violations to recur.

“We emphasize that we stand firmly with our club, Besiktas, and our supporters, who faced a series of problems, particularly serious security failures, and extend our best wishes for a speedy recovery to all our supporters subjected to interference and mistreatment.

“Let no one forget that we will not remain silent in the face of disrespect, discrimination and security violations directed at representatives and supporters of Turkish football.

“We will act decisively on national and international platforms to ensure that all necessary steps are taken, particularly with Uefa, and that those responsible are held accountable.”

Turkish clubs echoed the sentiments of the TFF, with Besiktas’ rivals Fenerbahce, Galatasaray and Trabzonspor all among those to stand with the club.

“We do not accept Turkish clubs being denied the right to play their home matches in their own country, in front of their own fans, when facing clubs from the occupying state of Israel,” Trabzonspor wrote in a statement.

“We do not consider Uefa’s double standards on this issue acceptable. We also strongly condemn the disproportionate intervention by security forces against Besiktas fans in Georgia this evening.”

The ⁠officiating team and the Besiktas players ‌left ​the pitch before ‌the game restarted.

Earlier, the Besiktas players refused to shake hands with their Hapoel counterparts, the state-run Anadolu Agency reported.

Hapoel Beer-Sheva and Israel FA had not commented on the incident at the time of publishing.

#918. Why malnutrition can go unnoticed, and what that means for our health

More than 2 billion people worldwide suffer from nutrient deficiencies, most of them in the Global South. The health consequences can be devastating.

Some 50,000 deaths can be attributed to malnutrition in Germany each year, according to the German Society for Nutritional Medicine (DGEM).

The problem is that malnutrition often doesn't become apparent until the consequences are already severe.

"In most cases, you don't notice anything at first," said Matthias Pirlich, a nutritional expert and internal medicine specialist, who once served as DGEM vice president. "You could have a severe vitamin D deficiency for months before any symptoms appear at all. The same applies for vitamin B12. By the time symptoms appear, such as nerve damage, it's already too late."

A long-term B12 deficiency can damage the spinal cord, leading to numbness in the limbs, muscle weakness or even paralysis. Less common deficiency-related brain damage can cause memory loss and mental health issues.

All B vitamins play an important role in metabolism, blood formation and healthy nerve function.

Vitamins, along with various minerals such as calcium, magnesium, iron, iodine and zinc, are classed as micronutrients. The body needs to source them from food, as it cannot produce them itself. Our bodies also need macronutrients like carbohydrates, carbohydrates, protein and fats that provide us with energy.

If the body consumes less food than it needs to maintain all bodily functions over a prolonged period of time, then this is known as undernutrition. A recent World Food Organization (FAO) report estimates that approximately 645 million people worldwide suffer from chronic undernutrition.

Malnutrition, on the other hand, occurs when we consume enough calories but lack certain macronutrients or micronutrients in our food. This, too, can make one sick over time and even prove fatal. About 2 billion people worldwide suffer from this so-called hidden hunger, most of them in the Global South. That said, even some people in industrialized nations lack important micronutrients in their nutrition.

One study, for instance, found that just under three-quarters of the US population did not meet the recommended daily intake of vitamin D between 2007 and 2010, with more than two-thirds falling short of the recommended amount of vitamin E. And in Germany, about one-third of the population suffered from vitamin D deficiency in 2017, according to the German Nutrition Society. Such deficiency can cause bone, joint and muscle pain. It may also lead to an increased risk of falls and bone fractures.

About one-third of Germans also had an insufficient intake of iodine, a trace element that is indispensable for the production of thyroid hormones. Iodine deficiency can therefore disrupt normal thyroid function. Not only that — during pregnancy, a baby's brain and nervous system can only properly develop with an adequate supply of iodine.

The cultivation of agricultural produce with partially long shelf life or high yields has in some cases caused a decrease in the micronutrient content of fruits, vegetables and grains. Whether this drop in micronutrients is impacting human health, however, is a matter of debate.

Malnutrition can result from an unbalanced diet that, while filling and providing energy, lacks essential micronutrients. Examples of such empty calories include fast food and highly processed foods, as well as white bread and white rice.

Poverty is often the reason for such an unbalanced diet, for example when people in the Global South can only afford to buy staples such as flour or rice.

Another study found that in Germany, households at risk of poverty are more likely to consume foods that are low in nutrients and high in calories.

Depression is also associated with an increased risk of nutrient deficiency. "People often lose their appetite, and when they neglect their self-care, they may end up eating a very unbalanced diet," Pirlich told DW. His research shows that older adults and people who live alone often develop malnutrition, too. The risk also increases the more medications a person takes.

Many diseases result in the body being less efficient at absorbing or utilizing nutrients through the intestines. This applies to people with inflammatory or chronic disease, such as Crohn's disease, celiac disease, liver disease and cancer.

The DGEM estimates that some 30% of all patients receiving inpatient care in Germany are affected by or at risk of malnutrition. Yet health insurance data shows that only about 1% of patients are screened and treated for nutrient deficiencies.

Often, patients' malnutrition worsens during their hospital stay. The consequences can be serious, potentially causing additional complications, delayed recuperation, longer hospital stays and even increased mortality rates. This results in higher healthcare expenditure, amounting to billions each year.

German policymakers and medical associations are therefore developing a plan to better screen for and treat malnutrition in hospitals. The road map will be ready by 2027 and copy the Dutch approach in the sense that all patients are checked for nutritional deficiencies upon hospital admission.

Pirlich wants to see such screenings for at-risk groups in outpatient clinics, too: "This includes all those with chronic and serious illnesses and, above all, older adults."

To prevent poverty-related malnutrition, Pirlich suggests increased access to healthy food, offering free school meals as an example.

The nutritional expert recommends eating a diet that is varied and largely plant-based. "Secondary plant compounds have a very positive effect, and if you eat a highly diverse diet, you consume many different foods that are [nutritionally] beneficial," said Pirlich.

There's a simple rule of thumb: The more colorful your food, the better.

Also, cook vegetables as gently as possible, because overheating and keeping them warm for too long destroys their vitamins. Long storage periods also lead to vitamin loss, so it makes sense to go for seasonal and regional foods in particular.

But even when ensuring a healthy and balanced diet, some people still develop a nutrient deficiency. A blood test can provide clarity, and dietary supplements may help make up for the deficiency.

This article was originally written in German.

#912. Will Australia push for fossil fuel exit at UN talks?

The heat is on Australia as chief negotiator at the COP31 UN climate conference to forge a path away from coal and gas, and to protect Pacific neighbors facing rising sea levels.

In its role as president of negotiations at the UN climate talks in Turkey, Australia is being pressured to guide nations toward unified action on slashing the greenhouse gas emissions that are generated in large part by burning fossil fuels.

The nation has pledged to lead by example at the summit through a strong commitment to renewable energy, electrification and reduced reliance on planet-heating coal, oil and gas.

"Renewable energy, grids, storage and electrification are creating opportunities to strengthen resilience, improve energy security, and reduce emissions at the same time," said Chris Bowen, Australia's climate change and energy minister, in October during a meeting in Fiji ahead of the COP climate conference.

"These are proven, commercial and scalable today. Now is the moment for faster implementation."

Yet Australia is also the world's third-largest exporter of fossil fuels. And unlike France and Germany, or island nations from Fiji to the Bahamas that are highly vulnerable to a changing climate, the COP31 co-president has not yet committed to phasing them out.

As calls grow for the country to set a clear route to a clean energy future, critics say its vague promise to transition away from polluting sources of power does not go far enough.

Australia is home to 56% of the world's coal mine projects currently in the pipeline, notes environmental nonprofit, 350.org.

Andreas Sieber, head of political strategy at the organization, is calling on the country, the world's second-largest coal exporter, to reverse course and announce an "overdue coal phaseout date" during the COP31 conference.

"Australia needs to walk the walk and follow Germany's example and commit to a phaseout," said Melanie Pill, founder of The Climate Project, an Australia-based climate policy advisory.

The argument to end fossil fuel production is not only about cutting emissions but reducing dependence on energy systems that rely on volatile oil and gas markets, she explained.

"A fossil phaseout in the face of the enduring and escalating conflict in the Middle East is in the interest of everyone," Pill told DW.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

This is especially true for Australia's diesel-reliant Pacific neighbors, who spend up to 25% of GDP on fossil fuel imports — as opposed 6% on health — according to a report by the Institute for Climate Risk and Response at the University of New South Wales.

As lead negotiator at the UN climate talks, Australia can "flip the narrative" on a fossil fuel phaseout, using the challenge of energy security as a justification, said Pill.

This opportunity could be lost, however, if Australia fails to address fossil fuel exports that accounted for 80% of its total carbon footprint in 2022 — and near 5% of global emissions.

While the nation is a world leader in rooftop solar, and generates around half of its electricity from renewables, this progress is "being undone by its continued approval of more fossil fuels for export," said Simon Bradshaw, COP31 lead and climate expert at Greenpeace Australia Pacific.

He noted that the Labor government of Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has approved the construction, expansion or extension of 38 coal, oil and gas projects since coming to power four years ago on a pro-climate platform.

"You cannot aspire to lead on climate abroad if you're not getting your own house in order," said Thomas Houlie, climate and energy policy analyst at Climate Analytics, a global climate policy institute.

In 2025, when Australia approved the extension of a major gas export project in the country's west until 2070, Albanese justified the move in the name of a balance between "security of energy supply" and "support [for] the transition which reduces our emissions."

The country has publicly backed a global transition away from the fossil fuels driving the global temperature rise linked to extreme heat and drought. Both through the Global Stocktake agreed at the 2023 UN climate summit, and via the inaugural "transitioning away" summit in Colombia this April, at which Australia and 56 countries pledged to develop a fossil fuel exit road map.

But these commitments are not reflected in Australian resources policy, or its domestic rollout of clean power infrastructure.

"While the government has set a renewables target for electricity, it leaves plenty of blind spots in other sectors," said Houlie, adding that emission reductions in industry and transport have been limited and that the push to achieve an 82% renewables target for the electricity grid by 2030 is behind schedule.

In its role as lead negotiator at COP31, Australia has promised to ensure that any final conference text serves to "elevate the views and the experiences" of small Pacific nations in its region, from Vanuatu to Tuvalu.

These island countries that generate low emissions yet suffer extreme climate impacts from worsening cyclones or rising seas are "sick of Australia's double talk on climate," said Shiva Gounden, head of Pacific at Greenpeace Australia Pacific.

Australia must commit to "substantial new funding contributions" to help Pacific neighbors adapt to the climate emergency and achieve energy independence, said his colleague Bradshaw. He reiterated the need to concurrently create a "national road map" away from coal and gas production and export.

A Climate Analytics report co-authored by Houlie outlines a fossil fuel phaseout pathway for Australia that can begin immediately. This includes an end to coal power generation by 2034 and a rapid reduction in oil and gas consumption, with renewables generating almost all the country's electricity by 2040. Fossil fuel export projects would be eliminated, and existing ones shuttered before becoming obsolete.

"This co-presidency is a golden opportunity for Australia to step up and commit to a phaseout," said Houlie.

George Russell says Lewis Hamilton is an equally "ruthless competitor" to Max Verstappen but that his former team-mate has "incredible values, grace and dignity".

Speaking exclusively to Martin Brundle during an interview that will air during Sky Sports F1's live coverage of the Qatar Grand Prix on Sunday, Russell said he found Verstappen's verbal attack on him "amusing", before drawing a comparison between the Dutchman and seven-time world champion Hamilton.

"He [Verstappen] is a ruthless competitor and I massively respect that, but there's also Lewis Hamilton, who I've spent three years team-mates with and watched my whole life," Russell said.

Newcastle United's owners PIF are seeking fresh investment to help the club achieve its infrastructure goals

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

At first glance, headlines stating that Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF) has put 25 per cent of Newcastle United up for sale were always going to draw intrigue and perhaps even alarm on Tyneside.

Five years on from the much-heralded takeover that ended Mike Ashley’s unpopular regime, any suggestion of the club’s sovereign wealth owners cashing in naturally invites fears that the project is running out of steam.

However, this proposed transaction is actually one of the more encouraging developments for Newcastle supporters in months.

First and foremost, PIF are not packing their bags and walking away from St James’ Park.

Rather than offloading existing shares to pocket a profit, the club is issuing brand-new equity - with US investment bank J.P. Morgan appointed to find an external partner.

This means not a single penny from the sale will flow back into PIF’s coffers - they are not recouping on their investment. Instead, funds raised through the share issue will supposedly be injected into Newcastle's ongoing projects.

PIF will see its majority stake diluted rather than exiting the club, remaining firmly in the driving seat as owners with majority control.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

While fans have grown increasingly frustrated by delays around major infrastructure upgrades, the club, led on the executive side by chief executive David Hopkinson, remains engaged in long-term plans to either substantially redevelop St James’ Park or build a brand-new stadium altogether, alongside the construction of a state-of-the-art training complex.

Bringing in additional investment allows Newcastle to raise hundreds of millions in fresh equity to accelerate those builds, sharing the heavy financial lifting.

After a difficult summer that saw stars like Bruno Guimaraes, Sandro Tonali and Anthony Gordon depart to help balance the books, developing Newcastle’s infrastructure and off-pitch revenue streams is the only sustainable way to compete with Europe's elite.

Since original consortium member Amanda Staveley sold her shares and left the board in 2024, ownership of the Magpies has been split between just two parties: PIF holds an 84 per cent majority stake, while the London-based Reuben family - represented on the board by Jamie Reuben, via RB Sports & Media - owns the remaining 16 per cent.

Issuing new shares to cover a 25 per cent stake will dilute both PIF and potentially the Reubens proportionally, leaving PIF with comfortably over 60 per cent of the club and still overall control.

#908. Why electrification is the climate game changer we need

From EVs and electric buses on the road, heat pumps warming homes and solar panels powering appliances, the shift to electrifying tech is already in full swing. But what exactly does "electrification" mean?

Electrification isn't just a buzzword, it's a lever that could slash energy bills while reducing the world's dependency on coal, oil and gas. Which also means significantly slashing the heat-trapping CO2 emissions that are linked to flooding and extreme heat around the world.

If fuel-importing countries "speed up the electrification of their economies considerably" they could knock more than $400 billion (€357 billion) off their energy import bills by 2035 compared with 2025 levels. That is according to a recent analysis by the International Energy Agency, which also found that such an acceleration could mean the world needs 18 million fewer barrels of oil per day.

In a nutshell, electrification means replacing technologies that burn fossil fuels such as oil and gas with electric alternatives. That means switching from diesel cars to electric vehicles (EVs), turning off gas heating and using electricity to power heat pumps.

But the way the electricity running these things is generated is also important. In theory, an EV using power created in a coal-heavy electricity grid could be worse for the climate than a car running on gas.

Electricity derived from renewable energy sources such as solar, wind or hydropower on the other hand produces clean power.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The booming EV market is the fastest-growing electrification sector. Globally, one in four cars sold in 2025 was electric and since 2020, international sales have increased by almost 600%.

Nonetheless, electricity only covers about 20% of final energy use in the wider global economy, including that used in businesses, factories and people's homes.

It would need to supply more than half of all power by 2050 if we are to avoid runaway heating and the more intense and extreme weather events connected to a hotter climate.

Some industries and activities are harder to electrify than others. While it's relatively easy to switch to EVs and decarbonize buildings, some industries such as petrochemicals and steel use fossil fuels as raw materials to make products like plastics, fertilizer, detergent or steel.

In addition, while heat pumps work well for low-temperature needs, they can't replace the temperatures needed in steelmaking or cement production.

The World Resources Institute, an independent research organization, recommends hydrogen, synthetic fuels or other low-carbon alternatives as more viable options than electrification in cases such as ocean shipping and aviation.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In addition to cutting down on greenhouse gas emissions resulting in cleaner air and limiting global heating, electrification is also more efficient and cheaper in the long run.

A combustion engine in a car wastes as much as 80% of its fuel energy, mostly to turn it into heat. Only about 20% is converted to actually move the car. Electric motors, on the other hand, convert about 80% of electrical energy into motion.

As the World Resources Institute points out, running all appliances on electricity will increase electricity consumption. Yet total energy costs are likely to be lower, even if electricity becomes more expensive.

As electricity needs grow due to the rapid expansion of AI, data centers and the overall shift to a more electrified world, outpaced grids struggle to keep up. This is increasingly holding back the energy transition, delaying the rollout of additional renewable generation, storage capacity and electrified demand.

According to the International Energy Agency, annual grid investment has to increase by about 50% by 2030 from today's $400 billion.

There's also a major mismatch between how long it takes to set up new grid infrastructure (five to 15 years), compared to renewable energy projects (one to five years), and EV charging infrastructure (one to two years).

Experts say we need smarter grids that support a two-way flow of electricity while remaining secure, stable and able to keep up with higher demand as electrification intensifies.

#905. Enzo Maresca backs ‘winner’ Erling Haaland and says there is ‘no panic’ over Man City slump

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The Italian said that ‘a few weeks ago Haaland was dancing’ and insisted that City’s poor run has not affected his players’ belief

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Manchester City manager Enzo Maresca has downplayed concerns about his team’s togetherness and insisted he is not worried about star striker Erling Haaland following downcast post-match interviews.

City had won 11 of their first 12 matches in all competitions this season but have suffered an alarming downturn in form, only winning two of their last seven games.

Talisman Haaland has also suffered a slump at the same time, scoring just one goal in five games, and cut a morose figure when he was interviewed after a battling 2-2 draw against Napoli in the Champions League on Tuesday.

However, Maresca has insisted their poor run and the Norwegian’s demeanour are not cause for concern.

He said: “I think Erling is a winner. It's normal that he's not happy when we don't win games but not just Erling, everyone.

“Remember just a few weeks ago he was dancing inside the pitch. You can write and think many different things.

“Erling is upset. I'm upset because we're not winning games. But this is our job, this is football. That's why I need to maintain the balance.

“He's a nine. They live day by day for goals and winning games. If they don't score or win games they're upset. So I don't think that affects his game but for sure he's not happy not winning games, but everyone is on the same page.”

Asked whether it has been business as usual in training, he said: “He has been good. Yes, normal like since day one. Again, a few weeks ago he was dancing inside the pitch, he was dancing in training. He's happy. It's normal that results affect the mood, that's why we need to win games.

“But I don't see any problem at all with Erling.”

The Italian insisted that “transition takes time” and added: “For me, it's completely normal, I'm completely relaxed, no panic at all. I understand that we need to win games because it's our business but for me, it's all normal.”

Asked whether their string of poor results, which includes a 10-game run without a clean sheet, had affected players’ confidence, he said: “For sure, when you don't win games, it's not the ideal situation. But we won games at the beginning. We have also seven or eight new players that need to be used to winning games, so it's just a process.”

City face another significant test as they visit league leaders Arsenal, who are six points ahead, on Sunday.

Maresca was insistent that City were not lacking in belief ahead of their trip to the defending champions, saying: “I think we have already shown this season that we are able to win important games, to win away. I don't see any reason why we are not able to win there.”

#904. Borussia Dortmund's Felix Nmecha and the question of religion

Felix Nmecha's "Crowns down" celebration has drawn criticism from a Borussia Dortmund fan club, reopening debate over faith, inclusion and religious messaging in football.

Felix Nmecha's renewed use of the "Crowns down celebration" — where a crown is pretended to be removed from someone's head and placed at Jesus' feet — has sparked a reaction from Borussia Dortmund's official supporters' group.

"Faith does not justify exclusion. Faith does not justify division. Borussia Dortmund is a club for everyone," read a statement after the Bundesliga club beat Elversberg, a game in which Nmecha scored twice. Nmecha's first documented "Crowns down celebration" was at the 2026 World Cup, for which "The King's Return" campaign was launched.

"In the past, the the Borussia Dortmund supporters club has deliberately refrained from commenting on sports-related issues and the athletic performance of individual players. We remain committed to this approach," the statement continued.

"However, when it comes to our club's values, discrimination, and the question of what view of humanity is fostered within and around Borussia Dortmund, we cannot and will not remain silent."

The fan club states their issue is not with Nmecha being a devout Christian, but rather his public support for "The King's Return" campaign, which the supporters club said "gives us cause to reassess the situation."

This campaign, according to research by German public broadcaster ARD in the summer of 2026, was designed by the "Ballers in God" (BIG) network. BIG was founded in 2015 by footballer John Bostock, a devout Christian who wanted to create a community where professional footballers could strengthen each other in their faith, pray together, and read the Bible. In over a decade since, the BIG community has grown to nearly 800,000 followers on Instagram.

Nmecha issued a response on social media not long afterwards, writing:

"I've been told that my most recent goal celebration has led to some misunderstandings," Nmecha wrote.

"My message was never intended to spread intolerance, discrimination, or hatred in any form. As Christians, our message is one of love and respect for every person—regardless of where someone comes from, what they believe in, or what worldview they hold."

Reports suggest that both the board at Dortmund and Germany head coach Jürgen Klopp will speak to Nmecha on the matter in the coming days.

The fan club say their criticism is "directed at religious networks that, under the guise of faith, promote a worldview in which people are devalued or marginalized because of their sexual orientation, gender identity, lifestyle, or personal choices... When religious beliefs are used to deny people their dignity or equality, that is where our tolerance for intolerance ends."

Here, they are referring to the recent ARD investigation. That work revealed the homepage for "The King's Return" campaign featured a link to a live counseling chat run by US-based evangelical nonprofit Groundwire. During the investigations, counselors told reporters that abortion is "Satan's plan" and that homosexuality is a sin.

Borussia Dortmund's statement of core values commits the club to diversity, human rights, and inclusion regardless of gender, sexual orientation, faith, or background. The club's largest and most influential fan group also promotes progressive, anti-fascist, and inclusive values. It is also part of a wider fan landscape in Germany where club members are more involved in club decisions than in many other countries. This was evidenced when the club signed a deal with arms manufacturer Rheinmetall two years ago and in the case of Nmecha as well. When the midfielder signed for Dortmund in 2023, many of the club's fans protested because the player had previously shared or liked several transphobic and homophobic posts on his Instagram account. In response, Nmecha deleted some posts and instead issued a statement emphasizing "I do not discriminate against anyone."

Article 4 of German Basic Law guarantees that each individual is allowed to decide how strongly, why and which god to believe in. In football, players cannot display political, religious, or personal slogans, statements, or images on their jerseys, undershirts, or gear. However, physical gestures are allowed so long as they don't delay the game or antagonize the crowd.

The use of physical religious gestures has history in sports, as professor Paul Putz described in his book "The Spirit of the Game: American Christianity and Big-Time Sports". Putz describes how the the pioneers of the Christian athlete movement realized they: "could influence others to Christian ideals more effectively on the field than in the pulpit."

And yet, such gestures can also be at odds with the atmosphere of modern sports arenas, particularly football. In their book "Sports and Christianity: Historical and Contemporary Perspectives", Nick J. Watson and Andrew Parker explain how modern sport has become a substitute for traditional faith.

"Sport seduces the teeming 'global village'; it is the new opiate of the masses; it is one of the great modern experiences … Sport, for many, has replaced religion as a source of emotional catharsis and spiritual passion," they wrote.

With the 26-year-old Nmecha a key player for both club and country, the conversation around faith and football looks set to continue for some time yet.

Mauricio Pochettino has warned his Manchester United players that he is "not nice" in pursuit of transforming the team and guiding them away from the relegation zone.

"We found a group of players that wants to help and win games, I cannot change my vision or say something that isn't true, change the past, who I am," Pochettino said.

"Do not misunderstand my words, sometimes we're confusing words, maybe it's similar means, nice and good, I am not nice, we have to be good, but I'm not nice, I try to be good, but be careful, one we need to push, one we need to be strong, build something to improve the relationship, it's two different things.

Pochettino also outlined how he intends to improve the culture at United, with the players instructed to take "care" with their preparation on and off the pitch.

"In only a few training sessions, they're working with the intensity, they cannot be perfect in three days, a few weeks, we're thinking long term, today we need to win, but thinking to win the game and prepare for tomorrow, working up the progression, the club has to fight for big things. The more things change, the more they stay the same - Watford is an unmanageable club

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Some things are certain in life; death, taxes and Watford sacking another head coach.

At 11:51am on Sunday morning, the news everyone expected had arrived and Alessio Dionisi was relieved of his duties as Watford head coach after five months in charge, following a dismal 4-0 away defeat to Sheffield United, which left the club just one place above the relegation zone.

It was the latest in a series of lifeless performances from a Watford side that have looked ill-equipped for Championship football from the moment the season started.

Now, at a time where Watford need Championship experience more than ever, owner Gino Pozzo has turned to former Romania boss Edward Iordanescu, a man that has had 13 jobs in 15 years, never managed more than 60 games at any team and most importantly, never played or coached in England or in one of Europe’s major leagues.

Given Watford’s reputation with head coaches, many would joke Iordanescu’s appointment sounds like a match made in heaven.

For Hornets fans, though, it’s an act of desperation from a club that has no plan, structure or hope.

In truth, Dionisi is the latest in a series of head coaches who have been let down by owner Pozzo, chairman Scott Duxbury and technical director Gianluca Nani, who seem incapable of building a squad or supporting a head coach.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Things could have been so different for the Italian, because at the start of the season, there was clearly something there. Watford were excellent in their opening day win over Southampton - playing with real flair and intensity in the first half - and followed that up with draws against Wrexham and West Ham. It was clear the players respected the Italian.

However, the warning signs were already there. In the summer, Dionisi and supporters were told that Watford would prioritise experienced players in the transfer market. None arrived.

Nestory Irankunda, Imran Louza and Giorgi Chakvetadze - three key players - were sold and not replaced, with Watford starting the season with just two centre-backs on the club’s books and two fit central midfielders.

The Italian sounded increasingly exasperated as his calls for reinforcements fell on deaf ears until the final few days of the window, where Watford eventually panicked and brought in Stephy Mavididi, Soumaila Coulibaly and Branimir Mlacic on loan. Myron Boadu and Michail Antonio arrived on free transfers.

Most of those players arrived unfit and come September, Dionisi was struggling to fill the bench as injuries took hold. The Italian never really recovered from embarrassing defeats to Burnley and Cardiff City, deploying a back five in recent weeks as he attempted to make the Golden Boys harder to beat.

Quite frankly, Watford are unmanageable. Not even Pep Guardiola would be successful at Vicarage Road, because no head coach is given the opportunity to implement a style of play when they have to contend with poor recruitment, a leadership vacuum and a dressing room with seemingly poor attitudes.

Rob Edwards was promised he'd be backed in the transfer market come hell or high water by chairman Duxbury in the summer of 2022. Most of the signings he received didn't fit his system and he was sacked within two months of the season starting.

After Edwards, Slaven Bilic thought he'd be able to sign players he wanted in the January transfer window. He received Joao Ferreira and Henrique Araujo - both of whom never looked suited to Championship football – as well as Ryan Porteous, Wesley Hoedt and Britt Assombalonga. Bilic was gone by March.

Then came Chris Wilder, who repeatedly called out the poor attitude within the dressing room and wasn't given a contract extension when his deal expired in the summer of 2023. After the wheels came off under Valerian Ismael, Tom Cleverley was promoted to head coach in 2024 and despite a thin squad, united the players and fans, having been a popular player at Vicarage Road during his playing days.

Once again, though, January arrived and Cleverley didn't get the options he so dearly needed, meaning Watford's form dropped off and he was sacked, somewhat harshly, at the end of the season.

Just last season, the popular Javi Gracia returned for a second spell in charge and had Watford in the play-off spots by January. He was promised additions, but none were forthcoming and ultimately the Spaniard decided the job wasn't worth his time. Gracia resigned, returning to Spain to spend time with his family.

In short, it's time the Watford ownership took a long, hard look at themselves, rather than the head coach. Has Iordanescu been appointed because no one sensible will take it? Any head coach worth his salt in England - and possibly now Italy, too - knows what they’re walking into.

In a recent interview with Roy Moore from the 1881 Movement, Pozzo tried shifting accountability for the club’s downfall, which can be traced back to the FA Cup Final in 2019. Since then, numerous decisions have, in the eyes of supporters, led to the erosion of the club's identity - fans have had enough.

Empty statements, the constant churn of players and head coaches, and what appears to be a lack of any real structure or plan - supporters are fed up.

The fact Watford closed their Under-21 setup, downgraded their academy and sold off the women's team this summer was a huge source of disappointment for fans, too, given the club’s rich history of bringing players through their youth system.

Unless there is a sudden change of approach overnight, Watford are only heading one way and that's down to League 1.

#900. Megaspeed and the battle to go high-end Nvidia chips into China

Jensen Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy has shone a light on Megaspeed, the company she worked for. It is under investigation in the US for smuggling Nvidia chips into China, which it denies.

As Nvidia, one of the world's most valuable companies, grapples with CEO Jensen Huang's romantic relationship with an alleged Chinese spy, attention is turning to the much smaller company she worked for.

Alice H., the alleged spy, worked as an executive for Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center and AI computing company. It manages data center access, including for some major Chinese tech firms such as Alibaba.

According to Megaspeed's website as of November 2026, the company advertises itself as an "Nvidia cloud partner", saying it provides "computing power product services covering Nvidia's entire GPU product line." GPU stands for Graphic Processing Unit, a specialized electronic circuit that are in high demand for artificial intelligence (AI) applications, because they are designed to handle high numbers of parallel mathematical calculations. Megaspeed says it provides access for clients to Nvidia's advanced GB200 NVL72 ​computing system.

This type of firm is often referred to as a "neocloud". It buys Nvidia chips and computing power and then rents it out — in this case, at multiple sites across south-east Asia, to different companies. The US has set up strict export controls to prevent that Nvidia's high-performance chips end up in China, because it sees China as a competitor in the global AI race. It also does not want data centers made up of Nvidia chips to be owned by Chinese companies. It does, however, tolerate that data center compute with Nvidia chips be rented out to Chinese companies like Alibaba, and occasionally allows the export of Nvidia chips for specific purposes.

Megaspeed has bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia's products in recent years and has been accused of breaching US export controls to divert Nvidia chips into China.

In December 2025, Bloomberg reported that the "once-obscure" Megaspeed had become the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in all of south-east Asia and that the US government was investigating its ownership structure and whether or not it was smuggling Nvidia chips into China.

At the same time, Singapore police began an investigation into whether or not Megaspeed had "violated local laws" without specifying which ones. Those investigations are believed to be still ongoing.

On December 23, 2025, Megaspeed strenuously denied any wrongdoing in a statement — which still appears as the first page for visitors to the company's website as of November 2026.

"There has been no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities, and this demonstrates that we are a compliant and legitimate company," it said. "We operate fully within the bounds of all applicable export control regulations and maintain the highest standards of legal and ethical conduct."

The US government investigation began in 2024. The Commerce Department initially began looking into Megaspeed, but the US Justice Department has since taken over. According to the New York Times, this switch came about after an Nvidia executive directly contacted the Commerce Department about the investigation.

Megaspeed was founded in 2015 and was originally called 7Road International. It changed its name to Megaspeed in March 2023. It is owned by the Singapore-registered Swiftdata, which was set up in October 2023.

Its rise in prominence coincided with a sharp increase in assets, which increased from $33 million in 2023 to $3 billion in 2024.

Alice H., the woman accused of being a Chinese spy, had an affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. She is widely seen as an influential figurehead at Megaspeed. She also served as the company's managing director of Megaspeed for eight months in 2023.

The Financial Times reported on Monday that Alice H. leveraged her close access to Jensen Huang and Nvidia to pitch AI chips deals to Chinese investors.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The newspaper said that in early 2025, Alice H. sought investment in China for a data center project in south-east Asia, and cited their easy access to Nvidia chips and close relationship with Alibaba.

Alibaba lent money to Megaspeed in June 2024, via subsidiaries. It has remained Megaspeed's largest client, according to reporting by the Financial Times.

In December 2025, Nvidia said its own inquiry into Megaspeed had found no evidence of chips being diverted and that the company was fully owned and operated outside of China, with no Chinese shareholders. The company told Bloomberg at the time that it had visited Megaspeed's facilities on multiple occasions and had seen nothing untoward.

Megaspeed is one of several companies accused of smuggling Nvidia's chips into China or finding ways to give Chinese companies access to them.

Nvidia's high-performance chips are seen as essential for companies looking for the most advanced form of supercomputing to use and develop various AI applications.

Back in 2022, the Biden Administration began severely restricting the sale of the US's most advanced chips to China, part of the two countries' growing rivalry to achieve AI dominance.

However, an illegal smuggling and underground network was soon set up, with many vendors operating to get the chips into China and selling them on to companies there.

In December 2025, US authorities shut down the operations of Hao Global, a US-based shell company with links to China which plead guilty to smuggling Nvidia chips to China.

In June 2026, Taiwanese government agencies raided the offices of Super Micro Computer as part of an investigation into the smuggling of Nvidia chips to China.

While export restrictions have been eased significantly under the Trump administration, there are still significant blocks and restrictions on the most advanced Nvidia chips.

In December 2025, the Trump administration approved several Chinese companies to buy or handle advanced Nvidia H200 chips, a move that sparked significant concern among the US security establishment.

However, that deal has not led to a significant flow of Nvidia chips moving legally to China, amid strict US licencing controls and official reluctance from Beijing to publicly promote Nvidia chips to the detriment of its own alternatives.

#899. How Singapore has turned a nation into a smart-city testing ground

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Sandy Ong is a freelance writer based in Singapore.

As a city state, Singapore can often implement digital infrastructure projects more quickly than cities in much larger countries.Credit: Roslan Rahman/AFP via Getty Images

Singapore is one of the world’s smallest countries by land area, spanning roughly 744 km2. Yet as a technologically advanced city, it consistently punches above its weight. Earlier this year, Singapore placed ninth in the IMD Smart City Index 2026 — the highest-ranked city in Asia — noted for the strong trust its residents had in the government’s use of digital technologies. The index, published by IMD, a Swiss research institute, uses citizen surveys to evaluate cities’ physical and digital infrastructure across areas such as health and safety, governance and mobility.

The centralized government of Singapore, as a city-state, allows it to coordinate nationwide digital infrastructure projects with a speed and consistency that would be difficult in larger, more fragmented countries, says Orlando Woods, director of Singapore Management University’s Urban Institute, which studies urban growth and governance. “It has a single layer of government,” says Woods. “To make decisions and implement things is just so much easier.”

Singapore was among the earliest countries to digitize public services and integrate technological advancement across multiple government sectors, including health care, public services, transport and urban planning. In 2014, it announced these strategies as part of its ‘Smart Nation’ initiative, a major part of which is Virtual Singapore — one of the world’s first national-scale ‘digital twins’.

A dynamic, 3D replica of Singapore, the Virtual Singapore model encompasses everything from real-time air-quality statistics to population data and traffic flow. Comprising more than 100 TB of data collected from aerial photography, remote-sensing technologies and the thousands of sensors installed across the island, it is continually updated with new geospatial, environmental and infrastructure data.

Local authorities use Virtual Singapore to inform urban-planning decisions, such as identifying the best rooftops for solar panels. It is also used in planning public-safety measures, including modelling flood impacts, drafting disaster-response plans and pinpointing potential risk areas for disease outbreaks, such as dengue fever. Some features and data sets are freely available to researchers, businesses and residents.

The captain was in the last year of his deal but United have triggered the option to extend his contract for a further 12 months

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Manchester United have triggered their option to extend captain Bruno Fernandes’ contract for another year to keep him at Old Trafford to 2028.

The 32-year-old was in the last year of his deal, but United had built in the chance to add a further 12 months, which they have now done.

United chief executive Omar Berrada said last week that the club was holding talks to give Fernandes a new deal but the midfielder promptly said he had put them on hold to concentrate on getting results.

“The club offered me a new contract so I think that, from their side, shows that they ⁠want me to stay,” he said then.

Fernandes has attracted interest in the past from Saudi Pro-League clubs and from Galatasaray but has chosen to stay at United.

If United had not taken up the option, Fernandes could have discussed a summer move to a foreign club from 1 January.

A 2020 signing from Sporting CP, he has scored 115 goals in 343 games for United, including the first two goals of new manager Mauricio Pochettino’s reign in a 2-2 draw with his former club on Wednesday.

However, he missed training on Friday due to a virus and is a doubt for Saturday’s match against Brentford.

United have three other senior players out of contract next summer, in Luke Shaw, Harry Maguire and Lisandro Martinez, though they also have an option to extend the Argentinian’s deal for a further year.

Mikel Arteta opted against giving a definitive answer over whether David Raya will be fit for Arsenal’s mammoth clash with Manchester City this weekend - but indicated there was hope of the No 1’s return.

Raya hurt his shoulder in a seemingly innocuous collision with Newcastle striker William Osula in Arsenal’s 2-2 draw at St James’ Park last weekend, but the Spaniard escaped serious injury with Arteta confirming earlier in the week that he would not require surgery.

Having initially feared the Spaniard would have been “out for months”, Raya has already returned to training and is in the picture for a return to the starting line-up.

He nevertheless was not fit for the Champions League draw with Borussia Dortmund in midweek and Arteta could not confirm if Sunday’s visit of City would come too soon for the 31-year-old.

Questioned on his involvement, Arteta replied: “I don't know... we have a few more hours. We're trying to get everybody back.”

Arteta was then asked if there was a “ray of hope” if Raya might play, to which he said: “Yeah.”

Raya was instrumental in Arsenal ending a 22-year wait for a Premier League title last season has carried his stellar form into the current campaign, boasting seven clean sheets in 10 matches prior to Arsenal’s trip to Newcastle.

He was deputised by Kepa Arrizabalaga for the Dortmund clash and Arteta backed his goalkeeping understudy as a more than adequate alternative.

“The experience that Kepa has is incredible, and for the teams he's been involved, the trophies that he's won,” he added.

#895. Neuer injury gives Urbig chance to shape Bayern and Germany future

Manuel Neuer's latest injury gives Jonas Urbig a run of games in Bayern's goal. Marc-André ter Stegen remains Germany’s No. 1, but Urbig now has a chance to strengthen his case for the future.

It's no secret that getting playing time is important to the development of any professional footballer – especially if your aspiration is to become the first-choice goalkeeper for your country . For most national team coaches, only a keeper who is playing regularly for his club merits consideration.

Unsurprisingly, Germany coach Jürgen Klopp is no exception. While he did give Urbig – the backup keeper at Bayern – two starts in his first international break as national team boss, for the upcoming UEFA Nations League matches against Serbia and the Netherlands, Marc-André ter Stegen remains the undisputed No. 1.

But when Klopp gave ter Stegen the nod, Urbig was still spending most of his time on the bench in Munich. But this is set to change after Bayern's recent Bundesliga win over Mainz. The 40-year-old Manuel Neuer asked to be subbed off just before halftime, complaining of severe pain in his right foot.

An examination revealed that Neuer has sustained a partial tendon tear in the foot.

"An injury never comes at the right time, but it's part of the game," Neuer wrote on Instagram.

"I've been through this before, and I'll get through this one too. From now on: full focus on recovery. Until then, I will support the boys on the pitch wherever I can."

A partial tendon tear usually results in a layoff of six to 12 weeks, depending on the severity of the injury. Given that Neuer's foot already has some pre-existing damage from previous injuries, his recovery could take even longer.

Although Urbig is now the de-facto first-choice keeper for Bayern, he will still have to bide his time in the national team as understudy to ter Stegen. However, there is a general consensus that someday, Urbig will also become Germany's No. 1. With Neuer's contract running out in the summer, the chance to truly make the Bayern goal his own appears likely in the not-too-distant future.

The match on Saturday was Neuer's 550th in the Bundesliga and he also became the oldest player in a league match in Bayern's history when he took the pitch aged 40 years and 225 days. In other words, he can't go on forever.

One of his most famous predecessors in the Bayern goal has already called on him to draw a line under his highly successful career.

"I would tell him: 'Call it a day, Manu!' You have given an incredible amount to football, you have won everything, and you don't have to prove anything to anyone anymore," Sepp Maier, a member of West Germany's 1974 World Cup winning team told Sport1.

At some point, the now 82-year-old Maier noted, there comes a moment "when your body no longer behaves the way you want it to. And even a Manuel Neuer cannot stave off that moment."

For now, with ter Stegen playing regularly and performing well for Ajax, Germany coach Klopp is under no pressure to make a change. However, the 34-year-old former Barcelona keeper has, like Neuer, become quite injury-prone in recent years. Whenever he's needed, Urbig will be more than happy to seize his opportunity.

#891. Israeli fans set to attend Bournemouth clash after Maccabi Tel-Aviv supporter ban controversy

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Maccabi Tel-Aviv fans were banned from attending their side’s Europa League clash with Aston Villa last season

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Supporters of Israeli side Hapoel Beer-Sheva are expected to be permitted to travel for their Europa League fixture against Bournemouth in January.

A previous decision to ban fans of fellow Israeli team Maccabi Tel Aviv from a Europa League game at Aston Villa last November caused controversy, with the move openly denounced by the then Prime Minister, Sir Keir Starmer.

That call prompted an investigation by the Independent Office for Police Conduct in August into former West Midlands Police chief constable Craig Guildford over allegations of gross misconduct.

Currently, Dorset Police are planning on the basis that Hapoel travelling fans will attend the 28 January match, though security assessments and intelligence reviews remain ongoing with two months remaining before kick-off.

Dorset Police’s Gold Commander for the game, Assistance Chief Constable Lindsay Dudfield, stated: "We are continuing to work closely with partners to ensure we can facilitate a safe and enjoyable match for all concerned.

"As with previous fixtures, we regularly review the latest information and intelligence to inform our policing operation and the resources required. All intelligence received will be carefully verified before informing any decisions we make around our plans.

"We are also in regular contact with interested parties in our communities to ensure we communicate clearly with them around what to expect and our policing plans for the fixture, as well as listening to any concerns they may have."

The match between Villa and Maccabi last year required the deployment of over 700 police officers.

On Thursday, Hapoel’s encounter with Besiktas was interrupted following altercations involving police and supporters of the Turkish side. The fixture had been relocated to Georgia following recommendations from Turkish authorities, having originally been scheduled as a home game for Besiktas.

Reports indicated that Besiktas supporters displayed Palestinian flags alongside pro-Palestine banners before unrest broke out, forcing play to be stopped. Georgia’s interior ministry stated that 16 individuals were arrested and three officers suffered injuries.

The Turkish football federation described the actions of Georgian police towards Besiktas supporters as "unacceptable".

Denouncing the unrest and violence during the fixture, European football's governing body Uefa released a statement saying: "Violence, aggression, hatred and any form of provocative, discriminatory or extremist behaviour have no place in football.

"Uefa competitions are founded on the principles of respect, fair play, integrity and safety. The events witnessed at the above-mentioned matches run counter to these fundamental values and to Uefa’s objective, enshrined in its Statutes, of ensuring that football matches are played in a spirit of peace, mutual respect and sporting fairness."

Uefa confirmed that an ethics and disciplinary inspector has been designated to investigate the incident.
