It might get worse before it gets better for Manchester City fans

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Never be the man after ‘the man’, the saying goes. Football history is stippled with cautionary tales of managers who followed an all-time great, only to discover that they were doomed from the very beginning.

Manchester City have stumbled through a bruising autumn under Enzo Maresca, uncharacteristically so. It is impossible not to wonder if the Etihad Stadium is experiencing its very own version of Manchester United's 2013/14.

For a decade, Pep Guardiola bent English football to his will, turning Man City into a relentless, trophy-winning machine. Succeeding a figure who loomed so large over the east side of Manchester was never going to be straightforward. Few, though, expected the drop-off to feel quite so jarring, or quite so familiar.

David Moyes arrived at Old Trafford in 2013 tasked with prolonging Sir Alex Ferguson’s dynasty, meanwhile Maresca was handed a three-year contract this summer to keep Guardiola’s juggernaut in motion. Four months into the job, the steering wheel is juddering uncomfortably.

Man City’s recent results make for grim reading compared to the standards set over the last 10 years. A 3-1 defeat away at Nottingham Forest earlier this month was double-take worthy, before Saturday’s 1-1 home draw with Fulham - rescued only by an Elliot Anderson volley - saw them lose yet more ground in the Premier League title race.

On Tuesday night in the Champions League, Man City needed an 86th-minute Rayan Cherki strike just to salvage a 2-2 draw at home to Napoli, currently eighth in Serie A and 14 points off the pace.

Ahead of Sunday’s trip to league leaders Arsenal, Maresca's men look a shadow of the team that so recently struck fear into the Gunners' title hopes.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Predictably, the question of Maresca’s future has already begun to take on more of a 'when rather than if' feel. Reports emerged this week suggesting the Italian is fighting to save his job barely a third of the way into his debut Etihad campaign. Sack talk at Manchester City circulating at all, never mind in November, speaks volumes about how rapidly things have changed.

There are parallels between Man City’s recent slump and Moyes’ 10-month spell across town, too. Like Moyes, Maresca inherited a squad undergoing significant churn after an era of dominance.

To bridge that gap, City made a throng of big summer purchases, bringing in additions such as Elliot Anderson, Enzo Fernandez, Iliman Ndiaye and Ayyoub Bouaddi.

Much like Moyes’ integration of Marouane Fellaini and Juan Mata into a fading champion side, Maresca’s new-look Man City feels disjointed - caught between Guardiola’s positional automatisms and a new manager’s attempt to stamp his own authority on the dressing room.

That disconnect quickly becomes apparent when the team aren't getting results, breeding doubt among players accustomed to certainty and success. All of which begs the question: was Maresca always doomed to fail?

Following Guardiola was always going to be an exercise in managing impossible expectations while rebuilding in real time. Perhaps the Etihad hierarchy believed their structure would insulate Guardiola’s successor from the same sort of post-Ferguson collapse that swallowed Moyes' efforts - which in hindsight weren't all that bad. Perhaps there is a lesson there for Man City chiefs to heed.

#889. Controversial kinship: From colonial rule to the Holocaust?

Hitler once called Eastern Europe "Germany's India." A new exhibition examines the links between colonialism and Nazism, and the bitter debate over where comparisons illuminate history and where they fall short.

Racial hierarchy, dehumanization, concentration camps, settler expansion in the name of "living space," collective punishment and mass violence: At first glance, the continuities between colonial and Nazi violence appear obvious. In 1941, Nazi dictator Adolf Hitler himself compared Eastern Europe to "Germany's India" after the British colonial model, declaring that "like the English, we shall rule this empire with a handful of men."

But the extent to which Nazism was shaped by the age of empire and whether the two systems of violence can even be compared remains the subject of intense debate.

This is particularly true in Germany, where the fear is often expressed that any comparison risks relativizing or minimizing Nazi crimes, and particularly the Holocaust. Others have argued that the intense focus on the Nazi era has, at least in part, come at the expense of a meaningful reckoning with Germany's colonial history.

"I do think this is nonsense," says Stephan Malinowski, a Professor of Modern European History at the University of Edinburgh. "If it were true, then all other colonial countries who are not discussing the Holocaust, like Great Britain for example, or France or Spain or Portugal, they would then supposedly be very, very attentive to colonial crimes and to colonial history, which it seems to me is not the case."

"Controversial Kinship: Colonial and National Socialist Violence," a new exhibition at the German Historical Museum in Berlin curated by Malinowski, does not aim to settle the debate but to tell its story.

The exhibition begins with a hippopotamus-hide whip used in African colonies displayed alongside a canister of Zyklon B, the poison used in Nazi gas chambers. The juxtaposition highlights the contrast between colonial violence and the industrialized mass murder of the Holocaust.

Yet it also points to connections: Whips were used in Nazi concentration camps, while Fascist Italy deployed chemical weapons against civilians and soldiers during its invasion of Ethiopia (then Abyssinia) in 1935-36.

In the 1930s, anti-colonial thinkers from India to the Caribbean argued that colonialism and fascism were two sides of the same coin. "There is nothing new or original about the blustering exploits of Hitler and Mussolini," observed the Trinidadian journalist and Pan-Africanist George Padmore in 1938. "They have all been used before by the British in their efforts to obtain the subjection of less powerfully armed and more industrially backward people."

European colonial rule was marked by the ruthless exploitation of people and resources, often enforced through extreme violence. In "The Origins of Totalitarianism" (1951), German-American philosopher Hannah Arendt argued that colonial territories served as laboratories for racial ideologies and practices of domination that could be applied beyond the legal constraints of Europe. Arendt described how these later "boomeranged" back into Europe and helped shape totalitarian politics in distinct and unprecedented form.

The Congo Free State, King Leopold II of Belgium's private colony from 1885 to 1908, became notorious for its extreme brutality, as colonial authorities used executions, amputations and sexual violence to ensure rubber production quotas were met.

Forced labor was also central to Nazi rule, with millions of Poles, Ukrainians, Russians and others from the Soviet Union, and Jews, subjected to exploitation and "Vernichtung durch Arbeit" ("extermination through work"). Within a few years, the regime mobilized around 13 to 14 million forced laborers, a scale comparable to the transatlantic slave trade over more than three centuries. The Nazis sought to extract value from their victims at every stage, confiscating their property, exploiting their labor, and even harvesting gold teeth and hair from the dead.

While racism underpinned both colonial empires and Nazism, Malinowski says the goals were different. The colonial powers tended to present assimilation as a path to advancement, forcing colonized people to adopt European culture, serve imperial interests, and suggesting that a select, educated few could gain opportunities, for example at elite institutions such as Oxford or Cambridge. "This is definitely not something that the Nazi regime is offering to Poles or to Russians or let alone to Jews," added Malinowski.

"In terms of violence, colonial violence was just as extreme as Nazi violence. But Nazi violence was annihilatory and exterminatory compared to colonial violence in the colonies," says Edward Kissi, a historian at the School of Interdisciplinary Global Studies at the University of South Florida. He points to the example of how, unlike European colonial powers in Africa, the Nazis pursued the elimination of Black-Germans or peoples of African descent in Germany through forced sterilization. "Even in racism, colonial color-based racism and colonial anti-Jewish sentiments were fundamentally different from what the Nazis pursued."

On October 2, 1904, German General Lothar von Trotha issued the "Vernichtungsbefehl" ("extermination order") following the Herero uprising in German South West Africa (present-day Namibia). Historians generally attribute the order to a combination of racial ideology, a desire to terrorize the population into submission, and efforts to secure colonial control over land, labor and resources. Between 1904 and 1908, an estimated 60,000 to 80,000 Herero (around 80% of the population) and 10,000 (around half the population) Nama died.

One area where the exhibition draws no direct parallel is the industrialized killing carried out in Nazi death camps such as Belzec, Sobibor, Treblinka, and Auschwitz-Birkenau. "Where the two things really diverge is the Holocaust and is the systematic mass murder of the European Jews and it's murder for the very purpose of murder," explains Malinowski. The deportation of around 1,800 Jews from the Greek islands of Rhodes and Kos in July 1944 illustrates how Nazi persecution often defied military or economic logic. Even after the war was effectively lost, the community was transported to Auschwitz, where most were murdered immediately upon arrival.

The issue of the "singularity" of the Holocaust came to the fore during the 1980s "Historikerstreit" ("historians' dispute"). Historian Ernst Nolte argued that Nazism should be understood in the wider context of 20th-century political violence, and as a response to Bolshevik terror in particular. Critics accused him of downplaying German responsibility for Nazi crimes.

Since 2020, a renewed debate dubbed the "Historikerstreit 2.0" has focused on whether the Holocaust should be viewed as a unique reference point in German memory culture or be understood alongside the histories of colonialism, racism and empire. The dispute now is less about the legitimacy of comparison than about its implications.

The mass murder of tens of thousands of the Herero and Nama during four years of German colonial rule is now regarded as the first genocide of the 20th-century. But in 2016, Nama representatives walked out of talks after Germany's chief negotiator said what happened was "incomparable" to the Holocaust. The German government has since recognized the events as genocide "from today's perspective," but it has not yet accepted legal liability or agreed to pay formal reparations.

Martinican intellectual Aime Cesaire argued in "Discourse on Colonialism" (1950) that Europe condemned under Nazism forms of violence it had long accepted in its colonies. More than 70 years later, the exhibition opens amid renewed debates over the definition of settler colonialism and genocide, and the meaning of "never again," sharpened by Nicaragua's case against Germany at the International Court of Justice over Germany's support for Israel during the war in Gaza and its alleged failure to uphold its obligations under the Genocide Convention to prevent genocide.

These tensions are reflected in visitors' comments in the exhibition's epilogue, even though the exhibition itself does not address Israel or Palestine beyond a reference to Mohammed Amin al-Husseini, appointed Grand Mufti of Jerusalem in 1921.

Germany has unequivocally accepted responsibility for the Holocaust, which is front and center of the country's culture of remembrance.  However, Kissi likens Germany's apparent reluctance to reckon with its colonial history to debates in the US over slavery, in Cambodia over the Khmer Rouge, and in Turkey over the Armenian genocide. According to him, Germany's contemporary identity cannot be fully understood without examining its colonial history and the ways the Nazis appropriated and transformed aspects of that legacy.

"I think Germans and all other human beings who have experienced violent pasts and difficult pasts should be very careful not to delink or dissociate those facts from their present," Kissi said. "These are historical patterns. It is better to deal with these historical patterns and discomforts than to just fight them and then say this has absolutely nothing to do with German national identity."

"Controversial Kinship: Colonial and National Socialist Violence" is on show at the German Historical Museum until April 11, 2027.

#888. Ex-Iceland goalkeeper Ingvar Jonsson who was part of Euro 2016 squad that stunned England dies aged 37

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Iceland beating England in Euro 2016 is widely considered to be one of the biggest shocks in international football history

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Ingvar Jonsson, the former Iceland goalkeeper who was part of the squad that defeated England at the 2016 European Championship, has died at the age of 37.

His former club Víkingur announced his death on Thursday. The team did not provide a cause of death, although Jonsson had reportedly been diagnosed with cancer earlier this year.

In a statement, the Icelandic club said: "It is with great sorrow and deep sadness that we announce that our dear friend and teammate Ingvar Jonsson, goalkeeper for Víkingur, passed away on Wednesday, November 25, in the arms of his loved ones."

They added: "The club and all of Víkingur are thinking of his family and loved ones. We send them our deepest condolences."

Jonsson served as an unused substitute during Euro 2016, when Iceland created one of the greatest shocks in tournament history by knocking England out in the round of 16. The team were later eliminated by France in the quarter-finals.

Paying tribute on X, European football’s governing body Uefa wrote: "We extend our deepest condolences to Ingvar’s family, friends and former team-mates. Our thoughts are with them at this difficult time."

Jonsson earned eight international caps for Iceland, having made his first squad back in 2012. He had to wait another two years before making his first appearance for his country in a friendly against Belgium.

His final cap for Iceland came in 2019, but he continued to make the squad through until 2022.

His club career saw him start at Njardvik in his homeland before moving to Norwegian outfit IK Start in 2015. He would go on to play for Sandnes Ulf and Sandefjord prior to leaving Norway in 2018 to join Danish side Viborg.

After two years in Denmark, Jonsson returned to Iceland to play for Vikingur and remained at the club until his passing.

#886. Jamal Musiala suffers hamstring injury amid difficult spell for Bayern Munich star

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The midfielder will be out of action ‘until further notice’, according to the Bundesliga club

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Jamal Musiala will be sidelined “until further notice” after suffering a muscle injury to his right hamstring, in another setback for the 23-year-old.

Musiala has struggled with repeated injury issues over the last two years as well as a neurological condition which has received enormous scrutiny in recent weeks.

He suffered a muscle tear in April 2025 and began suffering from absence seizures, which cause a brief and sudden lapse in awareness, the same month, two months after signing a contract extension with Bayern Munich.

The condition was not made public knowledge until this summer, with Musiala experiencing two of these seizures during pre-season games. Absence seizures can be managed with daily medication, and other elite athletes, including England rugby player Tommy Freeman, have been able to continue professional sporting careers while experiencing the condition.

Over the same period Musiala has endured repeated injuries: he broke his fibula during the Club World Cup in 2025 and suffered a subsequent ankle injury, then had a metal plate removed from his foot after this summer’s World Cup.

He has only recently returned from an absence induced by a hamstring tear, coming off the bench against Koln in the Bundesliga after two months out. He made an appearance as a second-half substitute in Bayern’s surprise 2-1 defeat to Lille in the Champions League this week, but has now suffered another setback.

Bayern Munich announced on Friday: “FC Bayern’s medical department diagnosed Jamal Musiala with a muscle injury in his right thigh today. Musiala will be out until further notice. Get well soon, Jamal!”

How Bayern have handled Musiala’s neurological condition has been heavily criticised after highly-publicised comments by several members of the club’s hierarchy.

Former board chairman Karl-Heinz Rummenigge cast doubt on the midfielder’s future, saying the “hefty sums of money” Musiala is paid are “not justifiable any longer”, and honorary president Uli Hoeness suggested his contract - which now runs until 2030 - should be reviewed if his illness and injury record prevents him returning to top form.

The comments sparked backlash, with players’ union Fifpro saying it was “deeply concerned” by the “pressure” placed on Musiala by such public remarks.

Stand-in captain Joshua Kimmich said after the Lille defeat: “What I don’t understand is the way this is being communicated in public. It must never happen that the burden is placed on a player. The club is obviously the top priority and bigger than a player, but it’s not bigger than a person. That’s an absolute no-go and it is not Bayern-like.”

Bayern have a raft of top players out with injuries including star striker Harry Kane, who tore ligaments in his ankle during the Koln game, as well as Michael Olise, Manuel Neuer, Luis Diaz and Serge Gnabry.

They sit second in the Bundesliga and 15th in the Champions League group phase table.

#885. Germany slips in climate protection rankings as other countries make gains

Record renewable energy growth is driving climate progress in some countries, but Germany and many major emitters are falling behind.

Germany has slipped down the climate action ranking for the third consecutive year, with the former green leader now being outperformed by Brazil, Colombia and Romania.

In its worst performance since 2019, the country fell to place 25 and received a "medium" rating overall on the yearly Climate Change Performance Index (CCPI), which assesses efforts to curb global warming in 64 countries plus the European Union.

Still, "a number of countries have been making good progress for years," said Jan Burck, CCPI lead author, in a statement. Denmark is leading the way across all four categories assessed — energy use, greenhouse gas emissions, renewable energy and national climate policy. A total of 15 states, including Lithuania, Chile, and Morocco, received an overall "high" rating, which is two more than last year.

The European Union also moved up a spot, while Hungary jumped 21 places after the ousting of former prime minister Viktor Orban's government, which had repeatedly vetoed EU climate plans, dismissing them as a "utopian fantasy."

The top three positions on the CCPI remained vacant again this year, as no country has yet done enough to meet global climate goals aimed at preventing worsening weather extremes and climate damage.

"We are seeing a striking contrast," said Burck. "Progress on climate action is often slow and in some countries, such as the United States, things are even moving backwards. But technologically and economically there is enormous momentum."

That momentum is apparent in record solar energy growth. Last year 75% of global electricity demand growth was met by the green energy source, according to energy think tank Ember's latest global electricity review. Investment in clean energy has also outpaced that in fossil fuels for multiple years.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The rapid expansion of renewable technology, as well as the Iran War and a reduction in deforestation are behind a projected slight fall in emissions for the first time since the COVID-19 pandemic, according to the CCPI.

"Governments have to act now to turn the momentum into sustained emissions reductions," said CCPI co-author Niklas Höhne of the NewClimate Institute, which compiles the report with environmental NGO Germanwatch.

Burck attributed Germany's worst ever performance in the category of national climate policy to current policies being pursued by Germany's economy minister Katherina Reiche.

"Measures that primarily aim to increase the use of natural gas, threaten to undermine progress in the energy transition and risk significantly worsening the conditions for renewable energy and electrification for many years to come," said Burck.

A European Commission report published on November 9 on the sidelines of the UN COP31 climate summit in Turkey said Germany was one of nine EU countries set to miss 2030 emissions reductions targets.

Germany is not alone in its disappointing ranking. The other G20 countries — the world's leading industrialized and emerging economies, responsible for around 80% of global CO2 emissions — also perform poorly.

The only exception among them is the United Kingdom, which ranks seventh and received a high rating, performing well in greenhouse gas emissions, energy use and climate policy. However, study authors rated it low for renewable energy expansion.

The G20's oil- and gas-producing countries occupy some of the lowest positions on the climate action table. The United States, which is the world's second largest emitter, languishes alongside Russia, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Canada around the bottom of the league, with an overall rating of "very low."

The hosts of this year's COP31, also received a "low" overall score. Australia, a major coal exporter with some of the world's highest per-capita emissions, ranks 54th, while Turkey, which is also heavily dependent on fossil fuels, comes in 53rd.

China is the world's largest emitter of greenhouse gases and ranks 56th in the CCPI, receiving an overall rating of "very low." Its main weaknesses include its now high per-capita emissions and substantial energy consumption.

However, among the G20, China leads the way in renewable energy expansion. The country, which is five years ahead of schedule in reaching its goal of adding 1,200 GW of wind and solar capacity to the grid by 2030, also produces over 80% of the world's solar panels.

Several oil-producing countries, including Kazakhstan, Saudi Arabia, Uzbekistan and the United Arab Emirates, are also performing better than expected in the renewables category and "are significantly expanding their previously limited" capacity, said the report.

The authors said these countries have significant potential to further expand renewables.

"In the Arab states in particular, very high per-capita emissions and an above-average level of electrification coincide with a relatively low existing share of renewable energy and enormous solar potential," said co-author Natalie Pelekh in a statement. "These are, in fact, ideal conditions for more ambitious climate action."

This article was originally published in German.

#883. An in situ redox-converted molecule for all-perovskite tandem solar cells

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

We’re sharing this article early to provide faster access to peer-reviewed, accepted research. It is citable and carries a permanent DOI. This version is subject to further edits and will be replaced automatically by the final Version of Record. All legal disclaimers apply.

All-perovskite tandem solar cells (TSCs) are gaining prominence due to their ability to surpass the efficiency limit of single-junction perovskite solar cells (PSCs)1,2. However, the efficiency and stability of all-perovskite TSCs are limited by chemical instability at the hole transport layer/perovskite interface in the tin-lead (Sn-Pb) narrow-bandgap subcell, which introduces deep trap states from tin cations and promotes non-radiative recombination3-5. Here we incorporate a redox-converted molecule of p-aminobenzohydrazide (ABH) into poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene):polystyrene sulfonate (PEDOT:PSS) that neutralizes PSS acidity, heals Sn4+ defects, and generates a dipole passivation effect upon oxidation. During the preparation of Sn-Pb perovskites, ABH suppresses interfacial oxidation by reducing Sn4+ defects and converts to p-aminobenzaldehyde (ABD), which suppresses photogenerated hole-induced Sn2+ oxidation, aligning energy levels for efficient hole extraction. The in situ redox-converted molecule stabilizes the buried interface during both device fabrication and operation, reduces non-radiative recombination and enhances stability. The resulting narrow-bandgap Sn-Pb PSC achieves a power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 25.4% (certified 25.2%) with an open-circuit voltage of 0.92 V and a fill factor of 83.4%. Integrated into monolithic all-perovskite TSCs, the device delivers a PCE of 31.1% (certified 30.8%) together with enhanced thermal (ISOS-D-2I, 85 °C) and operational stability (ISOS-L-1I) under inert conditions.

Terry Venables arrived at Middlesbrough in 2000 to work alongside manager Bryan Robson in an unconventional setup

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Mark Schwarzer has revealed that he feared a difficult reunion with Terry Venables when the former Australia manager arrived at Middlesbrough – only to find that the coach was willing to put their past disagreement behind them.

The pair had fallen out over Schwarzer’s availability for international duty in 1997, when the goalkeeper chose to honour a commitment to Boro rather than join an Australia squad under Venables.

Schwarzer had reason to worry about the potential for awkwardness when Venables was appointed to work alongside Bryan Robson at the Riverside in December 2000, tasked with helping Middlesbrough to beat the drop.

Schwarzer told FourFourTwo: “I was worried when Terry came in, because his previous job had been manager of Australia.

“I’d just joined Middlesbrough when we had that League Cup semi-final at the same time as an Australia call-up.

"Terry had made it clear that if he called you up, he expected you to be there

"Bryan Robson asked him if I could stay because it was one of the biggest games in Middlesbrough’s history.”

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“Terry initially agreed, then three days beforehand called and said I had to choose. I told him I’d made a commitment to my club. He didn’t pick me again, including for the World Cup play-off against Iran.

“When he arrived at Middlesbrough, I wondered if there might be a problem. To his credit, he was brilliant. He basically said 'These things happen, let’s move on'."

Instead of allowing the dispute to linger, Schwarzer says Venables did a fantastic job of working out how to get Middlesbrough back in form

He said: “He made a huge impact at Middlesbrough. He spoke to everyone about what they thought was going wrong, then made his own mind up about how to address it.

“Terry was exceptional at not undermining Bryan. Robbo was still at the front of things but had this incredible coach to learn from. If Terry hadn’t come in, we would have been relegated.”

Boro eventually finished the 2000-01 Premier League season in 14th, well clear of the drop.

Roberto De Zerbi has hailed Luca Williams-Barnett’s new contract as a clear sign of Tottenham’s ambition.

Williams-Barnett marked his full debut for Spurs with a goal and assist in Saturday’s 2-0 win over Ipswich to justify the growing hype around the highly-rated 18-year-old.

It was followed by a new long-term contract for the teenager on Tuesday, which is understood to run until 2031, and ahead of Sunday’s trip to Sunderland De Zerbi stressed the importance of keeping hold of him.

“It’s great news for us, the extension of his contract, because if you see other big teams, big clubs, they are losing young talent in the same situations,” De Zerbi said.

“We have to say thanks to the club, because I think it was an important step for us, for the pitch, for the football, but also for the fans, because I think we gave a great signal with this extension of the contract.

“And if the agent of Luca, if the family of Luca, accept to stay and to extend the contract, it’s because they believe in the Tottenham project. So I think the credit is for the club.”

Williams-Barnett looks to be in line for another start at Sunderland due to the absence of several attacking players.

De Zerbi added: “You have to analyse many things.

“I think he is ready to play because he is a mature guy, he has the personality to play in every stadium, every game, but we have to analyse everything he has done this week.

“The debut in the first XI, the goal, the assist, the extension of his contract. Everything is for the best. For us, for him, for the club.”

De Zerbi used Dejan Kulusevski as an example for Williams-Barnett to follow and the Sweden playmaker could start one of Tottenham’s three matches over the next week after a 17-month absence with a serious knee injury.

“I am thinking to start maybe not now, but I think we are very close to start a game,” De Zerbi added.

“Deki is working well. I watched his games in the national team just to understand the physical condition.

“He played the first game as a winger and the second game as a number 10 and especially in the second game he played very well, but we have to be good to understand the right moment to put him on the pitch.

“I think medical staff, physical staff, they are working very well with him and we can’t lose any time, but we can’t take any risk because he is a special player.”

While Kulusevski is close to a start, Tottenham are set to be without Savio for the rest of 2026 and beyond due to a hamstring issue sustained late on against Ipswich.

De Zerbi said: “I don’t know, 50 days, 60 days, 80 days, I don’t know. When he comes back I think he will be crucial for us for the last step of the season.”

#880. Man Utd activate Fernandes contract extension clause

Bruno Fernandes' contract was expiring at the end of this season but it will now run until the summer of 2028; the Man Utd captain and the club are in agreement that it makes sense to return to negotiations in the future, with full focus on improving the club's current position

Sky Sports News Reporter @DanyalHKhan

Manchester United have triggered their 12-month option to extend captain Bruno Fernandes' contract.

His deal was previously set to expire at the end of this season but will now run until summer 2028.

United have been in talks with Fernandes over extending his contract since the summer.

Sky Sports News understands both parties are in agreement that it makes sense to return to negotiations in the future - with full focus on improving the club's current position.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Triggering the club option now is logical from United's perspective, as clubs could have approached Fernandes over a pre-contract agreement in January. This contract clause activation prevents that.

Meanwhile, Fernandes was absent from United training on Friday - ahead of their game against Brentford on Saturday - due to illness.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Fernandes is understood to be under the weather and is being kept away from the squad ahead of the Brentford game.

On whether he'll make the game, Mauricio Pochettino said: "We don't know. He got a virus in Portugal. He finished the game with a problem and today he cannot be part of the training session.

"We'll see. We are going to see during the day, and [Saturday], how he wakes up. We are not going to take any risks."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"What triggering this option does is reduce the chance to zero that any club outside of the Premier League can approach Fernandes from Europe's top leagues around a potential move next summer for free.

"So this move protects both the club and the player from that situation.

"We know he's been the subject of interest in the last few summers, especially from Saudi Arabia.

"I think negotiations will continue in the future over Fernandes' long-term future, but for now he will remain at the club until the summer of 2028."

"They are protecting their asset. It is as simple as that. They are not in a position to fall out with their best player.

"They need him to go and perform to make sure they do not go down. I do not think they are in a relegation fight; they have the manager who will sort a lot of things out.

"Right now, they are a team devoid of all confidence. They could lose to Brentford, but I do not think they are in a relegation fight. They will end up finishing in mid-table.

"They have some very average players, hence the position, but they needed to trigger the clause to protect the asset and then get the money in the summer, if they have to."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Last week, Fernandes exclusively told Sky Sports that United have offered him a new contract - but he has put discussions on hold as he insists the club's priority must be returning to winning ways.

Fernandes has rejected two contract offers from United. The club's initial proposal was made in the summer when discussions first began over a new deal, but was turned down by the Portuguese, who signed his last contract in August 2024.

The United captain said: "I've seen people saying that he's asked for more money, he's asked for more years. If I wanted more money, I wouldn't be here.

"I had somewhere to go to get much more money than being at Manchester United. I could have been in a place that is much warmer than Manchester.

"Two summers ago, three summers ago, last summer, I always had the chance to leave and I always chose to be here. The thing is, I've always showed how much I care about the club and how much I want to win at this club. And I always said, in the moment the club thinks it's time for me to move on, I will move on.

"I'm not going to be the player that I've seen many in this time at Manchester United. They're going to stay here just by staying, just finish my contract and then we will see. In the moment the club says, 'Bruno, it's time to part ways', I'm going to be the first one walking out the door.

"Yeah, the club offered me a new contract, so I think that, from their side, shows that they want me to stay. And there are no negotiations going on. We spoke about the contract at the end of last season, we came in the beginning of this season speaking about the contract.

"But about the context of the team and the club, I just put that to one side because I don't think it's the right moment, neither for me, nor for the club, to be talking about negotiations because the most important thing now is that the club gets back to win games.

"My aim will always be to win the Premier League and the Champions League within the club I am."

Man Utd chief executive Omar Berrada also spoke to Sky Sports last week about Fernandes' contract talks and said: "Listen, I've said before, we have a tremendous amount of respect for Bruno. We're very fortunate to have him as a captain.

"What he's done for this team over the last six, seven years is absolutely incredible. Last year he won, I think, all the individual awards you can win.

"And we're very proud to have him as captain. It's true that we're having conversations about his new contract, but I prefer to keep that private. I think it's something that needs to be discussed behind the scenes between him and the club."

#879. DW Science explainer on the default mode network: what your brain does when you aren't focusing on anything, and why it's important.

Doing nothing might be the ultimate brain hack. When you're bored, the brain goes into default mode network. It's not only healthy for you, but it may also shape the very essence of your identity.

You know when you lock your phone and the screen goes black? It seems like it's not doing anything. But it's not doing nothing. It's syncing your messages, updating apps and running other background processes.

Imagine you're sitting on a bus, staring out of a window, taking a shower or walking, and you get that feeling of doing nothing and letting your mind drift?

Well, your mind, the brain, is doing a lot when it feels like you're doing nothing.

It's going over your memories, shaping your sense of who you are, imagining possible futures, helping you understand other people and connecting ideas.

That's your brain's default mode network.

Scientists conducted brain-imaging experiments in the 1990s and early 2000s to find out which regions of the brain were active during demanding tasks, like solving a math problem or memory exercise.

But to measure that, they needed a so-called baseline. They needed to know the level of brain activity at rest and during demanding tasks.

So, between the tasks, they asked participants to relax, close their eyes, stare at a fixed point on a wall, or try not to think of anything at all.

And they measured the participants' brain activity both when they were solving a task and doing nothing. That's how scientists noticed the brain was active in up- and downtime.

They noticed that when participants started to focus on a new task, after having done nothing, some brain areas lit up and other areas dimmed down. That suggests those areas that dimmed down must have been active while the participant was apparently — physically and mentally — at rest.

This realization eventually led to the discovery of the default mode network or DMN.

The DMN is crucial because it helps your brain make sense of your life and experiences.

It helps you connect and revisit memories, reflect on who you are, imagine what might happen in future scenarios, understand other people, build meaning from experience, and connect ideas in new ways.

It turns all your memories, experiences, knowledge, emotions and social information into your internal story. Think of that story as a constantly evolving, updated model of who you are and how you engage with the world around you.

But it's important to understand the DMN involves more than one area of the brain. It is a group of brain regions that light up when you're not focused on an external task.

There's another player in your brain that acts as a monitoring system. You can think of it as constantly asking "Is there anything that needs my attention?"

Imagine you're daydreaming while driving, and a car suddenly swerves into your lane.

In a fraction of a second, your daydream disappears and your attention snaps back to the road. That player is called the salience network, or SN.

The salience network helps you notice important signals, like a sound, a mistake, pain, an emotion, a threat, or something happening in your body, and helps shift the brain toward attention and control systems when action is needed.

The DMN, SN and attention/control systems constantly interact.

And the DMN doesn't just turn off completely with every hard task. Parts of it can also contribute when tasks involve memory, stories, meaning or other people.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Smartphones have filled many of the small empty moments of our days — waiting for the bus, standing in line, eating alone, lying on the couch. We are constantly looking at our devices.

So, it seems reasonable to ask: are we crowding out those moments of boredom where DMN kicks in?

Maybe. But so far, there's no strong evidence that scrolling directly affects mental health by reducing DMN time.

What we do know is that problematic smartphone use can increase stress, anxiety, task-switching and disrupt sleep.

And sleep loss and stress also have clearer evidence for altering DMN-related brain connectivity.

When your mind wanders, it might produce a great new idea.

But it might also replay an embarrassing thing you did five years ago. Again. And again.

In depression, the self-reflection part of the DMN can get caught in repetitive negative loops that are hard to stop — what's known as rumination.

Scientists have also found that Alzheimer's disease targets key DMN areas, particularly those responsible for your autobiographical memory and remembering other aspects of the past. Which may help explain why memory problems are so central to the disease.

Protect your sleep and take stress seriously. There is direct evidence that sleep loss and stress disrupt DMN-related connectivity.

Take real, quiet breaks after mentally demanding tasks, like studying. It can even help you memorize facts for your exam.

Try to reframe boredom as this essential, energy-intensive active work in your brain that builds your internal narrative and sense of self, consolidates memories, creates connections and sparks creativity.

Try waiting in line without checking your phone. Look out the window next time you take the bus or take a walk without listening to anything.

You can also try scheduling DMN time. It may be the closest thing to a real brain hack.

Liverpool are beginning to see the very best of Florian Wirtz if recent form is anything to go by

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Florian Wirtz's £116 million Anfield arrival last summer was, on paper, a marquee addition to the Premier League, until he took to the field.

Supporters of all clubs were expectant, not least Liverpool fans. His debut campaign proved an awkward adaptation to English football, one in which the German seemed caught between systems, clearly in transition.

Fast forward to today and the player who lit up the Bundesliga with Bayer Leverkusen appears to have finally arrived on Merseyside.

Wirtz produced a standout display in Sunday’s 4-0 thrashing of Manchester United, where he scored an improvised goal to extend the Reds' lead and created 10 chances - albeit against 10 men - before finding the net again in Wednesday night’s 3-0 Champions League triumph over Club Brugge.

The underlying numbers from Gradient Sports prove this is no fleeting purple patch, either, especially after three goals in two games over the November international break.

According to Gradient Sports’ data, Wirtz’s overall player grade dipped sharply from a league-leading 91.0 in his final Bundesliga season with Leverkusen in 2024/25 to 73.1 during his debut 2025/26 Premier League campaign.

While his overall 2026/27 Premier League grade sits at 73.9, his attacking execution indicates a resurgence back toward his Leverkusen peak.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

In the Premier League this season, Wirtz has had a 48 per cent increase in chances created - jumping from 1.99 to 2.94 per 90 minutes - ranking first among all Premier League wingers and attacking midfielders.

Even more telling is his cutting edge in the final third: Wirtz's passes directly leading to a half-chance have increased by 84 per cent, from 0.31 to 0.57 per 90.

His end product in front of goal tells a similar story. Gradient data notes that Wirtz’s positively graded shots have risen from 0.24 to 0.38 per 90 - closing in on the 0.45 he posted in 2024/25. Similarly, his 1.61 shots in the box per 90 actually surpasses his final Leverkusen tally of 1.60.

So, what has initiated the turnaround? New Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola deserves credit for tweaking Wirtz's role and adjusting the team's tempo, but Anfield may also owe a debt of gratitude to Jurgen Klopp.

Since taking charge of the German national team, Klopp has turned Wirtz into his talisman; he has four goals in his last four international appearances. And it's that confidence which has bled into his club form, aided by private counsel from the former Reds manager. Wirtz revealed recently that he regularly speaks with Klopp about life at Anfield, taking on board "small, private things" from a man who knows exactly how to win over the Kop.

Armed with Klopp’s guidance and backed by the evidence of improved creative metrics in the Premier League, Liverpool’s £116m man is finally beginning to look worthy of his price tag.

Slegers led Arsenal to Champions League glory in May 2025

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Renee Slegers has left her role as head coach of Arsenal following a difficult start to the Women’s Super League season for the north London club.

The Gunners occupy sixth place in the WSL standings, sitting 12 points behind leaders Chelsea after 11 matches, and remain winless at home in the league this term.

The Dutch manager assumed the role from Jonas Eidevall, initially on an interim basis, two years ago before guiding Arsenal to Champions League glory in May 2025.

A statement on arsenal.com read: "We can confirm Renee Slegers has left her position as head coach of our women’s first team by mutual consent.

"Renee departs following a disappointing start to the 2026-27 season, with assistant coach Aaron D’Antino also leaving the club.

"The process of appointing a successor is under way and we will update in due course. Assistant coach Melissa Clarke-Reed will take charge of the team in the interim period.

"Everyone at Arsenal would like to thank Renee and Aaron for their contributions to the club and wish them every success in their future careers."

Pressure had been mounting on Slegers, particularly with Arsenal struggling to convert in front of goal, and her final match ended in a goalless draw against West Ham last Sunday.

Gunners director of women’s football Clare Wheatley said: "It was an extremely difficult decision to part ways with Renee, who has led the team with dedication and commitment throughout her time here.

"In leading us to glory in the Champions League and the inaugural Fifa Champions Cup, Renee has made a significant and lasting contribution to the history of Arsenal, with close support from Aaron.

"After careful reflection, it is clear that results have been below the expected level and change is necessary."

Arsenal have two weeks until their next fixture due to the international break, with England set to face Ukraine in a two-legged playoff as Sarina Wiegman’s side aim to secure their place at next year’s World Cup.

Once the international break finishes, Arsenal will return to action without Slegers when they travel to Everton on 11 December.

England and Arsenal striker Alessia Russo speaks about football memories and handling pressure in front of goal as she partners with Lucozade

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Alessia Russo has two European Championships and a Champions League to her name and has established herself as one of England’s most prolific strikers.

In another impressive year for the 27-year-old, she became the highest-scoring English player in UEFA Women's Champions League history with a recent hat-trick against Benfica, was named England Women's Player of the Year and earned a place in the FIFPRO Women's World 11.

Speaking to former Three Lions striker Ian Wright at the launch of her new long-term partnership with Lucozade, the England and Arsenal forward discussed how she fell in love with football and the mentality behind her performances.

Russo grew up in Maidstone, Kent and football always featured in her life.

“Football has always been a massive part of my life,” she said. “Growing up, my dad would take me to watch women’s games at Charlton, and I remember looking up to those players and dreaming of doing the same one day.

“To see how far the game has come is incredible. Women’s football is now about so much more than what happens on the pitch. It’s influencing fashion, culture and bringing communities together in ways I could never have imagined growing up.

“To be part of that journey is really special.”

Now one of the leading strikers in world football, Russo believes her calm approach is one of her biggest strengths when it comes to finding the back of the net.

"I've always been really laid back. I'm always wanting to win. Just because I'm not angry or shouting or screaming, doesn't mean I don't want to win and I don't want to score," she said.

"I think that calmness is something that I try and bring to the game. And I think as a striker, you have to be calm in and around the box. When things aren't going your way, I just kind of strip it back. I like to train hard and then whatever happens in the game happens.

"You can't control a whole lot as a No.9. You're quite reliant on other players. But what you can control is the moments that you do get."

The partnership will see Russo work with Lucozade Sport to better understand her individual hydration and fuelling requirements, with the 2027 Women's World Cup in Brazil on the horizon.

She will also help inform future product innovation as the brand continues its longstanding support of the Lionesses, dating back to 2006.

Ayisha Gulati is the women’s football writer at FourFourTwo. Having covered England’s triumphant Euro 2025 campaign in Switzerland and the 2026 World Cup in North America, she has reported on the ground at some of football’s biggest tournaments. She covers the WSL, UWCL and international football, and has interviewed leading names including Alexia Putellas, Leah Williamson and Bunny Shaw. She enjoys telling stories that capture the personalities, passion and excitement of the women’s game, on and off the pitch.

#875. Soldier Reeves emerges as future star with Long Distance Hurdle win

Soldier Reeves banished doubts about his staying ability with a magnificent display in the Coral Long Distance Hurdle. In the feature race, Dan Skelton's charge proved too good for previous winners Impose Toi and Strong Leader - who was gallant in second.

Soldier Reeves emerged as the new kid on the block in the staying division with an impressive comeback victory in the Coral Long Distance Hurdle at Newbury.

Dan Skelton's five-year-old mixed it with the best around in novice hurdles last season, most notably finishing fourth behind King Rasko Grey when upped in trip for the Turners Novices' Hurdle at the Cheltenham Festival before finding only high-class stablemate Bossman Jack too strong at Aintree.

He faced another step into the unknown on his reappearance, taking on more hardened stayers on his first start over three miles under rules, but travelled powerfully throughout in the hands of Harry Skelton and was right on the heels of the redoubtable Strong Leader on the approach to the final flight.

The latter did his best to regain his crown, having emerged victorious two years ago and finished a close second to Impose Toi last term, but Soldier Reeves (3-1) was the stronger at the finish and passed the post with three and a quarter lengths in hand.

Skelton will now point his emerging stayer to Ascot's Long Walk Hurdle just before Christmas.

He said: "I was very impressed with him and I wasn't surprised he won, but I was surprised he could do it first time out.

"He still didn't relax all that well, but he relaxed well enough for Harry to be able to get him switched off and he came home strongly.

"I didn't go to three miles in the spring and this makes me glad I didn't. We may have left a big race behind not going three miles at Aintree, but I just knew if I did that when he was just a five-year-old I might have been asking too much. I trusted him today and he delivered."

He went on: "He was under the radar, but that's because he wasn't quite behaving well enough to win one of those last year.

"I put that down to the fact he was very raw at four and five. We only went hurdling last year because I was so annoyed with him for pulling so hard in a bumper at Newton Abbot that I sent him hurdling to try to slow him down with a few jumps in front of him.

"He has just improved and improved and improved and he has a brilliant engine. He had some good rivals around him at the last and I was very impressed he could come out on top as I thought it was a very competitive renewal.

"I have a lot of respect for the horses he has beaten there and now he will have to try to back it up. The one thing about this horse though is he has a fantastic attitude and we'll go now to the Long Walk."

Race regular Strong Leader could renew rivalry at Ascot, although Olly Murphy will also consider a trip to Ireland.

Murphy said: "He ran well but just bumped into a younger, better horse on the day. We have no excuse whatsoever and although people love to knock this horse and he's not always great at Cheltenham, nine times out of 10 he turns up and runs a great race.

"He always jumps the last looking like the winner, but today he has bumped into a better one and we'll dust ourselves down and go again.

"Whether we go Ascot at Christmas or Ireland, I'm not sure, but there is still life in him yet. He loves a left-handed flat track and yes he ran very well in a Long Walk last year, but Ireland is certainly something we'll have a good look at.

"We'll see how he comes out of today and he's run a cracker and I'm really proud of him. He deserves to win a big one again, but it's life and sometimes you bump into a nice young horse who is just too good on the day."

Taurus Bay followed in the hoofprints of illustrious stablemate The Jukebox Man by winning the Coral John Francome Novices' Chase.

It is two years since Harry Redknapp's subsequent King George hero made a winning debut over fences in this Grade Two contest and in his younger stablemate the popular owner, trainer Ben Pauling and jockey Ben Jones appear to have unearthed another potential star.

Taurus Bay lined up having already won over the larger obstacles in the Rising Stars Novices' Chase at Aintree three weeks ago, a victory which meant the 11-8 favourite had to concede 3lb to each of his four rivals in his bid for back-to-back Group Two wins.

Harry Skelton ensured the race was a stern test of stamina and jumping aboard the front-running Royal Infantry, but Jones steadily nursed Taurus Bay into contention and he toughed it out on the run-in to prevail by half a length.

Pauling said: "It's lovely to work with horses who try as hard as that when they need to. He didn't have the run of the race and was in a tight pocket and Ben was patient when he needed to be today, which was great.

"We all know the Skelton team are going to be very hard to pass and are never here to make up the numbers, but I was always confident jumping two out and after the last he was going to tough it out.

"Ben would have liked him to have travelled a little bit better early doors, but that might have been because the ground was a little lively for him. I would love to get some soft ground for this horse soon because that's when we'll see him at his best.

"We definitely won't be going up in trip and I would come back in trip before I go up. I even think two miles on soft ground could be where he's at his best.

"There were no punches held there and the very good two-milers do stay really well as well. As for the future I would love to keep him at two or two and a half and he could be an Arkle horse - it's an option.

"The obvious place would be (to target) the Manifesto and then you could Wayward Lad (Kempton), Scilly Isles (Sandown) and then Aintree. But it's just lovely to see a horse win two Grade Twos in his first two outings over fences and in doing so he has hardly made a mistake."

Koala Rose looked every inch a filly bound for the big spring festivals judged on an impressive second success over obstacles.

A 77-rated performer on the Flat, having been placed on each of her five starts for Ralph Beckett without quite managing to get her head in front, the daughter of Australia won by 62 lengths on her jumping bow at Hereford, earning her a step up to Listed level in the Coral "Daily Rewards Shaker" Fillies' Juvenile Hurdle.

Supporters of Dan Skelton's exciting recruit will have had few concerns, with the 8-13 favourite jumping nimbly in front throughout in the hands of Harry Skelton before powering 16 lengths clear of another previous winner in Echo Valley on the run-in.

Skelton said: "I thought she was very good and I was delighted to see her win as well as that.

"I think there was a bit of market negativity around some of the others, so you might have to take the form with a pinch of salt. Hereford taught us only that she loves to jump, which we already knew from home, but she was very nimble around Hereford and today she's answered another question.

"There's harder questions to come, but I was really impressed with her attitude and hopefully she is progressive as well and there's more lurking under there.

"Hereford was quick ground, but there on slightly softer ground you could see she was barely getting her toe off the ground and it does play on my mind a little bit. Maybe we shouldn't ask her difficult questions too soon on soft ground and wait for some nicer conditions that allow her to show us what she can do.

"There's a Listed juvenile fillies' race at Doncaster at the end of January and that could be most appropriate. There's sure to be other races open to her as well, but she's a pretty effective three-year-old filly and not many have the substance and aggression in their jumping like she does and it really helps."

#874. Can global leaders put their money where their mouth is on climate?

World leaders warn that geopolitical divisions are distracting from the climate crisis as negotiations focus on clean energy and financing, while Iran calls for compensation for war-related environmental damage.

The slow international response to climate change has placed the world on a path to destruction, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres told heads of state and government during opening statements at this year's COP31 climate conference.

"The ⁠brutal truth is that the climate crisis is outrunning us," he said, as world leaders gathered in the Turkish resort city of Antalya to set the tone for negotiations at the UN climate summit.

A UN reportlast month found ​the world will cross a temperature threshold countries agreed to pursue in order to prevent runaway global heating. At the same time, states like Germany are slipping down the rankings for climate action, according to the annual Climate Change Performance Index published Wednesday by New Climate Institute and Germanwatch.

Nonetheless, Guterres said the world has "the power to make sure the overshoot is a temporary breach."

Negotiators from close to 200 countries are meeting in Turkey at the end of a year characterized by extreme heat waves and a glacier collapse in Nepal that triggered a flood, killing more than 1,400 people and leaving thousands more missing.

At this year's talks, national representatives are discussing climate solutions such as increasing the share of electricity in an effort to move away from fossil fuels.

On Thursday, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, one of the few heads of government from Europe's major economies attending the summit, said that the world's dependence on fossil fuels was at the heart of both the climate crisis and energy security challenges.

"The shift to clean energy is the only route to energy security," he said, endorsing the conference's focus on electrification which he said would lower energy bills, create jobs and protect people from the volatility of fossil fuel markets.

Burnham promised a "new era of British leadership over the next decade," announcing the UK would put climate resilience high on the agenda during its G20 presidency next year.

The US, the world's largest historical emitter of damaging greenhouse gases, is not attending the summit — for the second year in a row after US President Donald Trump withdrew the country from the Paris Agreement in 2025.

Other nations, including big polluters like Germany, France, Italy, Canada and Japan, also opted not to send their top leaders to the talks.

On Wednesday, Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, who is hosting COP31 together with Australia, which is leading negotiations, called on developed nations to take greater responsibility on climate finance.

Financing disagreements center around who should pay for international climate action, whether funding should take the form of grants or loans and how to scale monetary support for developing nations. Many of these countries are among the most vulnerable to the climate crisis but have contributed very little to the emissions causing it.

Erdogan said while previous conferences had resulted in different ideas around financing, they have yet to be turned into action. "We set out to make this an implementation COP," he told leaders.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen addressed remarks that developed nations are not contributing enough to climate finance, saying that the transition away from fossil fuels is in "our common interest."

"Europe is the world's largest provider of climate finance. Last year alone, we contributed more than €32 billion [about $35.5 billion] to support developing countries," she said, adding that Europe will continue to support partners worldwide in tackling climate change.

A recent Carbon Brief analysis found that public funding pledged under the Paris Agreement to help developing countries tackle climate change fell by more than 70% in 2026.

Most multi-year pledges from donor countries expired in 2025. Since then, the US has stepped back from international climate efforts, while several European countries have cut their aid budgets, reported Carbon Brief.

Hilda Heine, president of the Marshall Islands in the Pacific, which face an existential threat from rising sea levels, said the response to overshoot "must be overwhelming" and quickly reversed otherwise "the world we know is over."

"Every fraction of a degree of warming brings more catastrophe," said Heine, adding that more warming makes it more difficult to adapt to living on a hotter planet, brings greater loss and damage from worsening weather extremes and greater financial need.

She called on leaders to triple climate finance by 2035 and make it easier for Small Island Developing States to access the money.

"We are told there is no money, but their spending on war grows; the greatest security threat we face remains underfunded. I appeal to you: Find money for life, not death. Replenish the climate funds," Heine said.

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese spoke of a "solemn responsibility to this and to future generations ​to act," adding that this is the critical decade.

Australia, the world's third-largest fossil fuel exporter, has vowed to promote the views of the "Pacific family" — small Pacific nations in the region such as Tuvalu or Fiji, where pre-COP meetings were held in October.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Albanese said it was crucial that climate cooperation delivered practical results — "unlocking investment in clean energy technologies, accelerating electrification, speeding up action for our oceans, unlocking climate finance for those who need it ​most."

As reasons to speed up electrification von der Leyen pointed to wildfires in Europe and floods in Nepal, as well as droughts stretching from Central America to Sudan, and to the disruption to energy supplies linked to the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz.

"The world is witnessing the cost of continuing with the status quo for our climate and our energy security," she said, adding that the European Union would double down on efforts to become climate neutral.

"Three-quarters ​of humanity live in countries that import fossil fuels, hostage to price shocks they did ​not create and cannot ‌control," UN Secretary-General Guterres said, adding that recent conflicts have made clear a shift to renewable energy would help improve energy security and the cost-of-living crisis.

Von der Leyen also expressed support for COP31's 35-by-35 electrification pledge. The pledge aims to increase electricity's share of final global energy use to 35% by 2035, with von der Leyen saying Europe would be the first "electro-powered" continent.

Heine of the Marshall Islands said electrification must must be strictly tied to renewable energy generation rather than fossil fuels, warning that continued oil, coal and gas extraction was a threat to her country's survival.

Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian said his country wanted compensation for environmental damage caused by US and Israeli strikes, including oil leaks from attacks on tankers. The strikes began in February.

Iran, which is a major fossil fuel producer and has pushed back against strict language on phasing out oil and gas at previous COPs alongside other petrostates, has also struck tankers in the Strait of Hormuz.

Pezeshkian linked the issue to climate finance and said his country expected "responsibility in times of war, to document and assess the environmental damages caused by military aggressions and to develop compensation mechanisms."

Brazil's President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who hosted last year's COP in the Amazonian city of Belem, said the momentum for climate action had dropped off at the start of the year, partly due to the Iran war.

"We started talking more about weapons and tariffs than the survival ‌of future generations," he said.

He also warned that "climate agreements are the favorite targets of reactionary forces at COPs," and urged leaders to work together. Lula promised to protect the Amazon rainforest. "Brazil is back to defend the continuity of a healthy planet," he said.

This article was last updated on November 12 to reflect incoming statements from world leaders.

Pep Guardiola has been out of work since bringing an end to a decade at Manchester City this summer – and has suggested that his next job could be in charge of a national team.

Guardiola won six Premier League titles during his time at the Etihad, before deciding to step down at the end of last season.

In an interview this week though, the Catalan indicated that he sees his next step as being “a national team”, after talks to become Italy boss during the summer.

Guardiola opted not to take the Italy job, believing at the time that he needed a break from football, but has since been linked with the USA vacancy.
