#840. How to become a football referee

Honestly, for me it's one of the most rewarding things I've probably ever done. You find so much more out about yourself that you probably never knew.

Louise Thompson, women's referee pathway officer for the Irish Football Association, international FIFA referee, and PremierLeague referee in Northern Ireland.

What does a women's referee pathway officer do?

Looking after female referees within Northern Ireland, trying to recruit, retain and give them experience within their games to pushthrough into top level refereeing.

What kind of training do you give to aspiring referees?

So from going through recruitment courses first of all, and then we do the beginners course with referees, just giving them all of the Laws of the Game knowledge, then we will also do a practical part of that course where they go onto the pitch and we'll go through scenarios, positioning, things around free kick management for example, other set pieces likecorners, penalty setup, what you do as a referee day to day, even pre match stuff as well, so when you arrive at the grounds, how you check the pitch, check all the equipment is there, how you would interact with players, coaches and then just again, maybe createlike a role play sort of environment so that they know that they're not going totally blind into that sort of situation.

Have you always been passionate about football?

Football was a passion of mine, even when I was younger, primary school age, we just didn't have very many female teams, so it normally meant playing with the boys and the boys teams and stuff up until I was about 14, which was the minimum age here you can join senior ladies football team, which is what I did, and played there for 14 years at a club here locally, including up until the Women's Premiership, so it was great to be involved in football, but I always loved watching football, playing football, anything to do with football, I was always there and interested.

How did you go from playing football to being a referee?

Becoming a referee for me sort of happened by chance to be honest. It was during a game, one time I got an injury, quite a bad injury to my knee and then I had seen luckily that the referee course was being advertised. So I signed up for it, but I also signed up for a coaching course pretty much at the same time, maybe about six weeks apart. I wasnât really sure which role I wanted to follow, but over that winter I had been pushed into refereeing a wee bit and said sure, why not, Iâll give it a go, it'd be a bit of extra fitness before my season restarts, and then just fell in love with it from there and never looked back.

What subjects did you study at school and university?

Coming through school I always picked PE, so I did my GCSE PE and then I also did A-level PE and then when I went onto university,I had the sport and exercise science as well within that, so I think it gives you a good understanding of obviously how your body works, and your plan and training, stuff like that as well so you know when you're working nutrition wise, things that you need to know,especially as you reach the top level, just to make sure that you're getting the most out of your body.

What are your top tips for becoming a referee?

I would say definitely give it a try for sure. You never know until you do it. I think even when I was a player, I probably never imaginedthat I would be a referee and that I would even achieve and have experienced what Iâve been able to experience. So you never knowuntil you give it a go, but it's also about probably pushing yourself out of your comfort zone, being comfortable with being uncomfortable in situations like that. It's maybe not always as bad as it probably seems it's going to be. There's probably a lot more stigma around being a referee - who wants to be a referee? - but honestly for me, it's one of the most rewarding things I've probably ever done.

With a lifelong love of football, Louise Thompson followed her passion for the game, first as a player and now as a referee. As well as refereeing Fifa and NIFL Premiership matches, she also works for the Irish Football Association as the women's referee pathway officer, recruiting and developing up-and-coming female refs.

Louise Thompson on refereeing the Women's Irish Cup final.

If you're interested in becoming a referee, it's something you can get involved with from a young age through local referee courses. The minimum age to become a qualified referee varies depending on where in the UK you live:

In her role as a women's referee pathway officer, Louise oversees new referees right from the initial recruitment courses stage: "We then do the beginners' course with referees, giving them all of the Laws of the Game knowledge," she says. "We also do a hands-on part of that course where they go onto the pitch and we go through different scenariosâ¦ exactly what you do as a referee, and day-to-day practical stuff as wellâ¦ The idea is to give them all the basics and fundamentals before they go into a game so that they're prepared."

All four UK nations have established pathways for referee development and progression. Starting out at grassroots level, it's possible to progress all the way to Fifa!

Louise's first games were youth games: "I still remember my first game to this day," she says. "It was an under-13 game, and I was definitely the most nervous person on the pitch." She explains: "Over time, you'll get mentors who will come and watch you, give you advice, give you feedback" which will help you to progress to higher levels of the game.

As well as PE, Louise has found that languages are really helpful in this line of work, "especially when you're dealing with a lot of international games and people coming along," she says. "If you can learn some languages, it's very, very useful."

You could get into this role by training with a professional body.

Sources: National Careers Service, GOV.UK, FA, IFA, SFA, and FAW.

FourFourTwo tried out Be Your Best's state-of-the-art VR scanning technology - it was an illuminating experience into the mind of a top-level footballer

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In the basement of a central London WeWork this week, FourFourTwo slipped on a VR headset and stepped onto a virtual pitch.

It felt like living inside an interactively playable game of Football Manager - or recreating Guy Ritchie’s iconic late-2000s point-of-view Nike advert.

Within seconds the novelty wears off and the pressure is on. When a virtual teammate fizzes a pass toward your feet in the middle of a crowded midfield, you quickly realise just how hard it is to think like a top-level footballer.

Be Your Best (BYB) boast some of the most cutting-edge performance-enhancing technology on the market. Their virtual reality software is designed to train scanning, awareness and in-game intelligence.

Behind it lies nearly three decades of pioneering research by Norwegian sports psychologist Geir Jordet, who began logging how frequently players check their surroundings back in 1997 - armed with nothing more than a notebook and a VCR.

Scanning is the subtle, constant habit of taking mental snapshots of your environment before the ball arrives, and it's what separates good footballers from the greats.

Of the 117 players Jordet studied in his landmark research, the standout was Frank Lampard, who scanned an astonishing 6.2 times every 10 seconds before receiving possession. Lampard Snr. used to bark "Pictures! Pictures!" from the touchline during Frank Jnr.’s West Ham academy days, drilling into the future England international a habit that directly correlates with higher pass completion rates and a greater volume of forward passes.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Timing, though, is everything. Scan at the wrong moment and you miss vital cues on the speed and direction of pressing defenders - FourFourTwo learned that the hard way, frequently dispossessed in traffic or making stray passes.

Inside the headset, BYB drop you directly into real on-field moments recreated from actual matches, complete with four distinct training modes and fresh scenarios released weekly.

Suddenly, you are in the boots of Arsenal captain Martin Odegaard - who famously asked developers to crank the simulation speed up to 120 per cent because standard 100 per cent match pace felt too easy. FFT was playing at 85 per cent. Show-off.

Built-in awareness tests freeze play, turning surrounding players into blank silhouettes, quizzing the user on which team each belongs to. When the ball finally arrives, you have a split second to pick out a pass or pull the trigger.

At the end of each round, the software delivers a brutally honest scorecard, at least that's how it felt to FFT. We were graded on our performance across the following metrics: BYB IQ, scan rate, scan timing, critical scans (checks made in the final moments before receiving the ball), decision-making and overall awareness.

Afterward, a bird’s-eye replay mode allows players and coaches to dissect every scenario from above, effectively handing professionals unlimited 'do-overs' to rehearse how they could have played a situation differently, all without physical fatigue or risking injury.

It is little wonder footballers have taken notice. In the past, Norwegian youth sides featuring Erling Haaland used the technology during their development, while Chelsea midfielder Romeo Lavia is an investor. On the consumer side, everyone from 10-year-old grassroots hopefuls practising in their living rooms to Real Madrid stars Endrick and Aurelien Tchouameni use BYB to sharpen their minds.

Meanwhile, clubs and federations, including Hoffenheim and the Portuguese FA, tap into BYB’s B2B side of things, which includes custom match-scenario builds for academies and Apollo, a separate analytical tool powered by synced 3D tracking and event data. Apollo lets club analysts step inside any player’s first-person POV to review flashpoints and decisions in full 3D.

After 30 minutes in Odegaard’s virtual boots, FFT had improved but we weren't quite at the level of a Xavi Hernandez with a head on a swivel - let's just say our BYB IQ left plenty to be desired.

Be Your Best is offering 30% off annual VR training subscriptions for Black Friday using promo code BF30.

#838. 'My job combines my passion for gaming and football'

Working on one of the world's biggest football video games is the perfect combination of my two biggest passions, gaming and football.

I'm CJ Ramson. I work on the creation of football video games. I work on Football Manager as an associate QA manager. QA stands for quality assurance.

We're the ones that test the game. We make sure everything works, and we work closely with the developers to try and make the most realistic simulation of football.

Growing up, I loved football, whether that was playing football or playing football video games with my friends. I'd always be doing one or the other. With the video games, the thing that really drew me to them was I've always been into the tactical side of the game, either being able to control the players or create your own tactics.

So a typical day for us, we'll get a new build in from the developers. We'll test it as a QA team, and we'll look for either bugsor ways that we can improve the game. That can be anything from the runs that players make, to decisions they make on the ball, what the team instructions and tactics do. So there's a lot of areas for us to cover. Our final goal is to make it as realistic to real football as possible.

So even though my background was in coaching, there was a lot of transferable skills that I learned and developed through my time coaching that I managed to transfer into this. So whether that's being really analytical and having a good eye for detail and knowingwhen to pick things out and what to look for, or it could be things like timekeeping and making sure things run perfectly on time, and working with other people as well. So social skills where you have to work within a team or even lead a team.

The animation he makes, and the ball physics as well, where the ball goes off after the save."

So as much as I loved playing football, I realised quite early on I probably wasn't going to be a professionalfootballer. But I wanted to work in football and find. So at college, I studied sports science, and that's where I found my love of coaching. I did my FA Level 1 and then went on to do my FA Level 2. After I left college, I got a job at Arsenal, which was unpaid, working with them, learning how to develop my coaching skills. Which then led to me having a full-time paid job at Fulham Football Club, working with the youth teams, working with the academy teams. And then that eventually led to me going to an event. I saw an opportunity where you could apply for a job in Football Manager. It was something that naturally I was interested in, had a conversation with them, and realised it was definitely something that I would love to do.

So I went to the networking event at Kick It Out, and that was an opportunity for me to network with other football coaches, other people within the gaming industries, and have a really good insight to different jobs in football gaming. Without doing that, I wouldn't have the opportunity to meet the people at Football Manager and see a new job in gaming, which I wouldn't have beenaware of.

One of the highlights of my career so far is working on the in-and-out-of-possession system on FM 26. This is something we see in real football all the time, so being part of the team that brought that to life and brought it into the game was super cool.

Working within the football industry is a dream come true. Being able to work on something that I'm passionate about, that is played and enjoyed by millions of people, is an amazing feeling for me and an amazing opportunity that I have. And yeah, I love it.

CJ works as an associate quality assurance manager on the video game Football Manager. His team test the game to make sure everything works, and collaborate with the developers to create the most realistic simulation of football.

There are lots of different ways to progress in the gaming industry.

CJ works in the QA (Quality Assurance) team, testing games. In this team, his career progression has followed this path:

His team is just one of the options, though. There are different roles in video game testing. CJ notes that: "Salaries can vary depending on your role and the company you work for. They can range from around Â£20,000 to Â£50,000 and upwards." The higher salaries in this range could apply when you've gained more experienced and progressed in your career.

Former Liverpool centre-back Dejan Lovren has offered his thoughts on Virgil van Dijk's remaining time at Anfield

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Former Liverpool centre-back Dejan Lovren has admitted it will feel 'strange' when Virgil van Dijk eventually leaves Anfield, insisting the Dutchman deserves a fitting farewell whenever the time comes to part ways.

Lovren's role in the team was largely usurped by Van Dijk following the skipper's arrival on Merseyside in January 2018, who has since gone on to help the Reds lift both the Champions League and the Premier League title.

Speaking in an interview via Hajper, the Croatian international suggested that while Van Dijk could still earn a further 12-month contract extension if he maintains his current standards, both the club and player must ensure the timing of his eventual exit is right.

"It will be strange when Virgil van Dijk leaves Liverpool, but at some point it has to come to an end," Lovren said. "It’ll be important for him, the fans and the club that he leaves at the right time. If he stays at his level then you can see a one-year extension, but of course he’ll have to keep proving that on the pitch.

"But saying that, it’s so important that he gets a good farewell - he deserves it for what he has given to the club for so long, year after year. He has been at the very top.

"He is without doubt one of Liverpool’s greatest ever players. You just need to look at the stats. Look at what he achieved and what he won, it speaks for itself. How many times was he up for the Ballon d'Or or in the FIFPro World 11? It’s not just Liverpool, he's top of the tree."

Liverpool are already planning for life after their captain, and Lovren also weighed in on whether young defender Jeremy Jacquet has what it takes to fill Van Dijk's boots.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

"I hope Jacquet can be the next Van Dijk at Liverpool, but it's really important to realise why Van Dijk is at the top level, because of his consistency," Lovren added.

"It's as simple as that. If Jacquet is there for the next seven years, then we can talk about whether he deserves to stay there forever.

"But if he plays well this year and not well in the next six months, things will change. We know he has the ability, it's about consistency at the end. That's why top players are different from normal players."

Further up the pitch, Lovren is far more certain of Liverpool's long-term firepower, pointing to the chemistry between Florian Wirtz, Alexander Isak and his former Lyon teammate Bradley Barcola - as well as the eventual return of injured forward Hugo Ekitike.

"When Hugo Ekitike is back? These are beautiful problems, every coach wants that choice," Lovren added.

"Once he comes back alongside Isak, Wirtz, and Bradley, I believe they will have an amazing attack. Quality-wise, find me something better than what Liverpool have to offer."

#834. Which Premier League players are set for yellow card suspensions?

Yeremy Pino is the latest Premier League player to receive a yellow-card suspension

Crystal Palace's Yeremy Pino has become the latest Premier League player to receive a yellow card suspension after accumulating five bookings since the 2026-27 season began.

Hull City's Matt Crooks and Aston Villa's Matty Cash were the first players to receive a ban for collecting five yellow cards before gameweek 19.

Players receive a one-match suspension if they pick up five or more yellow cards prior to the conclusion of their team's 19th league match of the season.

There are now 17 players sitting on four bookings after 11 rounds of matches, meaning they must avoid another yellow card prior to the halfway point of the season to avoid a ban.

Bournemouth have the most players on the brink of a ban, with three players one yellow card away from suspension.

After that date, the threshold increases to 10 yellow cards. Any player reaching that number before the end of their club's 32nd league match of the season will receive a two-match suspension.

From that point, there are further thresholds at 15 and 20 yellow cards.

For players reaching 15 cautions, they incur a three-match suspension. Punishments for players reaching 20 yellow cards are determined by a regulatory commission.

Those cut-offs do not reset until the end of the Premier League season.

In the Championship, League One and League Two, there are similar thresholds.

However, with those three divisions having 46 rounds of league matches instead of 38, players have to avoid getting 10 yellow cards before the end of the 37th league match in order to not receive a two-match suspension.

In those divisions, the yellow cards are reset at the end of the league season and do not include matches in the play-offs.

The following players have received a one-match ban and will now receive a two-match ban if they reach ten bookings before game week 32:

Yeremy Pino - Crystal Palace (five yellow cards)

Matt Crooks - Hull City (five yellow cards)

If any of the following players receive another Premier League yellow card before the season's halfway point, they will be banned for one match:

Oliver Boscagli - Brighton & Hove Albion (four)

Chema Andres - Brighton & Hove Albion (four)

The following players will miss their club's next set of fixtures:

#833. Daily briefing: A guide to the Riemann hypothesis

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Hello Nature readers, would you like to get this Briefing in your inbox free every day? Sign up here.

An analysis of protein-coding DNA from more than 1.4 million people has identified hundreds of genes that influence a person’s height. Researchers identified 207 genes that were linked to a height difference of two centimetres, on average. They also identified 17 rare variants that prevent proteins from functioning, which have more striking effects. These include one variant associated with a 17-centimetre reduction in height and another with an 11-centimetre increase. The findings might help with the development of treatments that mitigate height changes caused by some medical conditions.

The number of reported global cases of the viral disease dengue in 2024 — a 34-fold increase from the 430,000 reported in 1990. (Nature | 5 min read)

Reference: Research Square preprint (not peer reviewed)

Major prizes in economics, including the Nobel, are being awarded to researchers affiliated to an increasingly concentrated set of US universities. Just eight institutions dominate these top economics awards: Harvard University; the University of Chicago; Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT); Stanford University; Princeton University; Yale University; the University of California, Berkeley; and Columbia University. On the other hand, prizes in the natural sciences, engineering and social sciences outside economics have become less concentrated to certain institutions over the past 70 years.

Reference: National Bureau of Economic Research working paper (not peer reviewed)

Four years after NASA’s DART Earth-defence test mission smashed into an asteroid and succeeded in altering the space rock’s movement, a follow-up mission has confirmed it on camera. The European Space Agency has released the first images from its Hera mission, which show detailed views of the asteroid’s new crater. “Hera is a sort of Inspector Columbo going back to the crash scene to investigate what is the outcome of this impact,” says Patrick Michel, principal investigator of the Hera mission.

This clip shows the final five-and-a-half minutes of images leading up to the DART spacecraft's intentional collision with asteroid Dimorphos. This replay movie is 10 times faster than reality, except for the last six images, which are shown at the same rate that the spacecraft returned them. (NASA/Johns Hopkins APL)

Last week, the field of mathematics was rocked by two competing announcements about solving the Riemann hypothesis. The hypothesis is considered one of the most important open problems in maths. But if, like me, you have some trouble getting to grips with the famed conjecture — and what solving it could actually mean — Nature has you covered.

The hypothesis concerns the distribution of primes, and it is important because these numbers are central to all of maths. Riemann arrived at his idea by studying prime numbers as waves and, at its heart, it boils down to a statistical test. One that will be familiar to any scientist who’s ever analysed data.

“If we can solve Riemann, what can’t we do?” says Xin Zhang, one of five mathematicians who spoke to Nature in the aftermath of the proofs’ publication. His reaction was one of excitement, despite Anthropic’s use of artificial-intelligence to develop its proof. But his enthusiasm was by no means universal. The format of Anthropic’s proof — 17 million lines of code with no natural-language version for humans to work with — is “the worst-case scenario”, says Álvaro Lozano-Robledo. And the shift towards AI-use in maths is “a choice to disempower ourselves”, says Tasmin Chu.

Bashyal observes a species of Coelogyne orchid, often found in tropical lowland forests and mountainous regions.Credit: CJ Karki for Nature

Wildlife conservationist Reshu Bashyal works with people in Nepal to protect the more than 500 species of orchids that grow there. Prized for their ornamental value and uses in traditional medicine, hundreds of these flowering plants are illegally harvested and sold each year. But blanket bans on the orchid trade are unlikely to be effective, Bashyal says, so more innovative strategies are required. One of these is an ‘anti-poaching taskforce’ that can document illegal activity, conduct patrols and spread information about the importance of conservation. (Nature | Leisurely scroll)

A biomedical innovation model that utilizes scientists in industry with government as their main funder could accelerate the development of therapeutics for common diseases that industry considers too risky to invest in, argue physician Victor Dzau, health-policy advisor Emily Shambaugh and healthcare entrepreneur Will Ellaissi. This government funding could operate at a national level, or several countries could form a consortium. Such a model “moves beyond the market-determined trajectory of research translation and ensures the public’s role in shaping the future of health,” the authors write.

Commensality — the act of sitting down to eat a meal with other people — has myriad health and social benefits, such as protecting against cognitive decline and helping us build trust with others. The presence of other people might also increase the enjoyment we get from eating. In an increasingly digital world, it might seem that opportunities to dine with others are dwindling. But research suggests that people are much more open and willing to accept invitations than we think, and simply putting ourselves out there might be an easy way to a dinner date.

Evolutionary biologist Pamela Yeh shares advice on how to navigate grief in the demanding environment of academia. (Nature | 8 min read)

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03894-3

Today I’m appreciating the world in monochrome through the entries into this year’s Black and White Photo Awards. The overall winner, photographer Shengwai Dai’s Bishwa Ijtema, depicts a man’s leap of faith between the tops of two train cars — “a scene filled with energy, tension, and detail”, the competition’s judges said.

Let me know which snap is your winner, along with any feedback on this newsletter, at briefing@nature.com.

Jacob Smith, associate editor, Nature Briefing

#832. Could lack of money sink TFFF rainforest fund before it even launches?

The TFFF rainforest fund aims to make forest conservation more profitable than deforestation. But a lack of money may prevent it from getting off the ground.

The world's tropical forests play a vital role in slowing global heating and preserving biodiversity, storing climate-damaging carbon dioxide and providing a home for an extremely large number of species — when they're intact.

More than 140 countries committed to halting global deforestation by the end of the decade at the 2021 UN climate change conference in Glasgow, but five years later logging continues.

In 2024, over 8 million hectares (19 million acres) of forest were lost. And since 1990, nearly 490 million hectares of forest have been wiped out.

More recently, the trend has shifted in the opposite direction. Deforestation in the Amazon region of Brazil decreased by 41% from August 2025 through 2026 to reach its lowest rate since records began.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

To ensure lasting protection, the Tropical Forest Forever Facility was launched in 2025 at the COP30 climate conference in Belem, Brazil.

Because rainforests are so important for the world, the idea behind the fund was to give money to the countries where they are located to help them preserve and protect these ecosystems.

So far, these countries have made more profit through deforestation — for example, by mining natural resources on rainforest land or farming the area.

Starting in 2027, the TFFF is expected to generate the funds needed for rainforest conservation, in part via contributions from various countries. By the end of this year, a total of $10 billion (€8.9 billion) in government capital is due to flow into the fund, mainly in the form of low-interest loans.

In addition, the TFFF is expected to issue bonds to private investors, such as banks and investment firms, to raise additional funds — initially totaling about $40 billion.

Going forward, the plan is for governments to contribute a total of $25 billion to the pot, and for private donors to contribute $100 billion. The fund will then invest this money in international financial markets with the aim of generating profits.

Private investors who purchase TFFF bonds can expect to earn about 5% interest per bond per year, said Felix Finkbeiner, the founder of the German environmental organization Plant-for-the-Planet, where he is responsible for forest conservation and advocacy.

"Private investors' capital is very well protected," Finkbeiner said, adding that any losses the TFFF might incur on the capital markets — for example, if the price of its bonds should fall — would be offset by government funds.

About 2.7% of the TFFF's profits would be set aside for countries with tropical forests.

Countries would receive $4 per year for every hectare of forest that they preserve instead of chopping down. At least 20% of these funds must be allocated to Indigenous peoples and local communities.

According to calculations by the TFFF Watch website, an independent platform launched by Plant-for-the-Planet to track investments, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, for example, would receive about $333 million for its 2024 forest stock under this system.

Finkbeiner said the subsidies would be paid only for intact ecosystems and not for timber plantations, with forest areas and their condition mapped and assessed using satellite imagery. Though it can sometimes be difficult to identify plantations accurately on satellite photos, he said, the technology has improved significantly over the last decade.

That means any NGO or external party with access to the satellite data can check the condition of the region, providing further oversight. If forest areas are cleared or damaged, money is deducted from the total.

Another safeguard: If countries don't use the TFFF funds for rainforest conservation, their payments could be frozen for the next few years.

The TFFF is supposed to invest, whenever possible, in government bonds issued by emerging and developing countries. Above all, the idea is not to invest in projects that harm the climate — such as those linked to oil, gas, or coal investments.

The TFFF concept has received plenty of support from environmental organizations, in part because it gives countries in the Global South significantly more sovereignty than traditional forms of development financing.

"For example, if the government of Ghana wants to protect its rainforest today, it usually asks the World Bank for financial assistance — and then the World Bank in [Washington] DC decides whether Ghana is allowed to do so," Finkbeiner said.

The TFFF fund is also designed to be immune to donor countries' backing out in the event of a change in government, for example. Once a contribution is made, the money remains in the fund for 40 years before being paid back.

Continuing protection is also an incentive for countries receiving money from the fund. "When a new government comes into power that wants to cut back a little on climate protection, they will realize: We'll get more money if we protect the rainforest," said Finkbeiner.

For the rainforest fund to actually get off the ground, a total of $10 billion in seed capital must be raised by the end of 2026. So far, the confirmed pledges from countries, NGOs and foundations total only $7.9 billion.

Eight countries have expressed a willingness to contribute so far, including Brazil, Indonesia, France, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands and Luxembourg.

Norway, with a pledge of $3 billion, is the largest would-be donor. However, the government in Oslo is willing to honor its commitment only if the agreed-upon total amount is in place by the end of the year.

"This deadline isn't set in stone, but otherwise the Norwegian government will have real trouble getting it through parliament," Finkbeiner said.

Germany's commitment must also still be approved by the parliament. The German government has pledged about €1 billion to the TFFF starting in 2027, to be paid out over 10 years.

Other countries are also considering investing in the TFFF, including Canada, China, South Korea and the United Arab Emirates.

Philanthropic organizations have pledged $88 million to the fund so far, including $73 million announced this week during the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey. Finkbeiner remains upbeat.

"Promises like that always come at the last minute," he said. "I'm very optimistic that we'll secure more commitments at the COP — and in the course of December — and that we'll then reach that $10 billion."

This article was originally written in German.

The former Arsenal striker believes it is time to cut ties with Renee Slegers with the Gunners lacking identity and leaders

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Arsenal would have already parted ways with Renee Slegers if this situation was happening with the men’s team, according to former Gunners striker Lianne Sanderson.

After 11 Women’s Super League games, Arsenal have just 15 points and sit sixth in the table, 12 points behind leaders Chelsea.

The Gunners’ latest setback came against West Ham, with a sixth home draw of the season, a result that left striker Alessia Russo in tears at the Emirates.

Sanderson was part of the Arsenal side that became European champions in 2007, with Slegers’ Arsenal side historically repeating the feat in May 2025.

The Dutch coach took charge on an interim basis following Jonas Eidevall’s departure, before being permanently appointed in January, becoming European champions four months later.

Following their triumph in Lisbon, they finished second in the league last campaign, four points off champions Manchester City.

“I've been a big advocate for Renee to stay in the job, but I feel like after the Lyon game [a 2-0 home defeat in the Champions League], I just felt this feeling in my stomach that it’s time [to part ways],” Sanderson told FourFourTwo.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“That was probably the most defeated I have felt. The players weren't fighting, they had just shown nothing, there was no identity.

“I love Renee, everyone loves Renee. But, I feel like if this was in the men's game, they'd have already cut ties.

“I actually feel gutted about the situation, because I have close ties and good relationships with everyone at Arsenal.

“The definition of insanity is doing the same thing over and over again and expecting different results.

“Six weeks ago, I believed she could turn it around. But the reality is, we are now in another international break and it’s the same story. To be drawing with teams like West Ham, Birmingham and Crystal Palace is not acceptable, that’s no disrespect to those teams.”

Arsenal made several additions to their squad including Lioness Georgia Stanway and World Cup and two-time Champions League winner Ona Batlle over the summer, but also lost a number of experienced players, including Katie McCabe and Beth Mead.

“There is something to be said about the types of personalities like Katie McCabe and Beth Mead,” Sanderson added. “Losing them is not the only reason Arsenal are struggling but Beth is a quiet type of leader and Katie is…you need a Katie in your team.

“Someone who is a nightmare to play against but will do anything it takes to win. You need those types of players. When I see Arsenal right now, I don’t see nastiness.

“My old captain, Jayne Ludlow, would do anything for us to win, putting your body on the line, and I'm not seeing that. Players have to take responsibility too.

“If Arsenal don't qualify for the Champions League, that will be a big, big, big blow.”

If Arsenal were to part ways with Slegers, Sanderson pointed to Nick Cushing as a potential option for a replacement manager, also saying she would love someone like Canada manager Casey Stoney to come in.

“Nick is the type of manager they need, someone with that personality,” she added. “I would welcome a personality like Nick Cushing, who knows what it takes to manage at the top and has good player management.”

With Arsenal all but out of the title race, Sanderson believes it will go down to the wire between Manchester City and Chelsea, tipping the Blues to win it.

While she can’t see third-placed London City Lionesses winning this year, she is impressed by their upward trajectory and believes the side who signed Alexia Putellas in the summer are ahead of where they are expected to be and could be contenders next season.

London City owner Michele Kang also owns NWSL side Washington Spirit, who lost the Championship to Kansas City Current, missing out in the final for a third year running, leading to the dismissal of head coach Adrián González.

“Michele Kang doesn't hang around,” Sanderson added. “Washington Spirit just lost at the weekend and the coach got fired the next day.

“The demand from her, it might be ruthless, but that's why she's successful. If Michele Kang was at Arsenal, this wouldn't be happening. That's the difference.”

Lianne Sanderson was speaking to FourFourTwo via polymarket promo code.

Ayisha Gulati is the women’s football writer at FourFourTwo. Having covered England’s triumphant Euro 2025 campaign in Switzerland and the 2026 World Cup in North America, she has reported on the ground at some of football’s biggest tournaments. She covers the WSL, UWCL and international football, and has interviewed leading names including Alexia Putellas, Leah Williamson and Bunny Shaw. She enjoys telling stories that capture the personalities, passion and excitement of the women’s game, on and off the pitch.

#830. When is the Nations League quarter-final draw?

England are a seeded side for the Nations League quarter-finals after topping their group

The draw for the final eight teams in the 2026-27 Nations League will be on Friday, 20 November at 11:00 GMT.

It will take place at Uefa's headquarters in Nyon, Switzerland and be broadcast on Uefa TV.

England are the only home nation to have made it to the quarter-final stage, however Northern Ireland's draw against Hungary saw them top Group B2 and secure promotion to League A in the 2028-29 tournament.

Scotland will remain in League B following their third-place finish in Group B1, and Wales face a League A/B relegation play-off in March after being consigned to last place in Group A4.

The Republic of Ireland finished second in Group B3 and so will take part in a League A/B promotion play-off in March.

The winners of groups A1-A4 are seeded for the draw, playing the runners-up of other groups in League A.

England have sealed their place in the last eight as Group A3 winners and could face:

They cannot face A3 runners-up Spain as teams must be drawn against sides from other groups.

The quarter-finals will be played over two legs during the international break between 25-30 March.

Seeded teams get to play the second leg of their quarter-final at home.

Nations that reach the semi-finals can bid those penultimate matches as well as the final.

The remaining dates for the Nations League are:

Semi-finals, third-place play-off and final: 9-13 June

#828. Why Man City can't wear their new kit in Premier League

Manchester City will only be wearing their orange kit for selected Champions League games

Manchester City sported a new orange fourth kit during their Champions League draw with Napoli on Tuesday - but will not be able to wear it in the Premier League.

Top-flight clubs in England can only wear a maximum of three strips in a league campaign, meaning Enzo Maresca's side cannot play in their new kit.

However, there is no limit in the Champions League, meaning City can wear their new strip for the rest of their European campaign.

City can also wear the kit in the FA Cup, provided that an application is made to the Football Association, as well as a reason for its requested use.

That is why Arsenal were allowed to play in a white fourth strip in the 2025-26 FA Cup as part of their campaign to combat youth knife crime in London.

Fans could scan the badge on City's 2025-26 fourth kit to receive items in a video game

City also released a green fourth kit in 2025-26 with a gaming-inspired theme.

The kit, debuted during their Champions League victory over Villarreal, featured an NFC chip in the club badge that fans could scan to unlock gaming rewards.

The club released another fourth kit in the 2024-25 season co-designed by Noel Gallagher in tribute to the 30th anniversary of Oasis' 1994 album 'Definitely Maybe'.

It was worn in the Champions League by the men's team against Inter Milan and Paris St-Germain, and the women's team against Paris FC and Barcelona.

A fifth kit was also used by the men's team during the 2025 Club World Cup

During the 2023-24 season, the women's side also sported a Chinese New Year-inspired shirt in a League Cup victory against rivals Manchester United.

While the Premier League is more restrictive over the number of kits that can be released - the rules are more relaxed in other European leagues.

Napoli wore 13 strips during the 2021-22 season; including a Halloween kit, four different Diego Maradona tributes and four Europa League-specific kits.

A former US international has had his say on the Argentine's move to Old Trafford

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Mauricio Pochettino has had a difficult start to his time at Manchester United, but some in the USA are questioning why he was allowed to join the club at all.

Pochettino followed up a 4-0 loss at Liverpool in his first game with the Red Devils with a Champions League draw at Sporting in midweek, having quit the US national team to move to Old Trafford.

The Argentine took charge of the USA for the final two times during the recent international break, guiding them to two wins over Haiti.

Pochettino was appointed as USA boss in 2024 after leaving Chelsea, then guided the Stars and Stripes to the last 16 of this summer’s World Cup.

His USA side started the tournament in scintillating fashion and won their group, although eventually succumbed to Belgium.

It had initially seemed like Pochettino would step down at the end of that tournament to pursue a return to club football, but instead he penned a new four-year deal in August, in theory taking him to the 2030 World Cup.

There was a catch, though – the contract contained a buyout clause, which Manchester United activated within only three months.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

The insertion of that clause has since been the subject of some criticism Stateside, and former US goalkeeper Brad Friedel admits he is disappointed with how the last few months have unfolded.

“I think he did very well as US boss,” Friedel told FFT, speaking in association with APWin. “He’s a good manager, he’s incredible.

“I don’t understand the whole thing of US Soccer signing him again and giving him an out on a four-year contract. It leaves a huge gaping hole for the US.

“I think the US got themselves into a situation and here we are, now having to hire a new head coach going into a four-year cycle.”

There will be more from Friedel in FourFourTwo soon.

Chris joined FourFourTwo in 2015 and has reported from 20 countries, in places as varied as Jerusalem and the Arctic Circle. He's interviewed Pele, Zlatan and Santa Claus (it's a long story), as well as covering the World Cup, Euro 2020 and the Clasico. He previously spent 10 years as a newspaper journalist, and completed the 92 in 2017.

#826. Why are there 2:05pm kick-offs in the Premier League on Sunday?

Everton's derby with Liverpool has been moved from Saturday to Sunday

The Premier League kick-off times look a little unusual this weekend, with no Saturday 12:30 GMT slot, and games starting at 12:00 and 14:05 on Sunday.

Everton will host local rivals Liverpool on Sunday at 12 noon because the match has been selected for live broadcast by TNT, who have a mid-day broadcast slot on that day. The game was originally scheduled for Saturday.

This has had a knock-on effect on the remaining fixtures.

On a typical Premier League weekend, the first matches will begin at 14:00 followed by a final 16:30 kick-off.

Pushing start times back five minutes to 14:05 reduces the risk of overlap with the unusual early 12:00 start time, while avoiding clashing with the 16:30 fixture.

Midweek European games have also affected the schedule, as the Premier League aims to prevent clubs from playing two matches within 60 hours of each other.

Crystal Palace, Sunderland, Bournemouth and Brighton are all set to play in the Europa and Conference Leagues on Thursday, ruling them out of Saturday Premier League fixtures.

#825. Germany's Nmecha won't repeat controversial goal celebration

Germany head coach Jürgen Klopp has said midfielder Felix Nmecha will not repeat a goal celebration that sparked controversy over the past week. Germany are set to face Serbia and the Netherlands in the Nations League.

With the controversy sparked by Felix Nmecha's celebrations after his goals in Dortmund's 2-1 win over Elfersberg last weekend, the subject was always going to be top of reporters' minds when Germany coach Jürgen Klopp faced reporters ahead of Friday's match against Serbia.

Nmecha celebrated the goals by mimicking taking a crown off his head and kneeling to place it on the ground.

This was understood by many to be a nod to a Ballers in God (BIG) campaign called "The King's Return."

BIG, a Christian group for footballers, has said it aims to "demonstrate love and respect towards everyone," but critics claim it discriminates against the queer and transexual people. The discourse generated by the celebration did not go unnoticed by the Germany boss.

​Klopp told reporters in Belgrade on Thursday evening, that the 26-year-old Nmecha had assured him that he meant no harm by his actions.

"Last weekend I ​saw Felix score two great goals and saw the celebration and then the gesture. I thought nothing of it at the time, but then it all kicked off," he said.

"As the controversy escalated, I started looking into the details of the subject and trying to form a clear picture of it.

"I confronted him with all the things you (reporters) might have confronted him with. He told me that it had nothing to do with that at all, and that he loves all people and does not discriminate against anyone."

He then said that Nmecha had agreed not to repeat the celebration.

In Friday's match, Klopp's goal will be to keep alive Germany's chances of reaching the Nations League quarterfinals with a win over Serbia. Germany are third in Group A2 with 5 points, trailing the Netherlands and Greece, who both have 8. Serbia, who Germany beat 2-0 in Munich last month, are still without a win.

"We feel well prepared," Klopp said, adding that his team were committed to earning "a final" for the last group last group game on Monday in Berlin against the Netherlands.

Klopp also expressed his disappointment that only a few thousand Serbian children would be admitted to the stadium due to a spectator ban. Originally, the game was to be played behind closed doors after Serbia was sanctioned for racist and discriminatory behavior by its fans. However, a clause in the UEFA rules allows a selected group of guests to attend. Now children under 15 accompanied by teachers or football coaches are expected to be at the match.

"We're expecting some 5,000 guests," a spokesman for the Serbian FA told the DPA news agency. The stadium's capacity is 55,000. The German FA has been allocated just 50 tickets for its fans.

#824. Who is close to a yellow card suspension in Champions League?

Arsenal forward Kai Havertz is among the players to have received two yellow cards in this season's Champions League

Players will receive a one-match ban should they receive four yellow cards before the semi-finals of the Champions League.

This rule runs from the start of the league phase until the end of the quarter-finals. After then, all yellow cards are wiped out and players cannot be suspended for multiple yellow cards.

Yellow cards that result in a red card during a match do not count towards a player's tally, as a separate suspension will be served.

The same rules apply for both the Europa League and the Conference League.

During the opening three rounds of the Champions League, 16 players received two yellow cards, meaning they are now two cautions away from a one-match ban.

There are now seven players on three yellow cards, putting them on the brink of a ban.

Players can also be suspended if they pick up six, eight or 10 yellow cards. This would also result in a one-match suspension every time a player hits an even number of yellow cards above four.

Red cards result in a one-match suspension, with Bayern Munich's Michael Olise missing his side's earlier clash with Arsenal after being sent off against Viking in the previous round of fixtures.

Uefa may increase the length of a red card ban for serious offences such as violent conduct.

*denotes two yellows that resulted in a red card

#820. Will Infantino feel he's already won as Fifa challengers confirmed?

Gianni Infantino has been president of Fifa since 2016 and is standing for re-election for a third time

Philippe Diallo and Kozo Tashima will take on incumbent Gianni Infantino in next year's Fifa presidential election.

World football's governing body has confirmed the three candidates for the election, which will take place at the Fifa Congress in Morocco on 18 March.

European football's governing body Uefa only identified its candidate Diallo fewer than 48 hours before Wednesday's deadline.

French Football Federation (FFF) president Diallo, 63, received the unanimous support of Uefa's executive committee.

Japan Football Association honorary president Tashima, 68, announced his intention to stand against Infantino, 56, earlier this month.

Tashima is a member of the Fifa Council and a former international footballer and coach.

Former Tottenham Hotspur defender Ramon Vega had also said he intended to stand but was not named as a candidate by Fifa on Thursday.

A late and surprise choice, Diallo said: "I have the experience, the convictions and the values which offer a credible alternative...I'm entering this campaign not just to provide a different voice, but to win."

But he is not the Frenchman some believe Uefa really wanted, as it tries to remove Infantino in the wake of his failed plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

Senior figures in European football had hoped to persuade Arsene Wenger - Fifa's head of global development - to stand against his own boss. Some felt that only he possessed the credibility to pose a serious threat to Infantino's plans for a fourth term.

But after the former Arsenal manager chose not to proceed, Uefa had no choice but to seek an alternative.

So just how credible a challenger is Diallo? Does Infantino's position appear unassailable? And how could he still be stopped from winning another term?

FA explored legal challenge to Infantino staying on

Wenger decides not to challenge Fifa chief Infantino

Japan's Tashima to stand against Infantino for Fifa presidency

An administrator who has worked in French football since 1992 and became FFF president in 2023, Diallo is not a household name. But he has already shown he is prepared to stand up to Infantino.

In September, Diallo claimed he had "seriously damaged the image and unity of football", and said "trust has been broken" over the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) sell-off plot.

According to Uefa vice-president Laura McAllister, Diallo is a "candidate who can instigate real, meaningful and lasting reform" within the governing body.

"We've always made it very clear that our objectives and motivations are driving culture change. That means wide-ranging, systemic reform of football governance rather than simply the replacement of an individual leader," McAllister told BBC Sport.

"I've known Philippe since we were both elected to Uefa's executive committee, and he's an intelligent, honest, sharp-minded football person with an impressive experience of governance in one of the world's football power-houses. Most importantly, he is a person of integrity... Philippe is a fantastic advocate for the change agenda that football needs, and I know his campaign will reflect that."

Infantino remains the favourite to win a majority of the 211 votes, and is thought to have the support of most of Africa (54 members), Asia (47) and South America (10).

However, Uefa hopes that Diallo - whose father was a Senegalese boxing champion who represented France in the 1960 Olympics - could enjoy support in parts of Africa and beyond. He claims he already has the backing of countries beyond Europe.

Laura McAllister is a former captain of the Wales women's football team

While most of Europe's national associations are expected to vote for Diallo, it is clear that he was not Uefa's first choice. "I wasn't initially a candidate, but the insistence of my European colleagues led me to accept the offer," he admitted.

Uefa only approached Diallo about standing in the past week, and senior officials at some European national associations have also told BBC Sport they are frustrated with the failure to find a higher-profile candidate sooner.

Speaking anonymously, one said they only learned about Diallo's potential candidacy on Sunday, and that while they were supportive of him, "it would have been helpful if we'd had someone much earlier" and "a lot of eggs were put in the Wenger basket."

They also made the point that Diallo was yet to publish a manifesto, and questioned whether he could really win.

Another expressed similar sentiments, saying Diallo was a good man, but "not seen as a heavyweight". They claimed that Uefa had "lost the momentum. The process hasn't been great. I really hope they've got a rabbit to pull out of the hat."

McAllister is optimistic: "I have no doubt whatsoever that we will collectively mount a powerful campaign with the objective of winning the election next March". she said.

"The really critical period comes next, once candidate nominations close and eligibility checks are complete."

Despite high-profile critics like Germany manager Jurgen Klopp - who this week said "the opinion is unanimous that a change would make sense" - Infantino does appear to be in a position of strength.

As recently as August it all seemed very different. Fifa's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour strongly criticised Infantino for the FFE scheme, while a senior adviser, Carlos Cordeiro, resigned. The heads of three confederations - Uefa, the Asian Football Confederation and Concacaf, which runs the game in North and Central America - then signed a letter accusing the Fifa president of breaking trust "through deception".

Amid an increasingly acrimonious civil war, Infantino seemed vulnerable. But the revolt against him then suffered a series of setbacks.

First, Fifa's executives backed Infantino at a crunch meeting in Rabat. Uefa then called off a threatened boycott of Fifa competitions, while potential rivals such as Concacaf chief Victor Montagliani decided not to stand. Aleksander Ceferin chose to stay for a fourth term as Uefa president rather than challenge Infantino directly.

Meanwhile, Infantino's position as the incumbent enabled him to embark on what has appeared to be a world tour, shoring up support. His chances of re-election received another major boost when he proposed to increase the amount of money handed out by Fifa for football development across the world by Â£2.6 billion.

Sheikh Salman, the head of the Asian Football Confederation, then performed a U-turn, endorsing Infantino, who soon after told the BBC he had the backing of the "vast, vast majority" of world football.

"I'm a professor of politics so I never assume that there's a runaway favourite to win any election", insists McAllister.

"There are plenty of twists and turns to come in this story between now and the election at Fifa's Congress next year.

"This is about structural change and a commitment to modernising the way in which football is governed so it benefits all who play and watch...that imperative will remain and we will hold the new president accountable for much-needed change."

"The current weaknesses of global football governance have been brutally exposed of late. This has helped coalesce and unite opposition to Gianni Infantino, but also to articulate the widely-held demands that things must change."

So with just four months until the presidential election, where could Infantino still run into difficulties?

Litigation is arguably the most obvious. As part of its wider plan to remove Infantino, Uefa has filed court documents in the US, which includes a potential criminal complaint against him in Switzerland for alleged financial mismanagement.

The legal action has not yet appeared to trouble him. But some senior figures in the European game remain hopeful it could still force Fifa to hand over evidence related to FFE that could prove damaging to Infantino's re-election prospects.

There is pressure from elsewhere in football. Fifa has already agreed to make "key documents" relating to the FFE plan available to members of its council. Infantino's critics believe this disclosure may reveal details that could increase the pressure on him before the election. Last month, the Norwegian Football Federation also submitted a three-part ethics complaint to Fifa regarding the awarding of a Peace Prize to US President Donald Trump, the Folarin Balogun case at the World Cup, and the FFE plot.

The Democrats' victory in the US midterm elections means scrutiny from beyond the sport too. Earlier this year, Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee launched an inquiry into Infantino's ties with Trump. In September, a spokeswoman said FIfa's co-operation with the investigation had been "woefully inadequate." But armed with extra powers, they could now force him to hand over relevant documents or give evidence.

Recent months have also seen a series of potentially damaging stories emerge in the media about various aspects of Infantino's leadership. So far they seem to have done little harm to his re-election chances, with Fifa claiming "it is evident that there is a concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine [him]". But the scrutiny is likely to continue.

With uncertainty over how much support Tashima will have, it seems Diallo is the challenger most likely to test the strength of Infantino's supporter base. There is a danger that the vote against Infantino is split.

It has not gone unnoticed at Fifa that as recently as March, Diallo was quoted congratulating Infantino when the Fifa president visited Paris, external to highlight a mini-pitch programme and the need for more football infrastructure globally.

A lot has changed since then, however. And now the Frenchman has been tasked with finding a way of unseating Infantino, and becoming just the 10th Fifa president in its history.

Politicians, private jets and power - the life of a Fifa president

Well that was a busy year! What started with non-league Macclesfield knocking FA Cup holders Crystal Palace out in the third round of the competition, ended with Harry Kane lifting the Ballon d’Or in London.

In between all of that, we saw Arsenal win their first Premier League title in 22 years, then miss out on the Champions League weeks later as they were beaten on penalties by defending champions PSG.

Manchester City won both domestic cups, then were found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules. Manchester United began the year with Ruben Amorim in the dugout, end it with Mauricio Pochettino, and for 303 days in the middle had Michael Carrick in charge.

Then there was the main event of the year. A 48-team World Cup promised chaos and duly delivered, culminating with Spain conquering Argentina to sew a second star onto La Roja’s crest. England, meanwhile, gave us a wild ride to bronze in a 10-goal thriller against France.

In this issue, we highlight some of the best stories from the past 12 months. #818. Ice hockey impasse as Russia threatens sanctions on Canada, Germany

Two weeks after the CAS ordered ice hockey's governing body to reintegrate Russia into international play, a solution remains elusive. Now Russia has threatened to take legal action against two tournament hosts.

"Should Canada and Germany refuse to allow the Russian team to participate, we will demand compensation, enforce the postponement of the competitions, and impose sanctions on the organizers," Russian Ice Hockey Federation President Vladislav Tretiak told the TASS news agency.

"There are rules: if a team does not take the ice, it receives a forfeit loss and sanctions are imposed," Tretiak said after a presidential sports council meeting in Moscow on Thursday.

"The IIHF as a way out — either allow us to participate or, if we cannot enter Canada, move the championship, don't hold it at all, or impose sanctions on Canada."

The threat comes after the Canadian government confirmed Wednesday that it would not allow Russian players to take part in the IIHF World Junior Championship starting on December 26 in Alberta.

"Canada's position is unequivocal: as long as Russia continues ⁠its war of aggression ​against Ukraine, there can be no return to business as usual," Adam van Koeverden, Canada's secretary of sport, said in a statement on Wednesday. "Canada will continue to stand with Ukraine."

Following the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruling in late October, in which it said the security concerns the IIHF cited for barring Russian teams from taking part in international tournaments was not sufficient, the world governing body pledged to work to comply with the decision.

On November 8, Norway said it had been bumped from the World Juniors tournament and had been informed by the IIHF that Russia would take its place. Several other national hockey associations said they had received a revised schedule for the tournament and stated they would not play against Russia. The IIHF has not confirmed the change.

Germany has been watching developments related to the World Juniors and host nation Canada closely, as it is set to host the IIHF World Championship in Gelsenkirchen, Mannheim and Düsseldorf starting on May 14.

With several nations saying they will not play Russia and major sponsors threatening to pull out, a German government spokesman described the prospect of hosting the tournament under these conditions as "effectively impossible."

However, Germany has ruled out taking the Canadian approach.

Ronald Rauhe, Germany's minister of state for sport, said Wednesday that refusing to grant visas was "not a solution for the [German] ice hockey federation [DEB], nor is it a solution for successfully hosting a world championship anywhere."

At the same time, though, he expressed support for the DEB in its wish to host the tournament as planned.

"We believe that we should channel all our energy and efforts into helping sport — and ice hockey in particular — find a solution, which would, of course, entail excluding Russia from the World Championship."

What makes things even more complicated for German officials are concerns that taking a hard-line on Russia could jeopardize Munich's chances as it bids to host the Summer Olympics in 2036, 2040 or 2044.

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) recently lifted its sanctions on Russian athletes and suspension of the Russian National Olympic Committee, opening the door for their return to competition despite the ongoing war in Ukraine.

The thinking goes that the IOC would expect national Olympic committees bidding to host an Olympic Games to follow its lead. The IOC is set to decide in the next few weeks whether Munich advances to the next stage of the process.

For now, though, the ball appears to be in the IIHF's court, after Ottawa confirmed its refusal to grant Russians visas to play in the World Juniors. How the dispute regarding that tournament gets resolved could go a long way to finding a solution for the men's tournament in Germany in May.

#817. One of football's most-hyped 16-year-olds - what next for JJ Gabriel?

JJ Gabriel featured for Manchester United's senior team in pre-season

It has been one of the biggest transfer sagas of the year - around a player who has never played competitive football.

Forward JJ Gabriel, who has recently turned 16, walked out on Manchester United in September and now has a verbal agreement to join Real Madrid.

Before even playing a senior game - barring friendlies - he has told Spanish newspaper Marca his "dream is to win the Ballon d'Or".

Gabriel's real name is Joseph Junior Andreou O'Cearuill - with Cypriot and Irish lineage - but he changed his name, reportedly for commercial purposes.

His father, London-born Joe O'Cearuill, played twice for the Republic of Ireland - but the highest level he played at club level was a loan spell with Brighton in League One and one minute in the Uefa Cup with St Patrick's Athletic. He has been actively involved in his son's career.

Gabriel was scheduled to become Manchester United's youngest ever player in the Carabao Cup against Brighton on 16 September, but had told the club he planned to leave by then.

How long will Gabriel have to wait for a first-team debut now? In the past 10 years Real have only handed two debuts to 17-year-olds and none to a 16-year-old.

When Real boss Jose Mourinho was asked about Gabriel on Friday, he said: "I don't have a feeling [about Gabriel]. I don't have a feeling with players who don't work with me."

In fact, Real have not even announced anything yet - despite Gabriel posting a 50-second video montage on social media saying goodbye to United this week.

Madrid-bound Gabriel posts farewell Man Utd message

Why schoolboys have become a huge part of football's transfer market

For a while now Madrid have been getting the best young talents early and turning them into Galacticos before they cost in excess of 100m euros.

Vinicius Junior and Rodrygo came that way, then Endrick - and Gabriel is seen as the next.

It fits the policy run by Jose Angel Sanchez, the director general, and Juni Calafat, head of scouting. It is a long-term bet on one of the most promising young players in the international game.

Barcelona looked at him too, and backed away because the commissions were too high. Madrid believe in the player so much that they were willing to pay whatever it took to get the deal done.

The expectations are very high and the aim is for him to reach the first team. They want him at Castilla - Real's reserve team - but the situation right now does not allow it.

Castilla and Real Madrid C cannot sign players until January, so for the time being he is expected to play for the Juvenil - the under-18s.

Madrid also learned from the Martin Odegaard period that training with the first team while playing for the B side is a bad idea. So the plan is a spell in the B side, and when he is ready, Gabriel jumps straight into the first team.

Where Madrid are less happy is with how things have unfolded. Madrid wanted to set the timing themselves and be discreet, because they do not want problems with Manchester United and do not want to upset anyone. At Real Madrid, nobody is bigger than the club.

The idea was to keep everything quiet until January and announce it then. But with Gabriel already training in Madrid, the secret was never going to last.

"Players are moving to him because his reputation is that he'll get you a move to a bigger club," one Premier League club source told BBC Sport.

Dubai-based Barat does not just consider himself a super-agent, but a "boutique" super-agent.

Born in Iran and raised in London, Barat says he fell into football almost by accident after many years in international business.

After initially working as an intermediary at low-level clubs, he founded Epic Sports in January 2020.

His major football experience before that? The football game Championship Manager.

"I was always trading players," he told ESPN this year. "I was obsessed with every single player around the world."

This was not just about living out a fantasy in the real world. Barat was drawn into the profession because of the vast sums agents can earn in commission.

What makes his agency "boutique"? Unlike the top operations which have a huge number of players on their books, Epic Sports aims to have just 22 - two for each position.

This, Barat argues, ensures there is never any conflict of interest in how he represents his players.

Barat offers bespoke management of a player's career and came to prominence in the summer of 2025 when 15 of his players moved on.

This included Dean Huijsen joining Real Madrid, Nicolas Jackson moving to Bayern Munich and Xavi Simons signing for Tottenham Hotspur. Noni Madueke left Chelsea for Arsenal, and the Gunners signed Piero Hincapie.

This led to Barat being named Golden Boy Best Agent for the second time in three years.

Yet he is largely the figurehead, with agents working on his behalf around Europe. For instance, Epic has three other agents registered with the English Football Association (FA).

Barat, who also brokered Moises Caicedo's move to Chelsea, says he uses social media, and in particular influencer Fabrizio Romano, to amplify stories and agree transfers on his terms.

"Ali Barat redefines the game again," read an Epic Sports press release to announce Jackson's loan move to Bayern. No other agency seems to promote itself in this way.

The largely AI-generated video which announced Gabriel had joined Epic Sports was right on brand.

Gabriel's deal is part of a new venture: Epic Future - and this presents an ethical problem.

"It is about targeting the biggest young players, especially where they're not necessarily on the longest contracts," a Premier League source said. "And move them overseas for cheap fees.

"The original club will get a few 100,000 euros if that, and everyone else will hoover up millions and millions and millions - including his family."

Transferring a player to Europe also opens the door to future sell-on fees for an agent, which is against FA regulations.

It is this new focus on younger players which has started to cause friction at some top clubs.

No club wants to lose players they have spent years developing for nothing, only for an agent to reap the rewards.

Manchester United had to work hard 18 months ago to convince JJ Gabriel and his family that Old Trafford was the right place to further his football education.

The big question is, did they overpromise in doing so?

Sources close to the player eventually felt they were let down and United did not deliver on what was expected.

Certainly around Gabriel's pre-season minutes and presence in the squad for the Champions League opener against Azerbaijan title winners Sabah FK, which it was felt would be a perfect opportunity for the youngster to make his debut.

By the time the Carabao Cup tie against Brighton came round, there was no faith Gabriel would be brought on. Given United lost 3-2, there is merit in that stance.

The secondary elements are where will Gabriel develop the most?

United's academy is one of the best in England at producing young players, but given his size, will the forward benefit more from being in a less physical environment?

There has been a lot of sniping around his decision to leave United, but his stats are impressive and he is clearly a player of huge potential. United would certainly have wished the situation had not unfolded the way it has.

#816. Orangutans face bleak future after Indonesia’s devastating wildfires

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

An orangutan affected by smoke inhalation receives emergency oxygen.Credit: REUTERS/Willy Kurniawan

For most of October, parts of Indonesia felt dystopian as wildfires turned the sky a reddish orange.

“It felt like you were on Mars,” says Erin Vogel, a primatologist at Rutgers University in New Brunswick, New Jersey.

Vogel was visiting the Tuanan Orangutan Research Station in Central Kalimantan, Indonesia, at the time. She and her colleagues have been conducting research on the critically endangered Bornean orangutan (Pongo pygmaeus) there for more than 20 years, but this trip she spent much of her time fighting fires. There were roughly 300,000 blazes in the region between July and October, and October’s level of toxic particulate matter in the air was roughly 400 times higher than what the World Health Organization deems safe.

Indonesia is experiencing one of its most severe fire and haze season of the past three decades, in part because a super El Niño has dried out vegetation and brought winds that fuelled the flames. More than 2.8 million hectares have burnt across Indonesia so far, and Kalimantan has been affected the worst. Fires devoured 60% of Bornean orangutans’ habitats in Kalimantan, including healthy forests such as those at the Tuanan research station and in Gunung Palung National Park.

Nature spoke to Vogel about the disaster and what it means for orangutans. At the time of the interview, fires were still smouldering in Tuanan peat swamp forests.

It was depressing and horrid. I’ve never seen so much forest loss in the 23 years I have worked in Indonesia. In the sky, there was this orange-brown haze that was very thick and it burnt your lungs if you weren’t wearing a respirator.

When I arrived in Tuanan, it really struck me how quiet the forests had become. You didn’t hear birds; you didn’t hear insects; you didn’t hear anything except trees burning and falling.

The forest staff, the orangutan staff, the phenology staff and the fire teams were all fighting fires. I felt in awe of those heroes voluntarily fighting these fires day and night. They’d all been doing so for more than two months straight. It takes real strength to be able to do that and not give up, and our team is just so positive and hopeful.

We saw some orangutans who seemed to be very lethargic and sick. We came across one of the males we’ve been studying for more than 15 years, and he was on the ground, breathing heavily. But when we saw him a couple of days later, he seemed to have recovered a little bit. He was near the research station, eating some vegetation on the ground, climbing trees and eating fruits. That reassures us that he is doing better.

We’re seeing orangutans being displaced from one area to others. That means we’re going to have competition between individuals over limited resources. That’s also going to change their behaviour. It’s going to be interesting to see what happens.
